definition: [in the CK janiY~N ] Whatever is gathered, or plucked;
sourceDefinition: [in the CK janiY~N ] Whatever is gathered, or plucked; as also ↓ janaApN : (K:) or whatever is gathered, or plucked, from trees, (S,) &c.; (so in a copy of the S;) as also ↓ janaApN : (S:) so that these two words are of the same class as Hiq~N and Hiq~apN : or the latter of them is a n. un.: (TA:) or the former signfies what is gathered from trees while fresh; (Msb;) as also ↓ janiY~N : (Msb:) or this last is an epithet applied to fruit, signifying just gathered or plucked; (S, K;) or gathered, or plucked, while fresh: (TA:) and ↓ majonFY , also, pl. majaAnK , signifies fruit gathered or plucked: (Har p. 369:) janFY also signifies fruit [ ready to be gathered or plucked ]; so in the Kur lv. 54: (Jel:) and is applied to fresh ripe dates: (Fr, K:) and grapes: (TA:) and truffles, and the like: (S:) and even cotton: (TA:) and herbage: (S:) and gold, (K,) which is collected from its mine: (TA:) and cowries, (K,) as though gathered from the sea: (TA:) and honey, (K,) when it is gathered: (TA:) pl. A^ajonaA='N (K) and A^ajonK , originally A^ajonuYN . (TA.) Hence the saying, h`*aA janaAY wa xiyaAruhu fiyhi A_i*okul~u jaAnK yaduhu A_ilaY fiyhi [ This is what I have gathered, and the best of it is in it; when every gatherer but myself has his hand to his mouth ]: or, accord. to one reading, wa hijaAnuhu fiyhi (which has the same meaning, TA in art. hjn ): a prov., ascribed by Ibn-El-Kelbee to 'Amr Ibn-' Adee El-Lakhmee, the son of the daughter of Jedheemeh: he says that Jedheemeh had ordered the people to gather for him truffles, and some of them ate the best that they found; but ' Amr brought to him the best that he found, and addressed to him these words: and 'Alee is related to have repeated them on an occasion of his entering the government-treasury; meaning that he had not defiled himself with anything of the tribute belonging to the Muslims, but had put it in its places. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yajiYo'u , inf. n. majiYo'N (S, Msb, K, &c., [the most common form, but] deviating from the general rule [respecting inf. ns. of this class], for the inf. n. of a verb of the form faEala having its aor. of the form yafoEilu is [accord. to the general rule, if commencing with an augmentative m ,] mafoEalN , though some words, beside majiYo'N , deviate from this rule by being of the measure mafoEilN , [for majiYo'N is originally majoyiy^N ,] as maEiy$N and makiylN and maSiyrN and masiyrN and maHiydN and mamiylN and maqiylN and maziydN and maEiylN and mabiyEN and maHiySN and maHiyDN , S, * TA) and jayoy^apN (S, K, of the form of an inf. n. of un., but used as an inf. n. in an absolute sense, like rajofapN and raHomapN , S, TA) and jaYo'N , (K,) He, or it, came; or was, or became, present; syn. A^ataY ; (S, K;) or HaDara , said of a man [&c.]; (Msb;) or HaSala [meaning it came, came to pass, happened, took place, betided, befell, or occurred; it resulted; it ensued; &c.]; and it is used in relation to ideal, as well as real, substantives; so that A_i*aA jaA='a naSoru A@ll~`hi [ When the assistance of God shall come (in the Kur ex. 1)] is [not a figurative but] a proper phrase. (Er-Rághib, TA.) Sb mentions, on the authority of certain of the Arabs, huwa yajiyka [for hw yajiyow^uka He comes, or will come, to thee ], with the hemzeh suppressed: (TA:) and he also mentions yajuwo'u as a dial. var. of yajiYo'u . (Id. in art. jwA^ , q. v.) [As shown above,] jaA='a is used intransitively and transitively. (Msb, MF.) say, jaA='a zayodN Zeyd came; or was, or became, present. (Msb.) And jiy^otu majiyoy^FA HasanFA [ I came with a good coming; or in a good manner ]. (S.) And jiy^otu zayodFA I came to Zeyd. (Msb.) And sometimes one says, jiy^otu A_ilayohi meaning I went [as well as I came ] to him, or it. (Msb.) And jiy^otu mina Albaladi [ I came from the town, or country ]: and mina Alqawomi , meaning mino Einodi Alqawomi [ from the presence of the people, or company of men ]. (Msb.) And jaA='a Algayovu The rain [ came, or] descended. (Msb.) And jaA='a A^amoru Als~uloTaAni The order, or command, of the Sultán came, or arrived. (Msb.) And jiy^otu bihi (S, Msb, K) and ↓ A^ajaA^otuhu , both signifying the same, (S, K,) [ I came with him, or it; ] I brought him, or it, with me. (Msb.) And AlHamodu ll~`hi Al~a*iY jaA='a bika [ Praise be to God who brought thee ]; and AlHamodu ll~`hi A_i*o jiy^ota [ Praise be to God because, or that, thou camest, or hast come ]; but not AlHamodu ll~`hi Al~a*iY jiy^ota : (S, TA:) and [in like manner] you say, AlHamodu ll~`hi A_i*o kaAna ka*aA ; but not AlHamodu ll~`hi Al~a*iY kaAna ka*aA unless you say bihi or minohu or Eanohu [after Al*Y ]. (ISk, TA.) [Hence, jaA='a biwaladK He begot a child, or children; like A^ataY biwaladK . And jaA='to bihi She brought him forth; gave birth to him; like A^atato bihi . And jaA='a bimaEonFY It (a word) conveyed, or imported, a meaning. ] ― -b2- [ jaA='a bi$aYo'K also signifies He brought to pass, did, executed, performed, or effected, a thing: and he said, gave utterance to, or uttered, a thing: like A^ataY bihi in both these senses.] And jaA='a ka*aA He did thus, or such a thing. (TA.) Hence, [in the Kur xix. 28,] laqado jiy^oti $ayoy^FA fariy~FA (TA) [ Verily, O Mary, thou hast done ] a thing hitherto unknown; a thing deemed strange. (Bd. [See another ex. voce A_imorN , likewise from the Kur.]) And jiy^otu $ayoy^FA HasanFA I did a good thing. (Msb.) And jaA='a biAlbadiyEi He produced a new saying, or new poetry, not after the similitude of anything preceding. (TA in art. bdE .) And jaA='a jaroyFA baEoda jaroYK (K in art. tA^m ) or [more commonly] jA' bijaroYK baEoda jaroYK (M in that art.) [ He (a horse) performed, or fetched, run after run ]. ― -b3- jaA=' is also syn. with SaAra , like A^ataY ; as in the saying, jaA='a AlbinaA='u muHokamFA The building became, or came to be, firm, strong, or compact. (Kull p. 11.) [And hence the phrase,] maA jaA='ato HaAjataka , (M, K,) thus in all the copies of the K, with the noun in the accus. case; i. e. What became, or has become, thy want? syn. maA SaArato ; (M, K;) or What was thy want? syn. maA kaAnato : (Er-Radee, TA:) mA being here an interrogative, and the [implied] pronoun [in the verb] being made fem. because its predicate is fem.: but some say HaAjatuka , in the nom. case, [as it is in the CK, meaning What did, or has, thy want become? ] regarding HAjtk as the subject of jA't , and mA as the predicate of this verb. (TA.) ― -b4- See also 3.

sourceDefinition: [inf. n. of jaAyaA^a ] signifies The act of facing, or fronting; being opposite, or over against: (IAar, K:) and the act of coinciding; as also jiyaA='N . (AZ, K.) You say of a man, jaAyaA^aniY mino qurobK He faced me, fronted me, was opposite to me, or was over against me, at a short distance. (TA.) And mar~a biY mujaAyaA^apF He passed by me being in front, or opposite. (TA.) And jaAyaA^otu fulaAnFA I coincided with such a one in his coming. (TA.) And lawo jaAwazota h`*aA AlmakaAna lajaAyaA^ota Algayova Hadst thou passed beyond this place, thou hadst met with rain, or coincided with rain in its coming. (TA.) ― -b2- ↓ jaAA=niY fajiy^otuhu , [so in copies of the S, and in copies of the K, as from the S, but in the TA, as from the S, jaA='aA^aniY , and said to be with two hemzehs, though this is evidently wrong,] aor. A^ajiyow^uhu , the former verb of the measure faAEalaniY , (S,) is [said to be] a mistake for jaAyaA^aniY fjy^th , since the former verb has an infirm letter [ Y ] for its medial radical and ' for its final, not the reverse, (Sgh, K,) [therefore] what J says is not allowable unless it be an instance of transposition; (IB, TA;) but what is given by F [and Sgh as the correct form] is that which is accord. to rule, and what J says is that which has been heard from the Arabs, as ISd has pointed out; (TA;) [and rule is not to be regarded when it is contr. to classical usage;] the meaning is, He vied with me, or strove to surpass me, in frequency of coming, and I surpassed him therein. (S, K.)

definition: A dam constructed of wood or stones, in a channel of water, to confine the water, (S, K,) that people may drink from it and water their beasts;
sourceDefinition: A dam constructed of wood or stones, in a channel of water, to confine the water, (S, K,) that people may drink from it and water their beasts; (S, TA;) as also ↓ HabosN : (El-'Ámiree, K:) pl. A^aHobaAsN (S, TA) and HibaAsN : (Meyd, in Golius:) or a dam by which the water-course of a valley is obstructed, in any place where it is confined: (TA:) or stones put in the mouth of a river or rivulet or the like, preventing the overflowing of the water: (IAar, TA:) or a maSonaEap for water; [i. e. a thing like a HawoD , or water-ing-trough for beasts &c., in which the rain-water is collected; ] (S;) as also ↓ HaAbisN : (TA:) or a thing like a maSonaEap for water: (AA, K:) pl. A^aHobaAsN : (AA, TA:) and ↓ HubaAsapN and ↓ HibaAsapN signify the same as HibosN : or, accord. to Lth, the HbAsAt in a piece of land are what surround a [ portion of ground such as is called ] daborapN , which is the same as a ma$aArap , in which the water is confined until they are full, when it is made to flow to other parts: (TA:) or a Hibos is what is surrounded by dams [or by ridges of earth ] which confine, or retain, the water [ for irrigation ]; as also ma$aArapN and daborapN . (R, TA in art. $wr .) ― -b2- Also Water collected, and having no supply to increase it: (Ibn-'Abbád, K:) thus called by the name of that by which it is confined. (TA.)

definition: , (S, Mgh,) or Hada biAlA_ibili , (Msb,) or both, (K) and HudaA='N (S, K) and HidaA='N , (K,) He drove the camels;
sourceDefinition: , (S, Mgh,) or Hada biAlA_ibili , (Msb,) or both, (K) and HudaA='N (S, K) and HidaA='N , (K,) He drove the camels; (S, Mgh, K;) and chid them: (K:) [and ↓ AHtdAhA app. has the former signification:] and he sang to them: (S:) or he urged, or excited, the camels by singing to them, which is termed ↓ HudaA='N : (Msb:) or HadaA lahaA signifies he sang to them. (Mgh.) The Arabs in driving their camels used commonly to sing verses of the kind termed rajaz . (TA in art. rjz .) [It is said that] ↓ HudaA='N originated from the fact of a DesertArab's beating his young man, or boy, and biting his fingers; whereupon he went along saying daYo daYo , meaning yaA yadaY~a [“ O my two hands! ”]; and the camels went on at his cry; therefore his master bade him keep to it: (K in art. dY :) so says IAar. (TA in that art. [Other (similar) accounts of its origin are mentioned by MF in remarking on this passage of the K.]) HadaA signifies also He raised his voice with [ the singing termed ] AlHudaA=' . (Har p. 576.) [And He breathed short ( anhelavit ), and sent forth a voice or sound. (Golius, from a gloss in the KL.)] ― -b2- You say also of the north wind, taHoduw Als~aHaAba , i. e. (assumed tropical:) It drives along the clouds. (S.) ― -b3- And HadaAhu EalaY ka*aA (assumed tropical:) He urged him, incited him, or put him in motion or action, to do such a thing. (Msb, TA.) ― -b4- And HadaAhu (assumed tropical:) It followed it; namely, the night the day; (K;) as also ↓ AHtdAhu : (AHn, K:) and so the [wild] he-ass his she-asses; and anything any other thing. (TA.) Hence the saying, laA A^afoEaluhu maA HadaA All~ayolu Aln~ahaAra (assumed tropical:) I will not do it as long as the night follows the day ]. (TA.) ― -b5- See also 5.

definition: , in its primary sense, is form AlHudaA='u , and signifies He (a driver of camels) vied, competed, or contended for superiority, with him, or emulated him, (namely, another driver,) in driving camels, or urging them by singing to them;
sourceDefinition: , in its primary sense, is form AlHudaA='u , and signifies He (a driver of camels) vied, competed, or contended for superiority, with him, or emulated him, (namely, another driver,) in driving camels, or urging them by singing to them; each of them desiring to elicit the ability of the other in doing so. (Z, TA.) ― -b2- [And hence,] He vied, or competed, and contended for superiority, with him, (S, K, * mentioned in the K in art. HdY ,) in an action or a work [ of any kind ]. (S.) You say, taHad~ayotu Aln~aAsa AlquroA=na I sought to elicit the ability of the people in order that it might be known which of us was most skilled in reading or reciting [ the Kur-án ]: it means like as does the saying of a person contending with others for the superior glory of his people, “ Bring ye a people like my people, or like one of them. ” (Msb.) It is said of Mohammad, in a trad., taHad~aY AlEaraba biAlquroA=ni [ He vied, or contended, with the Arabs by means of the Kur-án ]. (TA.) And one says, taHad~aY SaAHibahu AlqiraA='apa , and AlS~iraAEa , [ He vied, or contended, with his companion in reading, or reciting, and in wrestling, ] in order that it might be seen which of them was the superior reader or reciter, and the superior wrestler. (TA.) ― -b3- Also He aimed at it; made it his object; sought, endeavoured after, pursued, or endeavoured to reach or attain or obtain, it; intended or purposed it; (AA, and K * and TA in art. HdY ;) as also ↓ HadaAhu , (AA, TA,) and ↓ AHdAhu . (Sgh, and K ib.) Hence the saying of Mujáhid, kunotu A^ataHad~aY AlquroA=na faA^aqoraA^u [ I used to aim at reading, or reciting, the Kur-án, and so to read, or recite ]. (AA, TA.)

definition: He was debarred from the means of subsistence;
sourceDefinition: He was debarred from the means of subsistence; because he of whom this is said is aloof ( biHarofK ) from the means of subsistence. (Mgh.) And Huwrifa kasobu fulaAnK Such a one was made to experience difficulty (S, TA) in his buying and selling, and was straitened (TA) in his means of subsistence; as though his means of subsistence were turned away from him: (S, TA:) or he had his gain, or earnings, turned away from him. (Msb.) It is said in a trad. of Ibn-Mes'ood, mawotu Almuw^omini Earaqu Aljabiyni taboqaY Ealayohi Albaqiy~apimina Al*~unuwbi fayuHaArifu bihaA Einoda Almawoti , i. e. [ The death of the believer is accompanied with sweating of the side of the forehead: some sins remain chargeable against him, and ] he is made to experience difficulty by them [ in dying ], in order that his sins may be diminished. (S.) -A2- muHaArafapN has also a meaning like mufaAxarapN : Sá'ideh says, faqado EalimuwA fiY Algazowi kayofa nuHaArifu [ And they certainly know, in warfare, how we vie for superiority in glory: or] accord. to Skr, it means how we deal with them; as when one says to a man, What is thy Hirofap (i. e. thine occupation ) and thy lineage? (TA:) [or the meaning may be how we requite; for] -A3- HArfhu bisuwo'K signifies He requited him for evil (K, TA) that he had done. (TA.) And it is said in a trad., A_in~a AlEabodi layuHaArafu Eano Eamalihi Alxayora A^awo Al$~ar~a , i. e. [ Verily the servant ] shall be requited [ for his deed; the good I mean, or the evil ]. (IAar, TA.) And ↓ AHrf also signifies He requited for good or evil. (IAar, K.) -A4- muHaArafapN signifies also The measuring a wound with the miHoraAf , i. e. the probe. (K, * TA.)

sourceDefinition: The extremity, verge, border, margin, brink, brow, side, or edge, (S, Mgh, * K, TA,) of anything; (S, K;) as, for instance, the side of a river or rivulet, and of a ship or boat, (TA,) and of the notch of an arrow; (Msb;) and the edge of a sword: (L, TA:) pl. [of mult. HuruwfN , and of pauc.] A^aHorufN . (TA.) Hence, (S,) [ A point, a ridge, a brow, and a ledge, of a mountain:] the pointed, sharp, or edged, summit of a mountain: (S, Msb, K:) a projecting portion in the side of a mountain, in form like a small duk~aAn [i. e. bench ] or the like: and a portion in the summit of a mountain, having a thin edge, or ridge, rising above the upper part of the back: (Sh, TA:) pl. (of the word thus used in relation to a mountain, TA) HirafN ; (Fr, S, Msb, K;) accord. to Fr, (Msb,) the only instance of the kind except TilalN as pl. of Tal~N . (Msb, K.) [Hence, also,] A nib, of a writing-reed, obliquely cut: so in the phrase qalamN laA Harofa lahu , in the S and K in art. jzm , a writingreed not having a nib obliquely cut. (TA in that art. [See 2 in the present art.]) And HarofaA Alr~aA^osi The two lateral halves of the head. (TA.) [Hence, also, the phrase] fulaAnN EalaY HarofK mino A^amorihi [and biHarofK minohu (see 3, first sentence,)] Such a one is [ standing ] aloof with respect to his affair, ( EalaY naAHiyapK minohu , ISd, TA,) [ in suspense, ] waiting, and looking to the result, if he see, in regarding it from one side, what he likes; (TA;) turning from it if he see what does not please him. (ISd, TA.) The saying, in the Kur xxii. 11, wamina A@ln~aAsi mano yaEobudu A@ll~`ha EalaY HarofK means And of men is he who serves God standing aloof with respect to religion, in a fluctuating state, like him who is in the outskirts of the army, who, if sure of victory and spoil, stands firm, and otherwise flees: (Ksh, Bd: *) or the meaning is, who serves God in doubt, or suspense, (Zj, K, Jel,) being unsteady like him who alights and abides upon the Harof [i. e. point, or ridge, or brow, ] of a mountain: (Jel:) or in a state of disquietude respecting his case; (Ibn- 'Arafeh, K;) i. e. not entering into the religion firmly, or steadily: (K:) or who serves God in one mode of circumstances; i. e. when in ample circumstances, and not when straitened in circumstances; (Az, S, K;) as though good fortune and plenty were one side, and an evil state were another side: (Az, TA:) [hence,] HarofN sometimes signifies a mode, or manner, and a way. (Msb.) ― -b2- A letter of the alphabet: pl. HuruwfN : (S, Msb, K:) the letters being thus called because they are the extremities of the word [and of the syllable]. (Kull.) The saying of the lawyers, tuboTalu AlS~alaApa biHarofK mufohimK [ Prayer is made null by a significant letter ] means only by an imperative of a verb of which the first and last radical letters are infirm; such as fi from wafaY , and qi from waqaY , and the like. (Msb.) ― -b3- As a grammatical term, (assumed tropical:) [ A particle; i. e.] what is used to express a meaning, and is not a noun nor a verb: every other definition of it is bad: (K:) pl. HuruwfN . (Msb, &c.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) A word [absolutely: often used in this sense in lexicons &c.]. (Kull.) ― -b5- A dialect, an idiom, or a mode of expression, peculiar to certain of the Arabs: pl. [of pauc.] A^aHorufN : so in the saying (of Mohammad, TA) nazala AlquroA=nu EalaY saboEapi A^aHorufK The Kur-án has been revealed according to seven dialects, of the dialects of the Arabs: (A'Obeyd, Az, IAth, K:) or this means, according to seven modes, or manners, (Mgh, Msb,) of reading: whence fulaAnN yaqoraA^u biHarofi A@boni masoEuwdK Such a one reads in the manner of reading of Ibn-Mes'ood. (Mgh.) -A2- Applied to a she-camel, (assumed tropical:) Lean, or light of flesh; or lean, and lank in the belly; (S, K;) and firm, strong, or hardy; likened to the Harof of a mountain; (S;) or to the Hrf of a sword, (Z, O, TA,) in respect of her leanness, or thinness, and her sharpness and effectiveness in pace; (Z, TA;) or to a letter of the alphabet, meaning the letter A , in respect of her leanness: (TA:) or excellent, or high-bred, or strong and light and swift, sharp and effective in pace, rendered lean by journeyings; likened to the Hrf of a sword: (L:) or emaciated: (S, K:) so As used to say: (S:) but this is inconsistent with Dhu-r-Rummeh's description of a she-camel by the epithets jumaAliy~apN HarofN sinaAdN : (TA:) [see HariyvapN :] or [in the CK “ and ”] great; big; of great size; (K, TA;) likened to the Hrf of a mountain: (TA:) it is applied only to a she-camel: one may not say jamalN HarofN . (IAar, TA.)

definition: and ↓ HirofapN (S, K) and ↓ HurofapN (Mgh, K) and ↓ HiraAfN (TA) Ill-fatedness;
sourceDefinition: and ↓ HirofapN (S, K) and ↓ HurofapN (Mgh, K) and ↓ HiraAfN (TA) Ill-fatedness; privation of prosperity; or the being denied prosperity; syn. HiromaAnN [as inf. n. of Hurima ]: (K, TA:) lack of good fortune, so that one has no increase of his cattle or other property: (S:) debarment from the means of subsistence. (Mgh.) Hence the saying of 'Omar, A^aHadihimo A^a$ad~u EalaY~a mino Eayolatihi ↓ liHirofapu , (S, K,) or, accord. to one reading, ↓ laHurofapu , (TA,) [ Verily the ill-fatedness of any one of them is more distressing to me than his poverty: ] i. e., the supplying the wants of the poor man is easier to me than the making the bad to thrive: or the meaning is, the want of the means of gaining subsistence by any one of them, and grief on that account, is more distressing to me than his poverty: so in the Nh. (TA.) -A2- AlHurofu A certain grain, resembling Alxarodal [or mustard ]; (Az, Msb, TA;) called by the vulgar, (AHn, TA,) or in the dial. of El- 'Irák, (TA in art. r$d ,) Hab~u Alr~a$aAdi , (AHn, S, K,) or Alr~a$aAdu : (Msb:) n. un. with p , (TA,) applied to a single grain thereof. (Msb.) [See art. r$d .] Hence Hir~iyfN [q. v.]. (S, Msb.)

sourceDefinition: quasi-pass. of HaS~ahu in the first of the senses explained above; It (hair) became shaven off; as also ↓ HaS~a , [sec. pers., app., HaSiSota , and aor. yaHaS~u ,] inf. n. HaSiySN [and app. HaSaSN , q. v. infrà]; or, as some say, HS [perhaps a mistake for HaSaSN or HaSiySN ] signifies the hair's going from the head by shaving or by disease: (TA:) and the former verb, it (the hair) went from the head; (K, TA;) became removed, or stripped off; (TA;) fell off, and became scattered, by degrees; (S, TA;) as also ↓ HaS~a : (TA:) the former is also said of the plumage of a bird; (A;) and of the foliage of trees; in the last of the senses mentioned above: (TA:) and [in like manner] ↓ taHaSoHaSa it (fur, and the nap of cloth,) became removed, or stripped off. (IAar.) You say also, AnHS~t All~iHoyapu The beard became short, its hair breaking off in pieces. (TA.) And AnHS~ Al*~anabu The tail became cut off. (K.) It is said in a prov., A^afolata wa A@noHaS~a Al*~anabu [ He escaped, but the tail became cut off ]: applied to him who has been at the point of destruction, and then escaped: (K:) or alluding to the coward's escape from destruction after being at the point thereof: related to have been said by Mo'áwiyeh, on the occasion of the safe return of an ambassador whom he had sent to the King of the Greeks, appointing for him a threefold bloodwit [if he should be slain] on the condition of his proclaiming the call to prayer on entering his court; which he did; whereupon the King's generals, who were with him, sprang forward to slay him; but he forbade them, and sent him back furnished with requisites for his journey. (A 'Obeyd.) [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov., ii. 201.] You also say, AnHS~ raA^osuhu [ His head shed, or lost, its hair: or part thereof ]: (A:) and AlHimaAru ↓ taHaSoHaSa , and AlbaEiyru , the ass's, and the camel's, hair fell off. (TA.)

definition: [ Having the hair shaven off, or rubbed off, or fallen off, either wholly or partly ], applied to the head;
sourceDefinition: [ Having the hair shaven off, or rubbed off, or fallen off, either wholly or partly ], applied to the head; pl. HuS~N : (A:) a man having little hair upon the head: (S, K:) or a man having no hair; (Mgh;) a man whose hair has all gone; fem. HaS~aA='u , applied to a woman: (Et-Tirmidhee:) also, [a man] having no hair upon his breast: and a man suffering from a protracted disease, whose hair does not grow long: (TA:) and a horse having little hair in the fetlock, and in the tail; which is a fault; (TA;) as also ↓ HaSiySN ; (K, * TA;) on the authority of IDrd: (TA:) and the fem., a she-camel having no fur upon her: and the masc., a tail having no hair upon it: and ↓ maHoSuwSN applied to the back of the neck, of which the hair has been shaven off. (TA.) You say also rajulN A^aHaS~u All~iHoyapi A man whose beard has become short, its hair having broken off in pieces: and liHoyapN HaS~aA='u a beard that has become short in like manner. (TA.) And TaAy^irN A^aHaS~u AljanaAHi (S, A, K) A bird having little plumage in the wing: (K:) or whose plumage of the wing has gradually fallen off and become scattered: (S, * TA:) pl. as above. (S.) ― -b2- (tropical:) A sword having in it, or upon it, no A^avor [or diversified wavy marks, streaks, or grain ]. (K, TA.) ― -b3- Applied to a man, (A,) (tropical:) Unlucky; (AZ, A, K;) unpropitious; in whom is no good : (AZ, A:) and the fem., applied to a woman, also signifies (tropical:) unlucky; (K, TA;) in whom is no good. (TA.) And hence, (A,) or because they keep pace together in their prices ( yumaA$iyaAni A^avomaAnahumaA ) until they grow old and weak, when their prices become diminished and they die, (S,) AlA^aHaS~aAni signifies (tropical:) The slave and the ass. (S, A, K.) ― -b4- (tropical:) [A man] who cuts, or severs, the tie of relationship. (TA.) ― -b5- raHimN HaS~aA='u : see HaAS~apN . ― -b6- sanapN HaS~aA='u (S, A, K) (tropical:) A sterile year, in which is no good: (S, K:) or a year of drought, in which is little herbage: or a year in which is no herbage. (TA.) ― -b7- yawomN A^aHaS~u (tropical:) A day intensely cold. (TA.) It was said to a man of the Arabs, “ Which of the days is the most cold? ” and he answered, AlA^aHaS~u AlA^azab~u ; (TA;) the former meaning, (tropical:) The day whose sun rises (K TA) the horizon being red, (TA,) and its sky ( samaAw^uhu ), accord. to the copies of the K, but correctly its north wind ( $amaAluhu ), (TA,) being clear, (K, TA,) and such that a touch is not felt by reason of the cold; and it is that in which there are no clouds, and of which the cold does not abate: and the latter meaning, the day in which blows the wind called Aln~akobaA=' driving along clouds in which is no water, wherein no sun rises, and in which is no rain. (TA.) Z says, (TA,) it was said to one of them, “ Which of the days is the coldest? ” and he answered, AlA^aHaS~u Alwarodu wa AlA^azab~u Alhil~awofu , i. e., The clear, [ in which the horizon is red, ] and the cloudy, in which blows the wind called Aln~akobaA=' . (A, TA.) ― -b8- riyHN HaS~aA='u (tropical:) A wind that is clear, without dust. (K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. (S, Msb, K, &c.) and , (IDrd, Msb, K,) [the latter irregular,] inf. n. Haq~apN (K, TA) and Haq~N (IDrd, TA) and HuquwqN , (TA,) i. q. SaAra Haq~FA [i. e., accord. to the primary meaning of Haq~N , as explained below, on the authority of Er-Rághib, It was, or became, suitable to the requirements of wisdom, justice, right or rightness, truth, or reality or fact; or to the exigencies of the case ]: (TA:) it was, or became, just, proper, right, correct, or true; authentic, genuine, sound, valid, substantial, or real; established, or confirmed, as a truth or fact: and necessitated, necessary, requisite, or unavoidable; binding, obligatory, incumbent, or due: syn. wajaba ; (T, S, Msb, K, &c.;) and vabata : (Msb, TA:) it was, or became, a manifest and an indubitable fact or event; as explained by IDrd in the Jm; (TA;) it happened, betided, or befell, surely, without doubt or uncertainty. (K.) It is said in the Kur xxxvi. 6, laqado Haq~a Alqawolu EalaY A^akovarihimo , i. e. The saying, “ I will assuredly fill Hell with genii and men together, ” [Kur xi. 120 and xxxii. 13,] (Bd,) or the sentence of punishment, (Jel,) hath become necessitated [ as suitable to the requirements of justice, or as being just or right, ] to take effect upon the greater number of them; syn. wajaba , (Jel, TA,) and vabata . (TA.) And this, namely, vabata , is the meaning of the verb in the phrase, Haq~a Ealayoka AlqaDaA='u [ The sentence was, or, emphatically, is, necessitated as suitable to the requirements of justice to take effect upon thee; or it was, or is, necessary, just, or right, that the sentence should take effect upon thee ]. (TA.) [In like manner,] one says, yaHiq~u Ealayoka A^ano tafoEala ka*aA It is necessary for thee [ as suitable to the requirements of wisdom or justice or the like ], or incumbent on thee, or just or proper or right for thee, that thou shouldst do such a thing. (TA.) [Thus one says,] AlHaqiyqapu maA yaHiq~u Ealayoka A^ano taHomiyahu [ The Hqyqp is that which it is necessary for thee &c., or that which it behooveth thee, that thou shouldst defend it, or protect it ]. (S, * K.) Accord. to Sh, the Arabs said, Haq~a EalaY~a A^ano A^afoEala *`lika and Huq~a : but accord. to Fr, when you say Haq~a , you say Ealayoka ; and when you say Huq~a , you say laka . (TA.) [Accordingly] one says, Huq~a laka A^ano tafoEala *aA and Huqiqota A^ano tafoEalahu : both mean the same: (Ks, S, K:) [i. e., each has one, or the other, or both, of the meanings next following:] or the former means It was, or, emphatically, is, rendered H~q~ [or suitable to the requirements of wisdom or justice &c.] for thee, or necessary for thee, or incumbent on thee, or just or proper or right for thee, [or it behooved or behooves thee, ] that thou shouldst do, or to do, this, or that: and [the latter, or] Huqiqota biA^ano tafoEala , Thou wast, or, emphatically, art, rendered Haqiyq [or adapted, disposed, apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, proper, competent, or worthy, ] that thou shouldst do, or to do, this, or that ]: (A, TA:) and in like manner, Huq~ato signifies in the Kur lxxxiv. 2 and 5: (Bd, Jel: *) or Huqiqota biA^ano tafoEala may mean thou wast, or art, known by the testimony of thy circumstances to be Haqiyq &c. (A, TA.) And maA kaAna yaHuq~uka A^ano tafoEalahu [virtually] means the same as maA Huq~a laka [best rendered in this case It did not behoove thee to do it ]. (TA.) One says also, Haq~a A^ano tafoEala [ It was, or, emphatically, is, necessary &c. that thou shouldst do or to do such a thing]: but they did not say, Haqaqota A^ano tafoEala . (Fr, TA.) ― -b2- But Haq~a EalaY~a A^ano tafoEala ka*aA means Thy doing so distressed, or hath distressed, or afflicted, me; or, emphatically, distresses, or afflicts, me; like Eaz~a EalaY~a . (S and K and TA in art. Ez .) And in like manner, Haq~a A^an~aka *aAhibN [or Haq~a maA A^an~aka *aAhibN ] means Eaz~a maA A^an~aka *aAhibN [ It is distressing to me that thou art going away ]. (TA in art. Ez .) And laHaq~a maA is used in the same manner as laEaz~a maA , q. v. (A and TA in art. Ez .) You say also, Haq~ati AlHaAjapu Want befell, or betided, or happened, and was severe, or distressing: (Msb, TA:) [which is said to be] from the phrase, Haq~ati AlqiyaAmapu , aor. , The resurrection included, or shall include, within its sphere [ all ] the created beings. (Msb.) -A2- Haq~ato , aor. , (K,) inf. n. Hiq~apN (S, * Msb, K,) and Hiq~N , (K,) or, accord. to ISd, it should rather be HaqaAqapN and HuquwqapN , because Hiq~apN is used as an epithet, [as will be seen below,] and the inf. n. in a case like this, by rule, should differ from the epithet, (TA,) She (a camel) became a Hiq~ , or Hiq~ap ; i. e., entered the fourth year: (K:) and ↓ A^aHaq~a , inf. n. A_iHoqaAqN , he (a camel) became a Hiq~ : because, so they say, he is then fit to be laden: (Msb:) and ↓ AHq~t she (a young camel) completed three years; (Aboo-Málik, K;) became a Hiq~ap ; (Ibn-'Abbád, K;) like Haq~ato . (TA.) You say, huwa Haq~N bay~inu AlHiq~api [ He is a Hq~ , bearing evidence of being such ]: (S:) and hiYa Hiq~N (K) and Hiq~apN (Msb, K) bay~inapu AlHiq~api [ she is a Hq~ or Hq~p , bearing evidence &c.]: (Msb:) [a phrase] to which a parallel is scarcely known, (Msb,) or to which there is no parallel (K) except A^asadN bay~inu AlA^asadi [a lion bearing evidence of being like a lion in boldness]. (TA.) ― -b2- Hiq~N [as inf. n. of Haq~ato ] also signifies A she-camel's overpassing the days [ corresponding to those ] in which she was covered [ in the preceding year ]: (K:) or her completing [ the time of ] her pregnancy; as also ↓ AisotiHoqaAqN . definition: He demanded it as his right, or due.
sourceDefinition: He demanded it as his right, or due. (TA.) [And hence,] He had a right, or just title or claim, to it; he was, or became, entitled to it; he deserved it, or merited it; syn. Aisotawojabahu : (S, Msb, K:) or these two verbs are nearly the same; (TA;) [the former meaning he was, or became, adapted, disposed, apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, competent, or proper, for it; which is the most proper meaning of the phrase SaAra HaqiyqFA bihi , as well as of the verb AstHq~ ; but this verb has also the former of these two meanings.] When a man purchases a house, and another lays claim to it, and establishes a just evidence of his claim, and the judge decides for him according to his evidence, one says of him, qadi A@sotaHaq~ahaA EalaY Almu$otariY [ He has a right to it in preference to the purchaser ]; meaning that he is to possess it in preference to the purchaser. (TA.) And of a camel such as is termed Hiq~ one says, AstHq~ A^ano yurokaba [ He was, or has become, fit to be ridden ], (K,) and A^ano yuHomala Ealayohi [ to be laden ]: (S, Msb:) and AstHq~ AlD~iraAba [ He was, or has become, fit for covering ]. (L, K.) ― -b2- [Hence, It (an action, and anything,) deserved it, merited it, or required it. ] And AstHq~ A_ivomFA He did what necessitated sin; (Ksh and Bd and Jel in v. 106;) [ was guilty of a sin; ] and deserved its being said of him that he was a sinner; (Ksh ibid.;) i. q. Aisotawojabahu . (TA.) And AstHq~wA They committed sins for which he who should punish them would be excusable, because they deserved punishment; like A^awojabuwA , and A^aEo*aruwA , and AisotalaATuwA . (IAar, TA in art. lwT .) ― -b3- AstHq~t A_ibilunaA rabiyEFA : see 4, last sentence. ― -b4- AstHq~t Aln~aAqapu laqaAHFA The she-camel conceived, or became pregnant; and AstHq~ laqaAHuhaA [signifies the same]. (TA.) ― -b5- See also 1, as an intrans. verb, last two sentences.

definition: , inf. n. HaqoHaqapN , He went the pace, or in the manner, termed HaqoHaqapN ; (TA;) which means a pace, or manner of going, in which the beast is made to exert himself to the very utmost, and which...
sourceDefinition: , inf. n. HaqoHaqapN , He went the pace, or in the manner, termed HaqoHaqapN ; (TA;) which means a pace, or manner of going, in which the beast is made to exert himself to the very utmost, and which is the most fatiguing to the Zahor [meaning the camel that is ridden, or the beast that carries one ]: (S, Mgh, K:) or a journeying in the beginning, or first part, of the night; (Lth, S, K;) which is forbidden: (Lth, S, TA:) or, as some say, the fatiguing a while, and abstaining a while: (Lth, TA:) but Az says that Lth is not correct in either of his explanations of this word: (TA:) or an obstinate persisting in journeying: or an obstinate persisting in journeying until the camel that one is riding perishes or breaks down: (K:) or, accord. to Az, the correct meaning, confirmed by what the Arabs said, is the making the camel to go on, and urging him to that which fatigues him, and that which is beyond his power, until he breaks down with his rider: or, accord. to IAar, the jading of the weak [ beast ] by hard journeying. (TA.) It is related in a trad., that Mutarrif Ibn-Esh-Shikhkheer said to his son, when he took extraordinary pains in religious exercises, (S, TA,) and was immoderate therein, (TA,) xayoru AlA^umuwri A^awosaATuhaA wa AlHasanapu bayona Al$~ayoy^ayoni wa $ar~u Als~ayori [ The best of affairs, or actions, or cases, are such of them as are between two extremes; and the good action is between the two things; and the worst kind of journeying is that in which the beast is made to exert himself to the very utmost, &c.]: (S, TA:) meaning, pursue thou the middle course in religious exercises, and burden not thyself, lest thou become disgusted; for the best of works is that which is continued, though it be small. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: contr. of baATilN [used as a subst. and as an epithet or act. part. n.]: (S, Msb, K:) or, as an inf. n. [and used as a simple subst.], contr. of buTolaAnN ; and as an act. part. n., and a simple epithet, contr. of baATilN . (Kull.) [As a subst.,] its primary signification is Suitableness to the requirements of wisdom, justice, right, or rightness, truth, reality, or fact; or to the exigencies of the case; as the suitableness of the foot of a door in respect of its socket, for turning round rightly: (Er-Rághib, TA:) [and particularly] the suitableness of a judgment, and of what involves, or implies, a judgment, [i. e., of a saying, and a religion, and a persuasion, or the like, (as will be shown by one of the explanations of its meanings as an epithet,)] to reality or fact; and the suitableness of reality or fact to a judgment: (Kull:) [the state, or quality, or property, of being just, proper, right, correct, or true; justness, propriety, rightness, correctness, or truth; reality, or fact; the state, &c., of being established, or confirmed, as a truth or fact; of being necessary, requisite, or unavoidable; of being binding, obligatory, incumbent, or due: (as shown above: see 1, first sentence:)] and existence in relation to substances, absolutely: and everlasting existence [in relation to God]: (Kull:) pl. HuquwqN and HiqaAqN : it has no pl. of pauc. (TA.) (TA.) (TA.) definition: A camel three years old, (S, Mgh,) that has entered the fourth year: (S, Mgh, Msb:) or a camel entering the fourth year: (K:) so called because fit to be laden (S, Msb) and made use of;
sourceDefinition: A camel three years old, (S, Mgh,) that has entered the fourth year: (S, Mgh, Msb:) or a camel entering the fourth year: (K:) so called because fit to be laden (S, Msb) and made use of; (S;) or because fit to be ridden; or because fit for covering: (K:) the female is termed ↓ Hiq~apN , (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) and Hiq~N also: (S, K:) the pl. (of Hiq~N , Msb) is HiqaAqN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and (of Hiq~apN , Msb) HiqaqN , (Msb, K,) and the pl. pl., (K,) i. e. pl. of HiqaAqN , (S,) is HuquqN , (S, K,) and sometimes HaqaAy^iqu , (S, TA,) or this is a pl. of Hiq~apN . (TA: see 3.) Or [so in the K, but it should rather be “ and, ”] Hiq~N signifies A she-camel whose teeth have fallen out by reason of extreme age. (K.) ― -b2- One says, raA^ayotahaA wa hiYa Hiq~apN as meaning (assumed tropical:) [ I saw her when she was ] like a she-camel termed Hq~p in bigness. (TA.) ― -b3- And [the pl.] HiqaAqN is applied to The young ones of trees: (TA:) and particularly of the [species of mimosa termed] EurofuT : (K, TA:) as being likened to the camels termed HqAq . (TA.) -A2- Also (tropical:) The time of year in which a she-camel was covered in the preceding year; (S, TA;) and so ↓ Hiq~apN : (TA:) or the usual period of her gestation. (L in art. nDj .) You say, A^atati Aln~aAqapu EalaY Hiq~ihaA (tropical:) The she-camel arrived at the time of year in which she had been covered in the preceding year: (S, TA:) and ↓ Att ElY Hiq~atihaA signifies the same; or she completed her period of gestation, and overpassed by some days the time of year in which she had been covered in the preceding year, to complete the formation of the fœtus. (TA.) And jaAzati AlHiq~a She (a camel) overpassed the year without bringing forth. (As, S.) [See also the last sentence but one in the explanations of 1 as an intrans. verb.] ― -b2- kaAna *`lika Einoda Hiq~i laqaAHihaA : see Haq~N

definition: Adapted, disposed, apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, proper, competent, or worthy;
sourceDefinition: Adapted, disposed, apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, proper, competent, or worthy; syn. xaliyqN , (Sh, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) and jadiyrN ; (K;) as also ↓ Haq~N , (Ibn- 'Abbád, K,) and [some say] ↓ maHoquwqN : (Sh, S, Mgh, K:) HaqiyqN is said to be of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN ; but accord. to the A, it is not so, because its fem. is with p ; but is from the supposed verb Haquqa , and is like xaliyqN from xaluqa , and jadiyrN from jadura : and ↓ maHoquwqN signifies [properly] rendered adapted &c.: (TA:) the pl. of Hqyq is A^aHiq~aA='u ; and that of ↓ mHqwq is maHoquwquwna . (S.) You say, huwa HaqiyqN bihi (Sh, S, Msb, K) and bh ↓ maHoquwqN (Sh, S, K) and bh ↓ Haq~N (Ibn-'Abbád, K) [ He is adapted, &c., for it; or worthy of it ]. And to a woman, A^anota HaqiyqapN bika*aA (A, TA) and HaqiyqapN li*`lika and li*`lika ↓ maHoquwqapN [ Thou art adapted, &c., for such a thing and for that thing; or worthy of it ]. (TA.) And A^anota HaqiyqN biA^ano tafoEala (A, Mgh) and ↓ maHoquwqN (A) [ Thou art adapted, &c., for thy doing such a thing; or worthy of doing it]. And huwa HaqiyqN A^ano yafoEala ka*aA [ He is adapted, &c., for his doing such a thing; or worthy to do it ]; (S;) in which case, An is for biA^ano . (Mgh.) [And HaqiyqN bika*aA also signifies Having a right, or just title or claim, to such a thing; entitled to such a thing. ] It is said in the Kur [vii. 103], HaqiyqN EalaY A^ano laA A^aqowla EalaY A@ll~`hi A_il~aA AlHaq~a , meaning I am disposed [ not ] to say [ of God aught save ] the truth: or, as some say, I am vehemently desirous [ that I should not say &c.]; for, accord. to Aboo-'Alee, A^anaA HaqiyqN EalaY ka*aA means I am vehemently desirous of such a thing: but one reading, that of Náfi', is HaqiyqN EalaY~a A^ano laA A^aquwla , It is binding, or obligatory, or incumbent, on me [ that I should not say ]. (TA.)

definition: The essence of a thing as meaning that by being which a thing is what it is;
sourceDefinition: The essence of a thing as meaning that by being which a thing is what it is; [or that in being which a thing consists; ] as when we say that a rational animal is the Hqyqp of a human being: (KT:) or that by being which a thing is what it is, considered with regard to its reality, is termed HaqiyqapN : considered with regard to its individuality, huwiy~apN : and without regard thereto, maAhiy~apN : (KT, TA:) the ultimate and radical constituent of a thing. (Msb, TA.) ― -b2- [Also The essence of a thing as meaning the property or quality, or the aggregate of properties or qualities, whereby a thing is what it is; the essential property or quality, or the aggregate of the essential properties or qualities, of a thing; that which constitutes the particular and distinguishing nature of a thing or of a genus or species; i. q. *aAtiy~apN : and] the truth, reality, or true or real nature or state [or circumstances or facts, the very nature, and the gist, and the pith, marrow, or most essential part ], of a case, or an affair: pl. HaqaAy^iqu : see 3. (TA.) One says, balaga Haqiyqapa AlA^amori He arrived at [the knowledge of] the truth, reality, or true or real nature or state [&c.], of the case, or affair. (TA.) And ↓ AlHaq~apu signifies Haqiyqapu AlA^amori ; (S, K;) as also ↓ AlHaAq~apu . (TA.) Hence the saying, lam~aA Earafa min~iY haraba ↓ AlHaq~apa [ When he knew the truth, reality, or true or real nature or state &c., of the case, or affair, from me, he fled ]. (S, TA.) And min~iY haraba ↓ lam~aA raA^aY AlHaAq~apa [ When he saw the truth, &c.]. (TA.) [ HaqiyqapF is often used as meaning In truth, or truly; in reality, or really; and in fact. ] You say also, Earafotuhu Haqiyqapa AlmaEorifapi [ I knew it with reality of knowledge ]. (Msb in art. knh .) And Haqiyqapu AlA_iymaAni means Genuine belief or faith; reality of belief or faith. (TA.) [And you say, h`*aA $aYo'N laA Haqiyqapa lahu This is a thing having no reality. ] -A2- [Also A word, or phrase, used in its proper or original, or in a proper or an original, sense; ] that which is constantly used according to its original application; or a name for that whereby is meant what it was [ originally ] applied to denote; (TA;) contr. of majaAzN : (S, K:) of the measure faEiylapN in the sense of the measure faAEilapN , from Haq~a Al$~aYo'u signifying vabata : the p is affixed for the conversion of the word from an epithet to a subst.: (TA:) [pl. as above]. [It is also called HaqiyqapN lugawiy~apN , and HaqiyqapN lugapF ; to distinguish it from what is termed HaqiyqapN Eurofiy~apN , and HaqiyqapN EurofFA , which is A word, or phrase, so much used in a particular tropical sense as to be, in that sense, conventionally regarded as proper; as, for instance, EadolN in the sense of “ just; ” it being properly an inf. n.] A majaAz , when much used, becomes what is termed HaqiyqapN EurofFA . (Mz 24th nwE .) [ HaqiyqapN means also A proper (opposed to a tropical) signification. ] -A3- AlHaqiyqapu also signifies (tropical:) That which, or those whom, it is necessary for one, or it behooveth one, to defend, or protect, (S, L, K, TA,) of the people of one's house, (L,) or such as the wife, and the female neighbour, and property, &c.: (Ham p. 181:) pl. as above. (L.) You say, fulaAnN HaAmiY AlHaqiyqapi (tropical:) [ Such a one is the defender, or protector, of that which, or those whom, it is necessary, &c., to defend, or protect ]. (S, TA.) [See also *imaArN . And see an ex. of this signification, or of the next, in a verse cited in p. 288.] ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) The banner, or standard: (S, K, and Ham ubi suprà:) this being included in the preceding meaning. (Ham.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) That which is sacred, or inviolable; that which one is under an obligation to respect, or honour. (TA.)

definition: [comparative and superlative of HaqiyqN ].
sourceDefinition: [comparative and superlative of HaqiyqN ]. You say, huwa A^aHaq~u bika*aA [ He is more, and most, adapted, disposed, apt, meet, suited, suitable, fitted, fit, proper, or competent, for such a thing; or more, and most, worthy, or deserving, of it: and he has a better, and the best, right to such a thing; or a more just, and the most just, title or claim to it; or he is more, and most, entitled to it ]: this phrase is used in two senses: first, as denoting the possession of an exclusive right or title, i. e., without the participation of another; as when you say, zayodN A^aHaq~u bimaAlihi Zeyd is entitled to his property exclusively of any other person: secondly, as denoting the possession of a right or title in participation with another person, but in a superior degree; as in the saying, AlA^ay~imu A^aHaq~u binafosihaA mino waliy~ihaA , (Msb,) i. e. The woman that has not a husband and is not a virgin [ is more entitled to dispose of herself than is her guardian ]; (Mgh in art. Aym ;) meaning that they participate [in the right], but that her right is the stronger: (Msb:) a saying of Mohammad, in which the Ay~m is opposed to the bikor , for it is added that the bkr is to be asked her permission: but one reading substitutes Alv~ay~ibu for AlAy~m . (Mgh ubi suprà.) In the saying, in the Kur [v. 106], la$ahaAdatunaA A^aHaq~u mino $ahaAdatihimaA , it may be formed from AisotaHaq~a by rejection of the augmentative letters, so that the meaning is, [ Verily our testimony is ] more deserving of being accepted [ than the testimony of them two ]: or it may be from Haq~a Al$~aYo'u signifying vabata , and so mean more true, or valid. (TA.) -A2- Applied to a horse, That does not sweat. (S, K.) ― -b2- And, likewise thus applied, That puts down his hind hoof in the place [ that has just before been that ] of his fore hoof. (S, * K.) [See HaqaqN .]

definition: He abstained from, shunned, or avoided, sin, or crime;
sourceDefinition: He abstained from, shunned, or avoided, sin, or crime; put it away from himself: (A 'Obeyd, S, K, TA:) he applied himself to acts, or exercises, of devotion; became devout, or a devotee. (IJ, TA.) Here the form tafaE~ala is deprived of the radical signification, as in the cases of the syn. words taA^av~ama and taHan~ava ; though its property is oftener to confirm the radical signification. (TA. [See tHn~v .]) You say, tHw~b mino ka*aA He abstained from such a thing as a sin, or crime. (A 'Obeyd, S, TA. [See also another explanation below.]) ― -b2- He humbled himself in his prayer, or supplication. (TA.) ― -b3- He expressed pain, grief, or sorrow; lamented, or complained. (S, K, * TA.) And tHw~b mino ka*aA He was enraged, and expressed pain or grief or sorrow, or lamented, or complained, by reason of such a thing. (TA. [See another explanation above.]) ― -b4- He cried out, expressing pain or grief or sorrow, or lamenting, or complaining: he cried aloud, or vehemently, in prayer, or supplication. (TA.) He wept, in impatience, or sorrow, and with loud crying: and sometimes, in a general sense, he cried out, or aloud, (TA.) ― -b5- He (a jackal) cried, or howled: because his cry is like that of a person expressing pain or grief or sorrow, or lamenting, or complaining, as though he were writhing from the pain of hunger or beating. (S, TA.)

definition: and Hawobu and Hawoba (S, K) and ↓ HaAbi (K) A cry used for chiding a camel: (S:) or a cry by which a male camel is chidden, (Lth, IAth, K,) to urge him on;
sourceDefinition: and Hawobu and Hawoba (S, K) and ↓ HaAbi (K) A cry used for chiding a camel: (S:) or a cry by which a male camel is chidden, (Lth, IAth, K,) to urge him on; (Lth, TA;) like as a she-camel is by the cry Halo and Hali and HaliY : the first form ( Hawobi ) is that used by the Arabs [in general]; but the other forms are allowable: Hawobo Hawobo also occurs, with the b quiescent; and HawobFA HawobFA occurs in a trad., in the same sense: also, laA ma$ayotu ↓ Habo and ↓ Habi and ↓ HaAbo and ↓ HaAbi [ On! mayest thou not walk, or mayest thou not be rightly directed; Hb &c. being syn. with Hawobi , and followed by an imprecation]. (TA.) Hence, Hawobaka halo yuEotamu biAls~amaAri Urge on! Should a delay be made in bringing milk much diluted with water? i. e., if thou entertain with milk much diluted with water, wherefore tardiness? a prov., applied to him who delays the fulfilment of his promise, and then gives little. (MF.)

definition: (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ HawobN , (Msb, * K,) said by some to be two dial.
sourceDefinition: (S, A, Msb, K) and ↓ HawobN , (Msb, * K,) said by some to be two dial. vars., (Msb, [see 1, first sentence,]) and ↓ HaAbN (S, K) and ↓ HawobapN (A 'Obeyd, K) and ↓ HuwbapN (A 'Obeyd, TA) and ↓ HaAbapN (K) and ↓ HiybapN , (TA,) Sin, or crime: or a sin, or a crime: (S, A, Msb, K:) accord. to A 'Obeyd, the first and second signify any sin or crime; (TA;) [as also, app., HaAbN ;] and Hwbp [i. e. HawobapN and HuwbapN , the former particularly mentioned in the Msb, and app. HaAbapN also], a single sin or crime: (Msb, TA:) accord. to Fr, HuwbN signifies great sin, or a great sin: accord. to Katádeh, wrong, injustice, or tyranny: thus in the Kur iv. 2; where El-Hasan read ↓ HawobFA instead of HuwbFA . (TA.) One says, rab~i taqab~alo tawobatiY ↓ waA@gosilo HawobatiY (T, TA) i. e. [ O my Lord, accept my repentance, and wash away ] my sin, or crime. (A 'Obeyd, TA.) El-Mukhabbal Es-Saadee says, ↓ falaA tudoxilan~a Ald~ahora qaboraka HawobapF yaquwmu bihaA yawomFA Ealayoki Hasiybu [ Then introduce not thou, ever, into thy grave, a sin with which a reckoner, or taker of vengeance, may one day rise up against thee ]. (TA.) -A2- HuwbN also signifies Perdition, destruction, or death. (K.) [Hence, app.,] Aibonapu HwbK A quiver; syn. kinaAnapN . (TA. [The vowel of the H is not indicated.]) ― -b2- Disease. (K.) ― -b3- A trial, a trouble, or an affliction. (K.) You say, h`w^ulaA='i EiyaAlu A^abiY HuwbK [ These are the family of the father of trouble; i. e., of one who is in trouble ]. (TA.) ― -b4- See also HawobN . -A3- And see HawobaA='u .

(TA.) ― -b4- A state, or condition; as also ↓ HiybapN : (K:) but only used in speaking of an evil state; as in the phrases, baAta biHawobapi suwo'K and suwo'K ↓ biHiybapi He passed the night in an evil state or condition. (TA.) ― -b5- [Hence also, for *uw HawobapK , and *aAtu HawobapK , and *awuw HawobapK ,] A weak man; (AZ, S, K;) as also ↓ HuwbapN : (K:) and a weak woman: (TA:) and weak persons: (S:) and [ a man who can neither profit nor harm; or] a man having neither good nor evil: (S:) pl. (AZ, TA.) ― -b7- A sacred, or an inviolable, right of a person, which it would be sinful to disregard; as in the saying, faEalotuhu liHawobapi fulaAnK [ I did it for the sake of the sacred, or inviolable, right of such a one ]. (A.) ― -b8- A horse, or similar beast; syn. daAb~apN : (K:) for this, also, cannot do without some one to take constant care of it, and to sustain it. (TA.) -A3- The middle of a house. (K.) A_ixoraAbN , (TA,) He reduced to ruin; or rendered waste, uninhabited, depopulated, deserted, desolate, uncultivated, or in a state the contrary of flourishing; (S, A, K;) a house, (S, K,) or a dwelling, or place of abode, (Msb,) or a country; (A;) as also ↓ xr~b , (A, Msb, K,) inf. n. taxoriybN ; (TA;) and ↓ xaraba , (K,) [inf. n. xaraAbN , as in the Kur ii. 108:] or ↓ xr~b signifies the same, but in a more extensive, or a superlative or an intensive sense: you say, xar~abuwA buyuwtahumo [ They ruined their houses; the r being doubled because the verb has many objects: or they demolished their houses ]. definition: A hole, perforation, or bore;
sourceDefinition: A hole, perforation, or bore; (Msb, TA;) whether round or not: (TA:) or any round hole or perforation or bore; (S, K, TA;) such as that of the ear; (TA;) [and] so ↓ xurobN : (A:) pl. [of mult.] of the former (in this and in other senses here following, K, * TA) xurabN (Msb, K) and xuruwbN , which latter is extr. [with respect to rule], and [of pauc.] A^axoraAbN [which is irregular as pl. of the former, but regular as pl. of the latter]. (K. [See also xurotN and xurotapN .]) [Hence,] xurobapN Als~inodiY~i The bore of the lobe of the ear, when not slit: [the Sindee being particularly noted by the Arabs for his pierced ears:] when slit, it is termed Als~inodiY~i ↓ xarobapN . (TA.) ― -b2- Width of the hole, or perforation, of the ear; (JK;) as also ↓ xarobN , (JK,) or ↓ xurobN , (A,) and ↓ A^axorabN , (K,) this last being a subst. like A^afokalN . (TA.) ― -b3- The eye of a needle: [like xurotN and xurotapN :] and the foramen of the anus: as also ↓ xurobN and ↓ xarobN and ↓ xar~aAbapN and ↓ xur~aAbapN and ↓ xuraAbapN ; (K, MF;) in both of these senses, though this is not clearly shown in the K: (MF:) and likewise, of the vagina; the dual of xurobapN occurring in a trad., as some relate it, applied to the foramen of the anus and that of the vagina together: (TA:) and the last, ↓ xuraAbapN , also signifies any perforation like the eye of a needle. (K.) ― -b4- Alxurobapu and ↓ Alxurobu and ↓ AlxuraAbapu and ↓ Alxur~aAbapu The hole [or socket ] of the hip, (S, TA,) where the head of the thigh-bone is inserted; as also xurobapu Alwariki and Alwrk ↓ xurobu and ↓ xarobu Alwrk and Alwrk ↓ xaraAbapu [or, probably, ↓ xuraAbap ] and Alwrk ↓ xur~aAbapu and Alwrk ↓ xar~aAbapu : and the pl., A^axoraAbN , also signifies the lower extremities of the shoulder-blades. (TA.) ― -b5- And Alxurobapu , (A 'Obeyd, S, Mgh, Msb, K,) or xurobapu AlmazaAdap , (A,) and ↓ Alxur~aAbap , and sometimes ↓ AlxuraAbap without tesh-deed, (TA,) [and perhaps ↓ Alxurobu also, (see xubonN ,)] The loop of the [ leathern water-bag called ] mazaAdap ; (A 'Obeyd, S, A, Mgh, Msb, K;) because of its round form: every mzAdp having two loops [whereby it is suspended upon either side of the camel], each of which is thus called; and two kidney-shaped pieces of leather ( kuloyataAni ) [at the two upper corners]; and the two loops are sewed to these. (TA. [See also xurotapN .]) -A2- A vice, or fault; (IAth, TA;) as also ↓ xarabapN : (K:) and corruption, or unsoundness, in religion; (JK, K;) as also ↓ xarabapN (JK, TA) and ↓ xarobapN [like HarobapN ] (Mgh, * K) and ↓ xurobN and ↓ xarobN (K) and ↓ xarabN : and a quality inducing suspicion, or evil opinion: [a meaning app. belonging to all of the foregoing words:] (TA:) pl., of the first, xurubaAtN ; and of the second, xarabaAtN : (JK:) also, the first (i. e. xurobapN ), a crime: a bad, an evil, or a foul, word or saying: and a trial, or an affliction. (TA.) You say, maA fiyhi xurobapN There is not in him a vice, or fault. (TA.) And maA raA^ayonaA mino fulaAnK xurobapF (JK, TA) and ↓ xarobFA , (TA,) or ↓ xarabapF , (JK,) We have not seen in such a one unsoundness of religion nor anything disgraceful. (JK, TA.) ― -b2- faAr~N bixurobapK , occurring in a trad., means One who flees with a thing desiring to appropriate it to himself and to take possession of it unlawfully. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: [ The flank; i. e. each of the ilia; ] i. q. Al$~aAkilapu ; (Zj, in his “ Khalk el-Insán; ” S, K;) i. e. the TafoTafap [or quivering flesh ] of the side, that reaches to the extremities of the ribs: (Zj, ibid.:) and [so in the K, but more properly “ or, ”] AlxaASirapu , (K,) or AlxaASiraAtaAni (JK, TA) and ↓ AlxaSoraAni , (TA,) what is between the Haroqafap [or crest of the hip ] and the lowest rib; (JK, K, TA;) i. e. the part from which retires each of the lowest ribs, and in advance of which projects each of the HajabataAni : [explained by the words mA qlS Enh AlquSayorayaAni wtqd~m mn AlHjbtyn : but for mn AlHjbtyn , I read minohu AlHajabataAni ; referring, for corroboration, to explanations of this last word; and therefore I have rendered the passage as above: the meaning seems evidently to be the part between the lowest rib and the crest of the hip, on each side: ] the thin skin which is above the xaSor is called the TafoTafap : so in the M, agreeably with the saying of Ibn-El-Ajdábee, that ↓ AlxaSoru and AlxaASirapu are syn.; i. e., in this sense: [this assertion, however, requires consideration; for all the explanations of AlxASrp are easily reconcileable:] pl. xawaASiru [which is also used in the sense of the sing. or dual]. (TA.) You say rajulN Daxomu AlxawASiri [ A man large in the flank or flanks ]: and Lh mentions the phrase A_in~ahaA lamunotafixapu AlxawaSiri [ Verily she is inflated, or swollen, in the flank or flanks ]; as though the term xASrp were applicable to every portion [of the flank]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A pain in the xaASirap [or flank ]: or in the kidneys. (TA.) ― -b3- And it is also said to signify A certain vein ( Eiroq ) in the kidney, which occasions pain to the person when it is in motion. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (K,) or AlmutaxaS~iruwna fiY AlS~alaApi , (Mgh,) Those who, in praying in the night, becoming tired thereby, put their hands upon their xawaASir [or flanks ]: of such it is said (in a trad., IAth, K) that light shall be [seen] on their faces (IAth, Mgh, K) on the day of resurrection: (IAth, K:) [in other cases, this action is forbidden, or disapproved: see 8:] or, in the instance mentioned above, it may mean those who shall rest upon their righteous works on the day of resurrection: (IAth, Mgh, TA:) this latter is apparently the right meaning: otherwise, two trads. contradict each other. (MF.)

(A.) Thus in the saying, A^axa*a biyadihi faxalajahu bayoni SaHobihi [ He took his hand, and pulled him out from amid his companions ]: and xalaja rumoHahu mina AlmaToEuwni [ He pulled out his spear from the person pierced ]: and rumoHFA marokuwzFA ↓ Axtlj [ He pulled out a spear stuck in the ground ]. (A, TA.) [See also an ex. in a verse cited voce maTorabN .] El-'Ajjáj says, faA_ino yakuno h`*aA Alz~amaAnu xalajaA faqado labisonaA Eayo$ahu AlmuxarofajaA meaning (assumed tropical:) And if this time has taken away, and exchanged for another, a state [in which we were, we have long enjoyed its plentiful life ]. (S.) ― -b2- [Hence,] xulija , said of a stallion-camel, He was taken away from the females that had passed seven or eight months since the period when they last brought forth, before he had become too languid to cover any longer. (Lth, A, L.) And xalaja , aor. , (assumed tropical:) He weaned his offspring, or the offspring of his she-camel: (K:) (tropical:) he separated a young camel from the mother. (A.) And xalajato waladahaA (tropical:) She (a mother) weaned her offspring: (M, A:) so accord. to Lh, who does not particularize any kind [of animal]. (M.) And xalaja naAqapF (assumed tropical:) He weaned the offspring of a she-camel. (S.) And mino bayonihimo ↓ Auxotulija (tropical:) [ He was taken away from among them ]: said of the dead. (A, TA.) ― -b3- xalajaniY ka*aA , (S, K, *) aor. , (K,) (assumed tropical:) Such a thing occupied me; busied me; or diverted me, by employing my attention, from other things. (S, K, * TA.) You say, xalajatohu A^umuwru Ald~unoyaA (assumed tropical:) [ The affairs of the world occupied him, &c.]. (S, TA.) And ↓ xalajatohu AlxawaAliju (assumed tropical:) Busying [or distracting ] affairs busied [or distracted ] him. (Lth.) And a poet says, wa A^abiytu taxolijuniY Alhumuwmu kaA^an~aniY dalowu Als~uqaApi tumad~u biAlA^a$oTaAni [ And I pass the night, ] anxieties busying me [ as though I were the bucket of the waterers, drawn from the well by the ropes ]. (IAar.) ― -b4- taxoliju Als~ayora , said of a fleet she-camel, (L, K,) (assumed tropical:) She goes, journeys, or travels, quickly. (L.) (L, K) and , inf. n. xalojN , (L, TA,) (assumed tropical:) He made a sign [ by a motion ] (L, K, TA) biEayonihi with his eye, and biHaAjibayohi with his eyebrows. (L, TA.) And xalajatoniY biEayonihaA (tropical:) She made a sign to me with her eye, or winked to me, to indicate a time or place of appointment, or something that she desired. (A, TA.) ― -b7- See also 8, in two places.

definition: The [ kind of tree called ] A^araAk : (Bd in xxxiv.
sourceDefinition: The [ kind of tree called ] A^araAk : (Bd in xxxiv. 15:) or a species of the ArAk , having a fruit which is eaten: (Lth, S:) or the fruit of the ArAk : (IB, K:) or any trees having no thorns: (IDrd, Bd, K:) or trees having thorns; cited from Fr; and by Z, in the Ksh, on the authority of A 'Obeyd: (TA:) or certain trees like the sidor , (K, TA,) the fruit of which is like the mulberry: (TA:) or certain deadly trees: (K:) or deadly poison: (TA:) or any plant that has acquired a taste of bitterness, (Zj, Bd, K,) so that it cannot be eaten: (Zj, TA:) or scanty fruit of any trees: (AHn, K:) or the fruit of what is called fasowapu AlD~abuEi : (K:) or a certain fruit called fasowapu AlD~abuEi , having the form of the poppy, friable, and of no use: (IAar:) or it signifies, in the Kur xxxiv. 15, fruit that is disagreeable in taste, and choking: (Bd:) or, [as an epithet,] bitter, and disagreeable in taste, and choking: (Jel:) or bitter; applied to anything: or acid. (K.) In the Kur, ubi suprà, some read, *awaAtaYo A^akuli xamoTK : (S, IB, Jel:) this is the right reading accord. to him who makes xmT to mean the ArAk : but accord. to him who makes it to mean the fruit of the ArAk , the right reading of Akl is with tenween, and xmT is a substitute for that word. (IB.) [The pl. is ximaATN : see an ex. voce xal~N .]

definition: , from xan~ava “he bent,” (S, K,) because of his softness, delicacy, tenderness, flabbiness, laxness, or limberness, and affectation of languor, or languidness;
sourceDefinition: , from xan~ava “he bent,” (S, K,) because of his softness, delicacy, tenderness, flabbiness, laxness, or limberness, and affectation of languor, or languidness; (TA;) or from xunovaY ; (Kh, JK, MS;) An effeminate man; (T in art. Anv , and TA;) one who resembles a woman in gentleness, and in softness of speech, and in an affectation of languor of the limbs: (TA voce muw^an~avN , q. v.: [see also xanivN :]) it is written thus and ↓ muxan~ivN : (TA:) this latter is explained by some as meaning one who makes his speech like that of women, in softness and gentleness: (Msb, TA:) it is also said that both these epithets are used to signify one who affects languor, or languidness, of the limbs; one who makes himself like women in the bending of himself, and in affecting languor, or languidness, and in speech: but that one uses the latter epithet only when he means one who does what is excessively foul, or obscene; [i. e. a catamite; though this is a meaning often borne by the former also;] notwithstanding that taxoniyvN , as signifying the “committing such an action,” was unknown to the Arabs [of the classical ages], and is not found in their language: (MF, TA:) [often, also,] the former epithet signifies a man incapable of venery: (MA:) it is said in a trad. that they used to reckon the mxn~v as one of those having no need of nikaAH . (TA in art. Arb .) The muxan~av is also called ↓ xunaAvapu and ↓ xunayovapu [each imperfectly decl.]. (K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: (AA, T, S, M, K) and ↓ diy^odaA='N (AA, S, M, K) and ↓ duw^oduwo'N , (M, K,) all with medd, (TA,) The last ( of the days, T) of the [ lunar ] month; (AA, T, S, M, K;) as also ↓ daA^odaA^u : (M:) or the day of doubt; yawomu Al$~ak~i [generally meaning the day of which one doubts whether it be the last of Shaabán or the first of Ramadán; but here app. relating to any month]: (TA:) or ↓ daA^odaA^N signifies the day, (M,) or night, (TA,) of which one doubts whether it be the last of one month or the first of the next month: (M, TA:) so says Kr: (M:) or the first word and the second (M, K) and the third (K) signify the twenty-fifth, and the twenty-sixth, and the twentyseventh, night: (M, K:) or the twenty-eighth night, and the twenty-ninth: or each of these two is called ↓ daA^odA^apN ; and the two together, Ald~aA=diy^u : (Th, M:) or [ each of ] three nights of the end of the month; (K, TA;) which are [also] called layaAliY AlmuHaAqi : (TA:) pl. daA=diy^u , (M, K,) and, by poetic license, daA=dK : (M:) or the daA=diy^ are three nights of the latter part of the month, before those called lyAlY AlmHAq : (T, S:) thus says A 'Obeyd; and IAar says the like: or they are the three nights that are after the mHAq ; and are so called because the moon hastens therein to become invisible; from the phrase daA^odaA^apu AlbaEiyri : As says that three of the nights of the month are called the mHAq ; and three, the dA=dy^ ; and these latter are the last; and AHeyth says the like. (TA.) -A2- See also R. Q. 1.

(TA.) ― -b2- And daxana Ald~uxaAnu , (JK,) and AlgubaAru (K) and Aln~aqoEu , (TA,) inf. n. duxuwnN , (K) The smoke, (JK,) and (tropical:) the dust, (K, TA,) rose; or spread, or diffused itself. (JK, K, TA.) ― -b3- And daxinati Aln~aAru , (JK, S, Msb, K,) with kesr to the x , (S, Msb, K,) aor. , (JK, Msb, K,) inf. n. daxanN , (Msb,) The smoke ( duxaAn ) of the fire (JK, S, Msb, K) became vehement, (JK,) or became excited, or raised, (S, Msb, K,) in consequence of its having firewood, (JK, S, Msb, K,) in a fresh, or green, state, (JK,) thrown upon it, (JK, S, Msb, K,) and being thus marred. (S, Msb, K.) ― -b4- daxina , aor. , said of food, (JK, K,) and of flesh-meat, (TA,) inf. n. daxanN , (JK,) means It was, or became, infected with smoke ( duxaAn ), (K, TA,) while being roasted or cooked, (TA,) and acquired its odour, (K, TA,) so that this predominated over its flavour: (TA:) [in this sense] it is said of cooked food when the cooking-pot is infected with smoke (↓ A_i*aA tadax~anati Alqidoru ). (S, TA.) ― -b5- [Hence, as is indicated in the TA, it is said of wine, or beverage, as meaning (assumed tropical:) It became altered for the worse in odour. (See daxinN .) ― -b6- Hence also,] (assumed tropical:) It was, or became, of a dusky, or dingy, colour, inclining to black, (K, TA,) like the colour of iron: (TA:) you say daxina Aln~abotu , and daxinati Ald~aAb~apu , (tropical:) The plant, and the beast, became of that colour; (K, TA;) as though overspread with smoke ( duxaAn ); (TA;) as also daxuna , aor. , inf. n. duxonapN . (K.) ― -b7- [Hence also,] daxina xuluquhu (tropical:) His nature, or disposition, was, or became, bad, corrupt, or wicked. (K, TA. [See also daxanN , below.])

sourceDefinition: (S, Msb, K) and ↓ dux~aAnN , (K,) which latter is the form [now] commonly used, (TA,) and ↓ daxanN , (S, K,) i. q. EuvaAnN [a less usual term, meaning Smoke ]: (K: [in the S it is said merely that the duxaAn of fire is well known:]) pl. (of the first, S, Msb) dawaAxinu , (S, Msb, K,) like as EawaAvinu is pl. of EuvaAnN , (S, Msb,) the only other instance of the kind, (Msb,) deviating from rule, (S,) and dawaAxiynu , [also irreg., and both pls. of mult.,] and A^adoxinapN [a pl. of pauc.]. (K.) [Hence, the tribes of] Ghanee and Báhileh ( ganiY~ and baAhilap ) were called AibonaA duxaAnK [ The two sons of smoke ] (S, K, TA) because they smoked a party of men ( dax~anuwA EalaY qawomK ) in a cave and so killed them. (TA.) Hence also, (S,) ↓ hudonapN EalaY daxanK (tropical:) A calm [or truce ] for a cause other than recon- ciliation: (S, K, TA: [in the CK, lagalabapK is erroneously put for liEil~apK :]) or (assumed tropical:) [as a cloak] upon [i. e. concealing ] inward corruptness; from daxinati Aln~aAru explained above; [see 1;] (Msb;) [for] IAth says that it likens inward corruptness beneath outward rectitude to the smoke [or smoking] of fresh, or moist, firewood: (TA:) or (assumed tropical:) upon latent rancour or malevolence: (S and TA in art. hdn :) but A'Obeyd, in explaining a trad. in which it occurs, takes it from daxanN as signifying “ a duskiness, or dinginess, inclining to blackness,” in the colour of a beast or of a garment; for he says that it means [a case in which] the mutual love of two parties will not become pure, like the duskiness, or dinginess, that is in the colour of a beast. (TA.) ― -b2- duxaAnN is also used by the Arabs for (assumed tropical:) Evil, or mischief, when it arises; as in the saying, kaAna bayonanaA A^amorN A@rotafaEa lahu duxaAnN [ There was between us an affair that had evil, or mischief, arising in consequence of it ]. (TA.) ― -b3- It also means (assumed tropical:) Dearth, drought, sterility, or unfruitfulness; and hunger: and so it has been said to mean in the Kur xliv. 9: for it is said that the hungry [once] saw smoke ( duxaAn ) between him and the sky: or hunger is thus called because of the dryness of the earth in drought, and the rising of the dust, which is likened to duxaAn [properly so termed]. (TA.) ― -b4- [In the present day, it is also applied, but generally pronounced ↓ dux~aAn , to Tobacco; nicotiana tabacum of Linn.]

definition: [The patella, or knee-pan;
sourceDefinition: [The patella, or knee-pan; ] the round bone which moves about in the head of the knee; (S, K;) or which turns aside and moves about above the raDof of the knee [which are said to be certain bones in the knee, like fingers put together, holding together one another]: (TA:) or the bone in the inside of the knee, on the right and left of which are the ligaments ( AlEaSab [app. meaning the internal and external lateral ligaments of the knee-joint, between which is the patella]): (IDrd, TA:) or a bone having at its extremity ( fiY Tarafihi [perhaps a mistake for fiY Tarafayohi at its two extremities ]) two ligaments ( EaSabataAni [app. the tendon of the extensor muscles of the leg and the ligamentum patellæ]), at the head of the waAbilap [a bone in the knee-joint]: (TA:) it is a subst., like kaAhilN and gaAribN : (TA:) also [explained as signifying] the piece, or portion, of fat beneath the skin that is above the knee: or, as some say, the ligament ( EaSabap ) [ in that part ]. (TA.) ― -b2- Also Compact flesh: pl. dawaAgiSu . (TA.) You say of a man whose flesh is compact, kaA^an~ahu daAgiSapN [ As though he were a dAgSp ]. (TA.) -A2- Also Clear, shallow, water: (IDrd, K:) pl. as above. (K.)

definition: A horse of a colour inclining to blackness, (S, K,) or of a black colour, (Mgh,) in the face and the part next the lips, (S,) or in the face and the lips, (K,) or in the face and the muzzle, (Mgh,)...
sourceDefinition: A horse of a colour inclining to blackness, (S, K,) or of a black colour, (Mgh,) in the face and the part next the lips, (S,) or in the face and the lips, (K,) or in the face and the muzzle, (Mgh,) differing from, (S, Mgh,) or blacker than, (K,) the colour of the other parts of the body; (S, Mgh, K;) called in Pers. dayozaj [or rather diyzaho , from which dayozajN is arabicized]; (AO, * S, Mgh, K;) in some instances, without any admixture of xuDorap [here meaning dark, or ashy, dust-colour ]: (AO, TA:) it is also applied as an epithet to a wolf: and the fem. is dagomaA='u : and the pl. is dugomN : (S:) the masc. is also applied to a ram, meaning having any, the least, blackness; especially in the end of the nose and beneath the chin: and the fem. to a ewe, meaning black in the end of the nose and in the chin; (TA;) or, thus applied, black in the face: (JK:) and the masc. also signifies black in the nose: (JK, K:) in which sense it has for its pl. dugomaAnN : (TA:) accord. to the K [and the JK], dugomN , a pl. of A^adogamu , signifies white; as though it had two contr. meanings; but this is a mistranscription for duEomN , with the unpointed E . (TA.) It is said in a prov., Al*~y^obu A^adogamu [ The wolf is blackish in the face and in the part next the lips, not being so in the other parts; or rather, is black in the nose ]: for, whether he lap from a vessel or not, dugomap is a necessary characteristic of the wolf, [all] wolves being dugom ; and therefore he is sometimes, or often, suspected of having lapped from a vessel when he is [really] hungry: the prov. is applied to him who is regarded with a wish for the like of that which he has not obtained. (S.) ― -b2- Also One who snuffles; i. e., speaks from [i. e. through ] his nose; (JK, K, TA;) i. e. i. q. A^axan~u . (TA.)

[and written dihoqaAnu &c.], because of the measure fElAnu ; (S;) [but this statement relates especially to the measure faEolaAn , with fet-h to the f ; except in the case of a proper name; and an epithet of this measure, moreover, that forms its fem. by the addition of p , as dhqAn does, is perfectly decl.; and it should be observed also, that,] accord. to IJ, dhqAn is of the measure fElAl , from tadahoqana , and there is no instance, in the language, of the measure tafaEolana ; (Har p. 102;) it signifies The headman, or chief, of a village or town: (Es-Sem'ánee, Msb, TA: [agreeably with the Pers. original:]) or the proprietor thereof, in Khurásán and El-' Irák: (Es-Sem'ánee, TA:) or, as used by the Arabs, a great man of the unbelievers of the ' Ajam [or Persians ]: but they disdained this appellation: (Mgh:) Lth says that it is a nickname, or name of reproach: (TA:) it became predominantly applied to such of them as was of the people of the districts of cultivated land and of villages or towns: and then to anyone possessing much land or other immoveable property: (Mgh:) [it signifies generally a dweller, or one having a fixed abode, in a district of cultivated land, or in a village or town of such a district; a rustic; a husbandman: ] or it signifies a chief, headman, or person in authority, over the husbandmen, or peasants, of the 'Ajam [or Persians ]: and the headman of a province: (K:) and a possessor of land or other immoveable property: (Msb:) and a merchant: (Msb, K:) and one who manages affairs firmly, or strongly, with sharpness: (K:) the fem. is with p : (JK, Mgh, K:) and the pl. is dahaAqiynu (Msb, K) and dahaAqinapN . (K.) [See a verse cited voce ja*aA in art. j*w . The same verse, but with qaroyatiY (my village or town) in the place of qaroyapK , is also cited in the TA in the present art.]

[In the K, diydaAnN is said to be pl. of duwdapN : and in the L, as from the T, duwdaAnN is said to be another pl. of duwdN : this, however, I regard as a mistake; for I do not find it in the T; but I there find added, after diydaAnN , “ and duwdaAnN is a tribe of Benoo-Asad. ”]) J says that the dim. is ↓ duwayodN , and that by rule it should be duwayodapN : but this is a mistake [unless it be meant that duwayodapN is the regular dim. of duwdapN ]: it is regularly duwayodN , like as tumayorN and quyayoHN are regular dims. of tamorN and qamoHN , which are pls. [or rather coll. gen. ns.] of tamorapN and qamoHapN . (IB.)

sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, &c.,) aor. , (T, M, Msb,) inf. n. *ab~N , (T, S, M, Msb,) He repelled from him: he defended him. (T, S, M, Msb, K.) You say, ya*ub~u Eano Hariymihi He repels from, or defends, his wife, or wives, or the like. (T, Msb.) [See also R. Q. 1.] ― -b2- And *ab~N signifies also The act of driving away. (T, TA.) You say, *ab~a Al*~ubaAba , and ↓ *b~bhu , He drove away the fly, or flies. (M, TA.) And AlwaHo$u ta*ub~u Albaq~a biA^a*onaAbihaA [ The wild animals drive away the gnats with their tails ]. (A.) ― -b3- And [hence,] A^ataAhumo xaATibN fa*ab~uwhu (tropical:) One demanding a woman in marriage came to them, and they rejected him, or turned him back. (A, TA.) -A2- *ub~a (assumed tropical:) He (a man, TA) was, or became, possessed; or mad, or insane. (K, TA.) -A3- *ab~a , (M, K,) aor. , [irreg., (the verb being intrans.,) unless the first pers. be *abubotu , like labubotu &c.,] inf. n. *ab~N , (M,) He (a man, K) went hither and thither, not remaining in one place. (M, K. *) -A4- *ab~a , [aor. ,] It dried; dried up; or became dry. (T.) You say, *ab~ato $afatuhu , (S, M, K,) aor. , inf. n. *ab~N and *ababN and *ubuwbN , (M, K,) His lip became dry, (M, K,) or lost its moisture, (S,) by reason of thirst, (S, K,) or by reason of vehement thirst, (M,) &c.; (M, K;) as also ↓ *ab~abato . (M, K.) And *ab~a lisaAnuhu (S, M) in like manner [ His tongue became dry &c.]. (M.) And *ab~a said of a plant, It withered, or lost its moisture. (S, K.) And said of a pool of water left by a torrent, It dried up in the end of the hot season. (IAar, M, K.) And *ab~a jisomuhu His body became lean, or emaciated, (S, K, TA,) and lost its moisture. (TA.) And *ab~a , (T, K,) aor. , inf. n. *ab~N , (T,) His colour, or complexion, became altered, by reason of emaciation or hunger or travel &c. (T, K.) ― -b2- See also 2.

sourceDefinition: Repelling: fem. with p : hence *ab~aAtu Als~abiybi , a phrase used by Dhu-r-Rummeh, meaning repelling with their tails: or this may be from the signification next following. (Ham p. 510.) -A2- Much in motion. (Ham ubi suprà.) *ab~N , (M, L,) or ↓ *aAb~N , (K,) [the former correct, and perhaps the latter also,] applied to a camel, That does not, or will not, remain still, or motionless, in a place. (M, L, K.) A poet says, fakaA^an~anaA fiyhimo jimaAlN *ab~apN [ And it was as though we were, among them, camels that would not remain still in a place ]: which shows that *ab~N is not an inf. n. used as an epithet; for, were it so, he had said jimaAlN *ab~N . (M, L.) ― -b2- Al*~ab~u (tropical:) The wild bull; [ a species of bovine antelope; ] also called *ab~u Alr~iyaAdi ; (T, S, M, K;) so called because he goes to and fro, not remaining in one place; (M;) or because he pastures going to and fro; (T, S, * M;) or because his females pasture with him, going to and fro: (T:) and called also ↓ AlA^a*ab~u , (T, K,) by poetic license, for Al*~ab~u ; (T;) and ↓ Al*~unobubu . (K.) ― -b3- *ab~u Alr~iyaAdi is also applied to (tropical:) A man who goes and comes. (Kr, M, TA.) And (tropical:) A man who is in the habit of visiting women. (AA, T, K.)
