definition: [The common fly;
sourceDefinition: [The common fly; ] the black thing that is in houses, that falls into the vessel and into food; (M;) well known: (S, K:) so called, accord. to Ed-Demeeree, because of its fluttering about, or because it returns as often as it is driven away: (TA:) and likewise applied to the bee; (M, K;) which is also called *ubaAbu Algayovi [ the fly of the rain ], (IAth, TA,) or *ubaAbu gayovK [ the fly of rain ]; because the rain is the means of producing herbage, and by herbage it is fed; (Mgh;) or because it accompanies rain, and lives upon that which the rain causes to grow: (IAth, TA:) [accord. to some, it is a coll. gen. n.; and] the n. un. is ↓ *ubaAbapN : (S, Msb, K:) one should not say *ib~aAnapN [as the vulgar do in the present day]: (S:) or one should not say ↓ *ubaAbapN , though El-Ahmar and Ks are related to have used this word [as meaning a kind of fly ]; for *ubaAbN is a sing. [properly speaking], and is used as such in the Kur xxii. 72: (M:) the pl. (of pauc., S, Msb) is A^a*ib~ahN and (of mult., S, Msb) *ib~aAnN (S, M, Msb, K) and *ub~N , (M, K,) the last mentioned by Sb, accord. to the dial. of Temeem. (M.) One says, A_in~ahu laA^awohaY mina Al*~ubaAbi [ Verily he is more frail than the fly ]. (A.) And huwa A^ahowanu EalaY~a mino Taniyni Al*~ubaAbi [ He is more contemptible to me than the buzzing of the fly ]. (A.) manojaY Al*~ubaAbi [ The refuge of the fly ] is a prov., applied to him who is protected by his ignobleness. (Har p. 332: there written manojaA ; and in two places, mnjA^ .) And A^abuw Al*~ubaAbi [ The father of the fly ] is an appellation used as meaning (assumed tropical:) He who has stinking breath; and some say A^abuw Al*~ib~aAni [ the father of the flies ]: (M, TA:) and is especially applied to 'Abd-El-Melik Ibn-Marwán: (M, A, TA:) whence the saying, A^aboxaru mino A^abiY Al*~ubaAbi (A, TA) and A^abiY Al*~ib~aAni (TA) [ More stinking in breath than Abu-dh-Dhubáb and Abu-dh-Dhibbán ]. ― -b2- [Hence,] (tropical:) Evil, or mischief; (A, K;) and annoyance, or harm; as in the saying, A^aSaAbaniY *ubaAbN (tropical:) [ Evil, &c., befell me ]; (A;) and A^aSaAba fulaAnFA mino fulaAnK *ubaAbN laA*iEN (assumed tropical:) Evil, or mischief, [lit. a hurting fly ] fell upon such a one from such a one: (T:) or (tropical:) continual evil, as in the saying, A^aSaAbaka *ubaAbN mino h`*aA AlA^amori (tropical:) [ Continual evil hath befallen thee from this thing, or event ]; and $ar~uhaA *ubaAbN (tropical:) [ Her, or its, or their, evil is a continual evil ]. (TA.) ― -b3- (assumed tropical:) Ill luck. (T, K.) Fr relates that the Prophet saw a man with long hair; and said *ubaAbN , meaning (assumed tropical:) This is ill luck: and hence, ↓ rajulN *ubaAbiY~N (assumed tropical:) [ An unlucky man ]. (T.) ― -b4- (assumed tropical:) Plague, or pestilence. (TA.) ― -b5- (assumed tropical:) Diabolical possession; or madness, or insanity. (K.) ― -b6- (assumed tropical:) Ignorance: so in the phrase rajulN maHo$iY~N Al*~ubaAbi (assumed tropical:) [ A man stuffed with ignorance ]. (M.) ― -b7- (tropical:) The A_inosaAn [as meaning the pupil, or apple, ] of the eye: (AZ, T, S, M, A, K:) so in the saying, huwa A^aEaz~u EalaY~a mino *ubaAbi AlEayoni (tropical:) [ He is dearer to me than the apple of the eye ]: (A:) [ISd says,] I think it to be so termed as being likened to the *ubaAb [properly so called; i.e. the fly]. (M.) And Al*~ubaAbu also signifies (assumed tropical:) A black speck, or spot, in the interior of the Hadaqap [or dark part ] of the eye of the horse. (M, K.) The pl. is as above. (M.) ― -b8- *ubaAbu Als~ayofi (T, S, M, A, Msb, K) and ↓ *ubaAbapN Als~ayofi (TA) (tropical:) The Had~ , (M, K,) or Taraf , (S, Msb,) [each app. here meaning the point, or extremity, though the former also means the edge, ] of the sword, (S, M, Msb, K,) which is the part wherewith one strikes: (S, Msb:) or its extremity with which one is pierced, or transpierced; and the Had~ [here meaning edge] with which one strikes is called its giraAr : (En-Nadr, T:) or its tapering, or pointed, extremity; expl. by Tarafuhu AlmutaTar~ifu : (M, K:) or the point ( Had~ ) of its extremity (M, A) which is between its $aforataAni : (M:) the parts of its two edges that are on either side of it are its ZubataAni : the ridge in the middle of it, on the inner and outer sides, is called the Eayor ; and each has what are termed giraAraAni , which are the part between the Eayor and each one of the ZubataAni on the outer side of the sword and the corresponding portion of the inner side, each of the giraAraAni being on the inner side of the sword and its outer side. (AZ, T, TA.) [The swords of the Arabs, in the older times, were generally straight, twoedged, and tapering to a point; and so are many of them in the present day; a little wider towards the point than towards the hilt.] Hence the saying, vamarapu Als~awoTi yatobaEuhaA *ubaAbu Als~ayofi (tropical:) [ The knot, or tail, at the end of the whip is followed by the point of the sword; i. e., whipping (if it effect not the desired correction) is followed by slaughter]. (A.) ― -b9- [Hence,] *ubaAbN signifies likewise (assumed tropical:) The Had~ [or point, or extremity, or edge, ] of anything. (A 'Obeyd, T.) ― -b10- (tropical:) The pointed, or sharp, part of the extremity of the ear (A 'Obeyd, M, K) of a horse (A 'Obeyd, M) and of a man. (M.) ― -b11- (assumed tropical:) The sharp edge of the teeth of camels. (S, TA.) ― -b12- And (assumed tropical:) The part that first comes forth of the flower of the Hin~aA=' (M, K.)

definition: Driven away: (TA:) or driven away, or repelled, much.
sourceDefinition: Driven away: (TA:) or driven away, or repelled, much. (T, TA.) It is said in a trad., tazaw~ajo waA_il~aA faA^anota mina Almu*abo*abiyna , i. e. [ Marry, or thou wilt be of ] those driven away from the believers because thou hast not imitated them, and from the monks because thou hast forsaken their institutes: from Al*~ab~u “ the act of driving away: ” or, accord. to IAth, it may be from the signification of “ motion and agitation. ” (TA.) And it is said in the Kur [iv. 142], mu*abo*abiyna bayona *`lika , meaning Much driven away, or much repelled, from these and from those: (T, TA:) or this is an ex. of the meaning next following. (S, M.) ― -b2- A man (M, K) wavering, or vacillating, between two things, or affairs; (T, S, M, K;) or between two men, not attaching himself steadily to either; (T;) and ↓ mu*abo*ibN signifies the same; (K;) as also ↓ muta*abo*ibN . (M.)

(K.) garovaAnu faA@robukuwA lahu [He is hungry, therefore make ye rbykp for him ], (S, K,) or, as IDrd relates it, fiA@bokuluwA lahu [i. e., “ therefore mix ye bakaAlap (a certain food) for him ”], (TA,) is a prov.; (S, K;) the origin of which was this: (S:) a certain Arab of the desert, (S, K,) said in the O to be Ibn-Lisán-el-Hommarah, (TA,) came to his family, or wife, (S, K,) from a journey, (TA,) and was congratulated with the annunciation that a boy was born to him: whereupon he said, “ What shall I do with him? Shall I eat him or shall I drink him? ” so his wife said, garovaAnu faA@robukuwA lahu : and when he was satiated, he said, “ How are the infant and his mother? ” (S, K:) the saying means, “ he is hungry, therefore prepare ye for him food, that his hunger may be allayed, and then congratulate him with the annunciation of the birth of the child: ” and IDrd says that it is applied to the case of him whose anxiety has departed and who has become unoccupied so that he may attend to other things. (TA.) ― -b4- And rabaka fulaAnFA , (Lth, K,) inf. n. as above, (Lth, TA,) He threw such a one into mire. (Lth, K.) -A2- rabika : see 8.

sourceDefinition: A great [ bowl such as is termed ] jafonap : (S, A, * K:) this is said to be the primary signification: (Har p. 609:) pl. ruduHN . (S, A.) ― -b2- A widened tent; as also ↓ maroduwHN and ↓ murodaHN [of both which see the verbs]. (A.) ― -b3- A woman heavy in the hips, or haunches: (S, K:) or a woman large in the hips, or haunches, and the posteriors: (A:) or a woman large in the posteriors, heavy in the hips, or haunches, and perfect in make; as also ↓ raAdiHapN and ↓ raduwHN . (TA.) And A she-camel, (T, TA,) and a ram, (A, K,) large in the posteriors. (T, A, K, TA.) ― -b4- A camel heavily laden, (K, TA,) that will not be roused, or put in motion or action, and rise. (TA.) ― -b5- An army, or troop, ( katiybapN ,) marching heavily by reason of numbers, (S, K,) or dragging along the apparatus of war, heavily laden, (K,) great, (TA,) compact, with many horsemen. (A, TA.) ― -b6- A great, wide, spreading tree. (A, K.) ― -b7- [A place, or land,] abounding with herbage, or with the goods, conveniences, or comforts, of life; fruitful; or plentiful. (K.) ― -b8- EukuwmN radaAHN Loads balancing one another that are heavy, much stuffed with goods or utensils and furniture; as also ↓ ridaAHN : so in the Towsheeh &c. (TA.) ― -b9- fitonapN radaAHN (A, K) (tropical:) Heavy and great [ conflict and faction, or sedition, or discord, or the like ]: pl. ruduHN : whence, in a saying of 'Alee, A_in~a mino waraAy^ikumo A^umuwrFA mutamaAHilapF ruduHFA , (K,) meaning (tropical:) [ Verily behind you are events whereof the exposition would be long, ] great conflicts and factions, or seditions, &c.: (TA:) or, accord. to one relation, rud~aHFA , (K, TA,) pl. of ↓ raAdiHapN , and meaning heavy, scarcely departing: and accord. to another, ↓ fitanFA murodiHapF , meaning oppressing by their weight; or covering the hearts; from A^arodaHa Albayota [in the latter of the senses assigned to it above: see 1]. (TA.) ― -b10- radaAHN also means (tropical:) Darkness. (A, TA.)

(JK, S, A, Mgh, Msb.) You say, qaEada yaroqubu SaAHibahu He sat looking, watching, or waiting, for his com- panion; as also ↓ yarotaqibuhu . (A.) And ka*aA ↓ A^ataraq~abu I look, &c., or am looking, &c., for such a thing. (A.) And yaroqubu mawota SaAHibihi [ He looks, &c., for the death of his companion ], (JK, S, A, Mgh, Msb,) and A^abiyhi liyarivahu [ of his father, in order that he may inherit his property ]: (A:) and ↓ turaAqibu mawota baEolihaA [ She looks, &c., for the death of her husband ], (K, TA,) liyamuwta fatarivahu [ that he may die and she may inherit his property ]. You say, maA laka laA taroqubu *im~apa fulaAnK [ What aileth thee that thou wilt not regard the inviolable right or due, &c., of such a one? ]. (A. (K, TA. [See this word below.]) ― -b5- And you say, baAta yaroqubu Aln~ujuwma and ↓ yuraAqibuhaA , like yaroEaAhaA and yuraAEiyhaA (tropical:) [i. e. definition: The neck: or the base of the hinder part thereof: (A, K:) or the hinder part of the base of the neck: (JK, S:) or the upper part of the neck: (TA:) pl.
sourceDefinition: The neck: or the base of the hinder part thereof: (A, K:) or the hinder part of the base of the neck: (JK, S:) or the upper part of the neck: (TA:) pl. [of mult.] riqaAbN (JK, S, Msb, K) and [coll. gen. n.] ↓ raqabN (JK, S, K) and [pl. of pauc.] A^aroqubN (IAar, K) and raqabaAtN . (S, Msb, K.) ― -b2- By a synecdoche, it is applied to (tropical:) The whole person of a human being: as in the saying, *anobuhu fiY raqabatihi (tropical:) [ His sin, or crime, &c., be on his own neck; meaning, on himself ]. (IAth, TA.) [Hence also] one says, h`*aA AlA^amoru fiY riqaAbikumo (tropical:) [ This affair is upon your own selves ], and fiY raqabatika (tropical:) [ upon thine own self ]. (A.) And A^aEotaqa A@ll~`hu raqabatahu (tropical:) [ May God emancipate him ]. (A.) And laka riqaAbuhun~a wamaA Ealayohin~a , in a trad., relating to camels, (tropical:) They themselves, and the burdens that are upon them, are thine. (TA.) And [hence], in another trad., lanaA riqaAbu AlA^aroDi (tropical:) To us belongs the land itself. (TA.) ― -b3- Hence also, i. e. by a synecdoche, (IAth, Mgh, TA,) (tropical:) A slave, (S, IAth, Mgh, K, TA,) male and female: (IAth, TA:) and a captive: (TA:) pl. riqaAbN . (Mgh.) You say, A^aEotaqa raqabapF (tropical:) He emancipated a slave, male or female. (IAth, TA.) And fak~a raqabapF (tropical:) He released a slave, or a captive. (TA.) Alr~iqaAb in the Kur ix. 60 means (tropical:) Those slaves who have contracted with their owners for their freedom. (T, Mgh, Msb, TA.) ― -b4- riqaAbu AlmazaAwidi (tropical:) [lit. The necks of provision-bags ] is a nickname which was applied to the Eajam [or Persians, or foreigners in general]; because they were red; (S, A;) or because of the length of their necks; (El-Karáfee, TA in art. zwd ;) or rather because of the thickness thereof, as though they were full. (MF in that art.)

definition: One's giving to another person a possession, (K,) such as a house, and land, and the like, (TA,) on the condition that, whichever of them shall die, the property shall revert to his [ the giver's ]...
sourceDefinition: One's giving to another person a possession, (K,) such as a house, and land, and the like, (TA,) on the condition that, whichever of them shall die, the property shall revert to his [ the giver's ] heirs: (K:) so called because each of them looks for ( yaroqubu ) the death of the other: (TA:) or one's assigning it, (K,) namely, a dwelling, (TA,) to another person to inhabit, and, when he shall die, to another: (K:) or one's saying to a man, If thou die before me, my dwelling [or my land, which I give to thee, ] shall revert to me; and if I die before thee, it shall be thine: so called for the reason above mentioned. (JK, KT. *) [It also signifies The property so given. ] See 4, in three places. The act thus termed is forbidden in a trad., which pronounces that the property so given belongs to the giver's heirs. (JK.) Accord. to the Imám Aboo-Haneefeh, and [the Imám] Mohammad, it is not a hibap : accord. to Aboo-Yoosuf, it is a hibap like the EumoraY ; but none of the lawyers of El- 'Irák says so: the Málikees absolutely forbid it. (TA.) You say, daAriY laka ruqobaY [ My house is thine as a rqbY ]: from AlmuraAqabapu ; because each of the two persons looks for the death of the other. (A.)

definition: (tropical:) A woman (S, A) of whom no offspring lives, or remains, (S, A, K,) and who looks for the death of her offspring, or of her husband [app.
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) A woman (S, A) of whom no offspring lives, or remains, (S, A, K,) and who looks for the death of her offspring, or of her husband [app. that she may have offspring by another ]: (A:) and in like manner applied to a man: (S:) because he, or she, looks for the death of the child, in fear for it: (IAth, TA:) in like manner also a she-camel of which no offspring lives: (TA:) or he who has no offspring: (Msb:) or he who has not sent before him [ to Paradise, by its dying in infancy, ] any of his children: this, says A'Obeyd, is the meaning in the [classical] language of the Arabs; relating only to the loss of children: (TA:) he who has had no child die in infancy: or he who has had children and has died without sending before him any of them [ to Paradise, by its dying in infancy ]. (So in the explanations of two trads., each commencing with Alr~aquwbu , in the “ Jámi' es-Sagheer ” of EsSuyootee.) warivotuhu Eano Eam~apK raquwbi is a prov., expl. by Meyd as meaning [ I inherited it from a paternal aunt ] of whom no offspring was living: such, he says, is most compassionate to the son of her brother. (TA.) ― -b2- Also A woman who looks for the death of her husband, (S, K,) in order that she may inherit his property. (S.) ― -b3- And (assumed tropical:) An old and a poor man who is unable to earn for himself, and has none to earn for him: so called because he looks for a benefaction or gratuity. (Msb.) ― -b4- And (assumed tropical:) A she-camel that does not draw near to the wateringtrough, or tank, on account of the pressing, or crowding [ of the other camels to it ], (S, K,) by reason of her generous disposition: (S:) so called because she waits for the others to drink, and drinks when they have done. (TA.) ― -b5- A^um~u Alr~aquwbi (assumed tropical:) Calamity, or misfortune. (K.)

definition: , of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure faAEilN , (TA,) A looker, watcher, or waiter, in expectation [of a person or thing]: (S, Msb, K:) pl.
sourceDefinition: , of the measure faEiylN in the sense of the measure faAEilN , (TA,) A looker, watcher, or waiter, in expectation [of a person or thing]: (S, Msb, K:) pl. ruqabaA='u . (Msb.) ― -b2- A guarder, guardian, keeper, or preserver: (JK, S, A, Msb, K:) a guard of a people; one stationed on an elevated place to keep watch: (TA:) a spy, or scout, of an army: (A, TA:) a watcher, or an observer. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] Alr~qiybu is an appel-lation applied to God; (A, K, TA;) meaning The Guardian, Keeper, Watcher, or Observer, from whom nothing is hidden. (TA.) ― -b4- Also The A^amiyn of the players at the game called Almayosir ; (JK, K;) or (K) he who is intrusted with the supervision of the Dariyb [or shuffler of the arrows ]: (JK, S, K:) or the man who stands behind the HuroDap [q. v.] in the game above mentioned: the meanings of all these explanations are [said to be] the same: pl. as above. (TA.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) The third of the arrows used in the game above mentioned: (T, S, K:) it is one of the seven arrows to which lots, or portions, appertain: (TA:) by some it is called AlD~ariybu : (Lh, L in art. Drb :) the arrows are ten in number: the first is Alfa*~u , which has one notch and one portion; the second, Alt~awo'amu , which has two notches and two portions; the third, Alr~aqiybu , which has three notches and three portions; the fourth, AlHilosu or AlHalisu , which has four notches [and four portions]; the fifth, Aln~aAfisu , which has five notches [and five portions]; the sixth, Almusobilu , which has six notches [and six portions]; and the seventh, AlmuEal~aY , the highest of all, which has seven notches and seven portions: those to which no portions appertain are Als~afiyHu and AlmaniyHu and Alwagodu . (TA.) A poet says, A_i*aA qasama AlhawaY A^aEo$aAra qalobiY fasahomaAki AlmuEal~aY waAlr~aqiybu [ When love divides the tenths of my heart, thy two arrows will be the mo'allà and the rakeeb ]: by the sahomaAni , [which properly signifies two arrows, and hence (assumed tropical:) two portions gained by two gaming-arrows, and then (assumed tropical:) any two portions, ] he means her eyes: and as the mEl~Y has seven portions and the rqyb has three, the shmAn would gain the whole of his heart. (TA. [See also a verse cited voce Eu$orN .]) ― -b6- raqiybu Aln~ajomi signifies (tropical:) The star, or asterism, that sets with the rising of that [ other ] star, or asterism: for example, the rqyb of Alv~uray~aA is AlA_ikoliylu : [and the former is the rqyb of the latter:] when the latter rises at nightfall, the former sets: (S, TA:) or raqiybN signifies the star, or asterism, which [ as it were ] watches, ( yuraAqibu ,) in the east, the star, or asterism, setting in the west: or any one of the Mansions of the Moon is the rqyb of another: (K, TA:) whenever any one of them rises, another [of them] sets: (TA: [see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl ; and see also nawo'N :]) and Alr~aqiybu is (assumed tropical:) a [ certain ] star, or asterism, of the stars, or asterisms, [ that were believed to be the givers ] of rain, that [ as it were ] watches another star, or asterism: (K:) [it was app. applied to AlA_ikoliylu , as being the rqyb of the most noted and most welcome of all the Mansions of the Moon, namely, Alv~uray~aA : see nawo'N .] The raqiyb of Alv~uray~aA is [also] an appellation applied to Ald~abaraAnu (assumed tropical:) [i. e. The Hyades; or the five chief stars of the Hyades; or the brightest star among them, α of Taurus ]; because a follower thereof: (A:) [and] AlEay~uwqu (assumed tropical:) [i. e. Capella ] is so called as being likened to the rqyb of the game called Almayosir . (TA.) [Hence,] one says, laAA=tiyka A^awo yaloqaY Alv~uray~aA raqiybuhaA (tropical:) [ I will not come to thee unless their rqyb meet the Pleiades ]. (A.) ― -b7- raqiybN also signifies (tropical:) A man's successor, (A, K,) of his offspring, and of his Ea$iyrap [i. e. kinsfolk, or nearer or nearest relations by descent from the same ancestor, &c.]. (K.) So in the saying, niEoma Alr~aqiybu A^anota liA^abiyka wasalafika (tropical:) [ Excellent, or most excellent, is the successor; such art thou to thy father and thine ancestors ]: because the successor is like Ald~abaraAn to Alv~uray~aA . (A.) ― -b8- And (assumed tropical:) The son of a paternal uncle. (K.) [App. because two male cousins by the father's side are often rivals, and watchers of each other; the son of a girl's paternal uncle being commonly preferred as her husband.] ― -b9- Also (assumed tropical:) A species of serpent: as though it watched by reason of hatred: (TA:) or a certain malignant serpent: pl. raqiybaAtN and ruqubN . (T, K.)

A poet says, A_i*aA qasama AlhawaY A^aEo$aAra qalobiY fasahomaAki AlmuEal~aY waAlr~aqiybu [ When love divides the tenths of my heart, thy two arrows will be the mo'allà and the rakeeb ]: by the sahomaAni , [which properly signifies two arrows, and hence (assumed tropical:) two portions gained by two gaming-arrows, and then (assumed tropical:) any two portions, ] he means her eyes: and as the mEl~Y has seven portions and the rqyb has three, the shmAn would gain the whole of his heart. (TA. [See also a verse cited voce Eu$orN .]) ― -b6- raqiybu Aln~ajomi signifies (tropical:) The star, or asterism, that sets with the rising of that [ other ] star, or asterism: for example, the rqyb of Alv~uray~aA is AlA_ikoliylu : [and the former is the rqyb of the latter:] when the latter rises at nightfall, the former sets: (S, TA:) or raqiybN signifies the star, or asterism, which [ as it were ] watches, ( yuraAqibu ,) in the east, the star, or asterism, setting in the west: or any one of the Mansions of the Moon is the rqyb of another: (K, TA:) whenever any one of them rises, another [of them] sets: (TA: [see manaAzilu Alqamari , in art. nzl ; and see also nawo'N :]) and Alr~aqiybu is (assumed tropical:) a [ certain ] star, or asterism, of the stars, or asterisms, [ that were believed to be the givers ] of rain, that [ as it were ] watches another star, or asterism: (K:) [it was app. applied to AlA_ikoliylu , as being the rqyb of the most noted and most welcome of all the Mansions of the Moon, namely, Alv~uray~aA : see nawo'N .] The raqiyb of Alv~uray~aA is [also] an appellation applied to Ald~abaraAnu (assumed tropical:) [i. e. The Hyades; or the five chief stars of the Hyades; or the brightest star among them, α of Taurus ]; because a follower thereof: (A:) [and] AlEay~uwqu (assumed tropical:) [i. e. Capella ] is so called as being likened to the rqyb of the game called Almayosir . (TA.) [Hence,] one says, laAA=tiyka A^awo yaloqaY Alv~uray~aA raqiybuhaA (tropical:) [ I will not come to thee unless their rqyb meet the Pleiades ]. (A.) ― -b7- raqiybN also signifies (tropical:) A man's successor, (A, K,) of his offspring, and of his Ea$iyrap [i. e. kinsfolk, or nearer or nearest relations by descent from the same ancestor, &c.]. (K.) So in the saying, niEoma Alr~aqiybu A^anota liA^abiyka wasalafika (tropical:) [ Excellent, or most excellent, is the successor; such art thou to thy father and thine ancestors ]: because the successor is like Ald~abaraAn to Alv~uray~aA . (A.) ― -b8- And (assumed tropical:) The son of a paternal uncle. (K.) [App. because two male cousins by the father's side are often rivals, and watchers of each other; the son of a girl's paternal uncle being commonly preferred as her husband.] ― -b9- Also (assumed tropical:) A species of serpent: as though it watched by reason of hatred: (TA:) or a certain malignant serpent: pl. raqiybaAtN and ruqubN . (T, K.)

definition: , (S, M, Mgh, Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, Mgh, Msb,) aor. (M, Mgh, Msb) and , (M, Msb,) inf. n. ramosN , (A, Msb, K,) He buried him, or it; (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K;) namely, a dead person; a corpse: (S, Mgh, Msb:) this is [said to be] the primary signification: (A:) as also ↓ Armshu : (S, Msb:) or he buried him, and made the earth even over him. (TA.) It is said in a trad. of Zeyd Ibn-Soohán, vum~a A@romusuwniY Then do ye bury me: or it may mean, conceal my grave, and make it even with the ground. (Mgh.) ― -b2- He poured, (M,) or scattered, (A,) dust, or earth, upon it; (M, A;) namely, anything. (M.) You say also, ramasahu biAlt~uraAbi [in this sense]. (A.) And ramasonaAhu biAlt~urobi We filled it up with dust, or earth. (M.) And it is said in a trad. of Ibn-Maakil, AuromusuwA qaboriY , meaning Make ye my grave even with the ground; not gibbous, or elevated. (TA.) ― -b3- He concealed, and covered, him, or it: this is [also said to be] the primary signification. (TA.) You say, ramasa Al$~aYo'a , aor. , inf. n. ramosN , He, or it, effaced, or obliterated, the traces, or remains, of the thing. (M.) And Alr~iyHu taromusu AlA=vaAra bimaA tuviyruhu [ The wind effaces the traces, or remains, by what it raises, of dust or sand &c.]. (A.) And ramasuwA qabora fulaAnK They concealed the grave of such a one, and made it even with the ground. (S.) And ramasotu Alxabara , (K, * Msb,) and AlHadiyva , (TA,) I concealed the news, or information, (K, * Msb,) and the story. (TA.) And ramasotu Ealayohi Alxabara , (S, M,) and AlA^amora , (As A,) I concealed from him the news, or information, (S, M,) and the affair. (As, A.) ― -b4- rumisa Hub~uka fiY qalobiY The love of thee hath become vehement, and firmly settled, [ as though buried, ] in my heart. (A, TA.) -A2- ramasotuhu biHajarK , (S,) inf. n. ramosN , (K,) I cast a stone at him. (Ibn- 'Abbád, S, K. *)

definition: A kind of [ plant, or] tree, (T, * S, M, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: A kind of [ plant, or] tree, (T, * S, M, K, &c.,) that grows in plain, or soft, land, (T, M, TA,) having a white fruit: or, as some say, a kind of dust-coloured tree, having a red fruit: (M, TA:) n. un. raA='apN : (T, S, M, K:) and dim. ↓ ruwayoy^apN : (M, TA:) AHn says that the rA='p is not taller nor broader than a sitting man: and accord. to one of the Arabs of the desert of 'Omán, it is a tree that rises on a stem, and then there branch forth [so in the M, but accord. to the TA, rise, ] from it round, rough leaves: others, he adds, say that it is a small tree of the mountains, resembling an EZlmp [q. v.], having a soft white flower like cotton: (M, TA: [but in the latter, the word rendered “ soft ” is omitted:]) some say that it is a species of the kind of tree called TaloH [ acacia, or mimosa, gummifera ], and is the tree that grew at the cave in which were the Prophet and Aboo-Bekr: so say Suh and others: it is, they say, of the height of a man, and has white flowers, resembling cotton, with which cushions are stuffed, like feathers in lightness and softness: it is said by IHsh to be the same [ tree ] that is called A^um~u gayolaAn [see art. gyl ]; but they have found fault with him. [for so saying]: it is not the Eu$ar [ asclepias gigantea ], as one author has supposed; but a tree resembling this: (MF, TA:) such is the truth: the rA=' is not the E$r : I have seen them both [says SM] in El-Yemen; and with the fruit of each of them cushions and pillows are stuffed: but the fruit of the E$r commences small; then increases to the size of the bA*njAnp [or fruit of the egg-plant, and much larger, like a bladder]; and then breaks open, disclosing what is like cotton: and the fruit of the rA=' is not thus: the E$r [he adds] is not found in Egypt; but it and the rA=' are peculiar to El- Hijáz and the neighbouring parts; [in saying this, however, he errs; for I have seen the E$r in abundance in the deserts of the upper part of the Sa'eed;] and the saddles of camels &c. are stuffed with the fruit of the rA=' in El-Hijáz. (TA.) ― -b2- Also The foam of the sea. (AHeyth, K.) -A2- And One of the letters of the alphabet. (TA.) [See the letter r .] -A3- See also art. ryA^ .

sourceDefinition: , (T, S, M, &c.,) aor. yariybu , (M, Mgh, Msb, K,) inf. n. rayobN (T, M, Mgh, Msb, &c.) and riybapN , (M, K,) or the latter is a simple subst., (S, Msb,) It (a thing) occasioned in me disquiet, disturbance, or agitation, of mind: (Ksh and Bd in ii. 1:) [this is the primary signification; (see riybapN ;) a signification also borne by ↓ A^araAbaniY ; (see the verses of Khálid cited in this paragraph;) whence the other significations here expl. in what follows:] it (a thing) made me to doubt: (Msb: and in like manner raAbahu is expl. in the Mgh:) or it (a thing, M) caused me to have what is termed riybap [i. e. doubt, or suspicion or evil opinion, or doubt combined with suspicion or evil opinion ]; as also ↓ A^araAbaniY : (M, K: in both of which this meaning is indicated, but not expressed:) but the latter is said by Lth to be bad: (T:) or, (T, M, Msb,) accord. to AZ, (T, Msb,) the former signifies he, (T, M, *) or it, i. e. his case, (M, * Msb,) made me to know that there was on his part what is termed riybap [i. e. something occasioning doubt, or suspicion or evil opinion, or doubt combined with suspicion or evil opinion ]; (T, M, Msb;) made me to be certain, or sure, of it: (Msb:) and ↓ the latter signifies made me to think that there was in him what is so termed; (Sb, T, M, Msb, K;) without my being certain, or sure, of it: (Msb:) [Az says that] these are the right explanations of the two phrases: (T:) [or] the latter signifies also jaEala fiY~a Alr~iyabapa [ he put into me, i. e. into my mind, doubt, or suspicion &c.]; (Sb, M, K; and in a similar manner A^arabotuhu is expl. in the latter;) or A^awohamaniY Alr~iybapa [ he made me to think that which occasioned doubt, or suspicion &c.]: (K: and in like manner ArAbhu is expl. in the Ham p. 363:) and ribotuhu signifies A^awoSalotu A_ilayohi Alr~iybapa [ I made doubt, or suspicion &c., or that which occasioned doubt, or suspicion &c., to come to him, or to reach him ]; (K;) [app. by some act; for it is said that] raAbahu signifies A^ataAhu biriybapK [ he did to him a thing that occasioned doubt, or suspicion &c.]: (Ham ubi suprà:) or, (K,) accord. to Lh, the Arabs say, (M,) raAbaniY A^amoruhu , aor. yariybuniY , inf. n. rayobN and riybapN : when they speak allusively [with respect to the cause of doubt &c., not expressing it,] ( A_i*aA kanawoA [misinterpreted in the TA as meaning “ when they affix a pronoun to the verb, ” for the meaning here intended is clearly shown by what follows,]) they prefix A [to the verb, saying ↓ A^araAba , and A^arabotu , &c., expl. in the latter part of this paragraph]; and when they do not speak allusively [with respect to the cause of doubt &c., but express it,] ( A_i*aA lamo yakonuwA ) they reject that letter; but [so accord. to the M, but in the K “ or, ”] it is allowable to say, AlA^amoru ↓ A^araAbaniY ; sourceDefinition: Of the colour termed zuroqap [q. v.]; (Msb, TA;) and ↓ A^azoraqiY~N signifies the same: (TA:) an epithet applied to a man, signifying having what is termed zuroqap of the eye: (S:) blue, (KL,) [whether light or dark or of a middling tint, but generally the first;] sky-coloured, or azure; (TK;) blue-eyed; (MA, KL;) gray-eyed; (MA;) [or having a greenish hue in the eye: &c.: (see zuroqapN :)] fem. zaroqA='u : (S, Msb:) pl. zuroqN . (Msb.) [In the present day it is often improperly used as meaning Black: and is applied to a horse, an ass, a mule, a bird, and any animal, and sometimes to other things, as meaning gray, or ash-coloured. ] ― -b2- [And Blind; properly by reason of a bluish, or grayish, opacity of the crystalline lens; i. e., by what is commonly termed a cataract in the eye. ] wanaHo$uru A@lomujorimiyna yawomay^i*K zuroqFA , in the Kur [xx. 102], means [ And we will congregate, or raise to life, on that day, the sinners, or unbelievers, ] blind; (Bd, K, * TA;) because the black of the eye of the blind becomes blue, or gray: (Bd:) Zj says that they will come forth from their graves seeing, as they were created at the first, and will become blind when congregated: (TA:) or the meaning is, thirsty: (Th, TA:) or with their eyes become blue, or gray, by reason of intense thirst: (ISd, TA:) or blue-eyed, or gray-eyed, ( zuroqa AlEuyuwni ,) because Alz~uroqapu is the worst of the colours of the eye, and the most hateful thereof to the Arabs, for the Greeks were their greatest enemies, and are zuroq . (Bd.) ― -b3- Applied to the iron head or blade of an arrow &c., Very clear or bright: (ISk, S, K:) and zuroqN [used as a subst.] means spearheads (S, K) or the like; (K;) because of their colour; (S, TA;) or because of their clearness, or brightness; (TA;) or polished iron heads or blades of arrows &c. (Ham p. 313.) And Clear water: (IAar, S, Msb:) pl. as above. (TA.) ― -b4- Hence, AlEaduw~u AlA^azoraqu The sheer enemy: or [ the fierce enemy; ] the enemy that is vehement in hostility; because zuroqap of the eyes is predominant in the Greeks and the Deylem, between whom and the Arabs is a confirmed enmity. (Har p. 148.) ― -b5- AlA^azoraqu The baAziY [i. e. hawk, or falcon: because of his colour]: pl. as above. (TA. [See also zur~aqN .]) ― -b6- And The leopard. (TA.) ― -b7- Alz~aroqaA='u Wine: (K:) [app. because of its clearness:] so says AA. (TA.) ― -b8- And the name of A horse of Náfi' Ibn-'Abd-El-'Ozzà. (Ibn-'Abbád, K.)

sourceDefinition: and Alz~inoju , (AA, S, Msb, K,) the latter being a dial. var. of the former, (Msb,) both of them chaste, (TA,) [but the latter is the more common,] and ↓ Alz~unuwju (S, K) and ↓ Almazonajapu , (K,) A certain nation of the blacks; (S, Msb, K;) [ the inhabitants of the country called by us “ Zanguebar, ” including the “ Zingis ” of Ptolemy, near the entrance of the Red Sea, and a large portion of inner Africa: ] their country is beneath, and to the south of, the equinoctial line; and beyond them is [ said to be ] no habitation, or cultivation: [sometimes applied to the Negroes absolutely; for] some say that their country extends from the western parts of Africa nearly to Abyssinia, [ comprehending the whole of Nigritia properly so called, or at least the whole of the countries of the Negroes known to the Arabs of the classical ages, ] and that part of it is on the Nile of Egypt: (Msb:) the n. un. is ↓ zanojiY~N and zinojiY~N , (AA, A'Obeyd, ISk, S, K,) like as ruwmiY~N is of ruwmN : (TA:) and ↓ A^azonujN occurs as a broken pl., meaning the divisions and subtribes [ of that nation ]: so says AAF, and so in the M. (TA.)

definition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and Eanohu , (S, Mgh, Msb,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) and Eanohu , (S, Mgh, Msb,) aor. ; (S, K;) [the most usual form of the verb;] and zahada , aor. ; (S, Msb, K;) which is the most approved form, though MF says otherwise; (TA;) and zahuda , aor. ; (Th, K;) inf. n. zuhodN and zahaAdapN (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and zahodN ; (Sb, TA;) He abstained from it; [meaning, from something that would gratify the passions or senses;] relinquished it; forsook it; shunned, or avoided, it; did not desire it; (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K;) contr. of ragiba [i. e. of ragiba fiyhi ], (S, K,) and i. q. ragiba Eanohu , (A, Mgh,) and lamo yuridohu , (Mgh,) and tarakahu and A^aEoraDa Eanohu : (Msb:) or he abstained from it, meaning a thing of the lawfulness of which he was sure, so far as to take the least that was sufficient thereof, leaving the rest to God: (MF:) or zahaAdapN relates only to worldly things; and zuhodN , to matters of religion: (Kh, Msb, K:) or both signify the exercising oneself in the service of God, or in acts of devotion; as also ↓ tazah~udN : (KL:) he who makes a difference between zahida fiyhi and zahida Eanohu errs. (Mgh.) ― -b2- zahaAdapN and zuhodN also signify [particularly The being abstinent in respect of eating; ] the eating little. (A, TA.) ― -b3- And zahada and ↓ Azhd He straitened his household, by reason of niggardliness or poverty. (TA in art. znq .) -A2- zahadahu , aor. , (K,) inf. n. zahodN , (TA,) (tropical:) He computed, or determined, its quantity, measure, size, bulk, proportion, extent, amount, sum, or number; or he computed by conjecture its quantity or measure &c., or the quantity of its fruit; as also ↓ Azhdhu , (K, TA,) inf. n. A_izohaAdN ; and ↓ zh~dhu , inf. n. tazohiydN : all used in relation to palm-trees. (TA.) You say, zahadotu Aln~axolu , aor. and inf. n. as above, (tropical:) I computed by conjecture the quantity of the fruit upon the palm-trees. (Esh-Sheybánee, S, TA.) And zahadotu AlmaAla (assumed tropical:) I computed by conjecture the quantity, or amount, of the property; or the number of the camels or cattle. (JK.)

definition: [and Eanohu ] He made him, or caused him, to abstain from it;
sourceDefinition: [and Eanohu ] He made him, or caused him, to abstain from it; to relinquish it; to forsake it; to shun, or avoid, it; or to be not desirous of it; (L, Msb;) i. q. zag~abahu Eanohu ; (L;) trans. of zahida fiyhi : (Msb:) [i. e.] Alt~azohiydu fiY Al$~aYo'i and Eanohu is the contr. of Alt~arogiybu fiyhi . (Bd.)

definition: A grandchild; (S, Msb, K;) a son's child, and a daughter's child: (M, TA:) pl. A^asobaATN ; (S, Msb, TA;) which is commonly used by the vulgar as signifying daughters' children; distinguished by them...
sourceDefinition: A grandchild; (S, Msb, K;) a son's child, and a daughter's child: (M, TA:) pl. A^asobaATN ; (S, Msb, TA;) which is commonly used by the vulgar as signifying daughters' children; distinguished by them from A^aHofaAdN [which they apply to son's children, pl. of HafiydN ]; but the leading lexicologists expressly declare that it includes sons' children and daughters' children, as it is said to do by ISd: IAar explained siboTN and siboTaAni and A^asobaATN as signifying the particularly distinguished, and choicest, of children. (TA.) It is said in a trad., (TA,) AlHasanu waAlHusayonu siboTaA rasuwli A@ll~`hi El-Hasan, and El-Hoseyn are the two grandsons of the Apostle of God. (M, TA. *) ― -b2- A tribe of the Jews: pl. A^asobaATN : (M, Msb, K:) siboTN (M) and A^asobaATN (S, Msb) in relation to the Jews, (M, Msb,) or [rather] the Children of Israel, (S,) being like qabiylapN (M) and qabaAy^ilu (S, Msb) in relation to the Arabs: (S, M, Msb:) and the former are thus called to distinguish them from the children of Ishmael. (M, TA.) In the phrase, waqaT~aEonaAhumu A@vonataYo Ea$orapa A^asobaATFA [ And we divided them into twelve divisions, tribes ], (S, M, K,) in the Kur [vii. 160], (S, M,) AsbATA is a substitute (S, M, K) for AvntY E$rp , (S, M,) not a specificative, (S, M, K,) because the specificative may only be a sing.; (S, M;) the meaning being wqT~EnAhm AvntY E$rp firoqapF AsbATFA , (Akh, Zj, S,) and therefore the numeral is fem.; (Akh, S;) or this is a mistake; for it should be firaqFA AvntY E$rp ; and therefore the numeral is fem. (Abu-l-'Abbás, TA.) Accord. to Ktr, you say, h`*aA siboTN and h`*ihi siboTN , and h`w^ulaA='i siboTN and using sbT as a pl., meaning firoqapN . (TA.) The saying kaA^an~ahu siboTN mina AlA^asobaATi is [asserted to be] a mistake, inasmuch as its author imagined that siboTN meant a man: (M:) IDrd ascribes it to El-'Ajjáj or Ru-beh: it occurs in an A^urojuwzap by the latter. (Sgh, TA.) [But it is applied to a single man: for] it is said in a trad., (TA,) HusayonN siboTN mina AlA^asobaATi , i. e. Hoseyn is [as though he were] a nation of the nations ( A^um~apN mina AlA^umami K) in goodness; so expl. by Aboo-Bekr: (TA:) or one of the fathers of tribes; because of the multitude of his descendants: or one of the sons of daughters. (So in a marginal note in a copy of the “ Jámi' es-Sagheer ” of Es-Suyootee.) ― -b3- Also A generation ( qaron ) that comes after another. (Zj, TA.) -A2- And siboTN riboEiy~apN , (TA in the present art. and in art. rbE ,) or riboEiy~apN ↓ sabaTN , (so accord. to a copy of the M, in the present art.,) A palmtree of which the fruit ripens in the end of the summer, or hot-season. (M, TA.)

definition: and ↓ saboTN and ↓ sabaTN , (the first and third of these in one copy of the S, and the second alone in another copy of the S, and all in the M and Msb and K,) the first of the dial.
sourceDefinition: and ↓ saboTN and ↓ sabaTN , (the first and third of these in one copy of the S, and the second alone in another copy of the S, and all in the M and Msb and K,) the first of the dial. of El- Hijáz, (TA,) from sabiTa , and the second from sabuTa , the last being an inf. n. used as an epithet, (Msb,) Lank, not crisp; (S, M, * Msb, K; *) applied to hair: (S, Msb:) pl. sibaATN , which is said by Sb to be of the measure most common for a pl. of an epithet of the measure faEalN , (M,) or faEolN . (TA.) ― -b2- sabiTu Al$~aEari , (S, M,) and ↓ saboTuhu , (M,) A man having lank hair: (S, M:) and in like manner sibaATN , alone, applied to a number of persons. (TA.) ↓ saboTN is also metonymically applied to (tropical:) A foreigner, like as [its contr.] jaEodN is to an Arab. (TA.) ― -b3- sabiTN also signifies Tall; (M, K;) applied to a man: (M:) or, as also ↓ saboTN , (TA,) or sabiTu Aljisomi , (M,) so applied, long in the [ bones called ] A^alowaAH [pl. of lawoH ], (M, TA,] and even therein: (TA:) or sabiTu Aljisomi or ↓ saboTuhu , (accord. to different copies of the K,) or both, (S, TA,) goodly in stature, or person, or proportion, (S, K,) and evenness. (S.) Also Having extended limbs, and perfect in make. (TA.) And sabiTu AlqaSabi , and ↓ saboTuhaA , A man [ long and even, or] extended, and without protuberances, in the bones of the fore arms and the shanks. (TA.) And sabiTu AlbanaAni and ↓ saboTuhaA , (tropical:) Long in the fingers. (TA.) And sabiTu Alxaloqi A man lank in make: (L in art. rd :) and sabiTapu Alxaloqi , and ↓ saboTatuhu , (tropical:) a woman lank, or soft, or tender, in make. (M, Z, TA.) And sabiTu Als~aAqayoni A man soft, or flaccid, or uncompact, in the shanks. (Ham p. 238.) ― -b4- Alyadayoni ↓ saboTu , (M, K, TA,) and sabiTuhumaA , (TA, and so in the CK,) and sabiTu Alkaf~ayoni , (TA,) (tropical:) A man who is liberal, bountiful, or munificent. (M, K, TA.) And sabiTN biAlomaEoruwfi (tropical:) A man easy, or facile, in beneficence. (M, TA.) ― -b5- maTarN sabiTN , (Sh, TA,) and ↓ saboTN , (Sh, K,) (tropical:) Rain pouring abundantly and extensively, (Sh, K,) and consecutively. (Sh, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. sajoEN , He pursued an even, uniform course; he pursued an even course, following one order: this is the primary signification. (TA.) [It seems to be properly intrans.; but is sometimes used as a trans. verb, li or A_ilaY being perhaps understood; as in the following phrase;] sajaEa *`lika AlmasojaEa He pursued, or aimed at, that object of pursuit or aim; (K, TA;) occurring in a trad. (TA.) ― -b2- And It was even and uniform, one part thereof being like another. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence,] sajaEati AlHamaAmapu , (IDrd, S, Msb, K,) aor. , (Msb, K,) inf. n. sajoEN , (Mbr, TA,) and quasi-inf. n. ↓ sijoEN , (TA,) The pigeon continued its cry uninterruptedly in one uniform way or manner; or called, and prolonged its voice or cry, modulating it sweetly: (Mbr, in the “ Kámil; ” and TA:) or cooed: or reiterated its voice or cry: syn. hadarato : (S, Msb:) and Saw~atato : (Msb:) or rad~adato SawotahaA . (IDrd, K.) It is said in a prov., laA A=tayka maA sajaEa AlHamaAmu [ I will not come to thee as long as the pigeon cooes; ] meaning I will never come to thee. (Lh.) ― -b4- You say also, sajaEati Aln~aAqapu , (S, TA,) inf. n. sajoEN , (TA,) The she-camel prolonged her yearning cry in one uniform manner. (S, TA.) ― -b5- And sajaEati Alqawosu (tropical:) The bow prolonged its twang in one uniform manner, monotonously. (TA.) ― -b6- And hence by way of comparison to the sajoE of the pigeon, sajaEa kalaAmahu (tropical:) He (a man) made his speech, or language, [ to be rhyming prose, i. e.,] to have fawaASil like the rhymes of verse, without its being measured. (Msb.) And sajaEa [alone], (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. sajoEN ; (S, TA;) and ↓ sj~E , inf. n. tasojiyEN ; (S, TA;) (tropical:) He (a man, S) spoke, or uttered, [or composed, ] (S, * K, TA,) rhyming speech or language, (S,) [i. e., rhyming prose, i. e.,] speech, or language, having fawaASil (K, TA) like the fawaASil of verse, without measure: as is said in a description of Sijistán, watamoruhaA wa liS~uhaA baTalo maAw^uhaA wa$alo wa A_ino qal~uwA DaAEuwA A_ino kavura Aljayo$u bihaA jaAEuwA daqalo [Its water is such as scantily distils, in interrupted drops, from mountains or rocks, and its robber is a man of courage, and its dates are of the worst kind: if the army be numerous in it, they hunger; and if they be few, they perish]: so says Lth. (TA.) You say also, sajaEa biAl$~aYo'i , meaning (tropical:) He uttered the thing in the manner above described. (TA.) [See also sajoEN , below.]

so called as being likened to the sajoE of the pigeon; (Msb;) or because of its uniformity, (TA,) and the mutual resemblance and agreement of the words which end its clauses: (IJ, TA:) or a consecution [ of clauses ] of speech or language, with one rawiY~ [which is the principal, or only, rhyme-letter ]: (Jm, K:*) or it consists in the agreement of the endings of words [or clauses ], in a certain order, like the agreement of the rhymes ( qawaAfK ) [ of verses ]: (Mbr, in the “ Kámil; ” TA:) each clause ends with a quiescent letter; and consists of at least two words: (Kull p. 208:) [see an ex. in the first paragraph of this art.:] you say also ↓ kalaAmN musaj~aEN (S) and ↓ kalaAmN masojuwEN , meaning the same as sajoEN : (TA:) the pl. of sajoEN is A^asojaAEN (S, K) and , accord. to IJ, sujuwEN , but ISd says, I know not whether he have related this from another or coined it, (TA,) and A^asaAjiyEu , (S,) or this last is pl. of ↓ A^usojuwEapN (K) [and is also a pl. pl., i. e. pl. of A^asojaAEN , like as A^azaAhiyru is pl. of A^azohaArN which is pl. of zahorN , and many similar instances might be added, such instances being numerous app. because A^afoEaAlN is properly a measure of a pl. of paucity]. (TA.) He is also related to have said, A_iy~aAkumo wa sajoEa Alkuh~aAni (tropical:) [ Avoid ye the rhyming prose of the diviners, or soothsayers ]. (TA.) One says also, ↓ bayonahumo A^usojuwEapN [ Between them is a discourse, or colloquy, oral or written, in rhyming prose ]. (S.)

definition: Pursuing [ an even, uniform, course, or] a direct, or right, course, (AZ, S, K, TA,) in going, or journeying, (AZ, S, TA,) [and] (tropical:) in speech, &c.
sourceDefinition: Pursuing [ an even, uniform, course, or] a direct, or right, course, (AZ, S, K, TA,) in going, or journeying, (AZ, S, TA,) [and] (tropical:) in speech, &c. (K, TA.) Dhu-r-Rummeh says, qaTaEotu bihaA A^aroDFA taraY wajoha rakobihaA A_i*aA maA EalawohaA mukofaA^F gayora saAjiEi i. e. [ I traversed, or have traversed, with her a land in which thou wouldst see the face of every one of the company of travellers riding over it, when they get upon it, ] jaAy^irFA gayora qaASidK [ turning aside from the right course, (or rather turned aside, unless, which is not improbable, the right reading be mukofiy^FA ,) not direct ], (AZ, S, TA,) or not direct towards one point: (TA:) but in the O we find, as on the authority of AZ, gayora saAjiEi gyr jaAy^irK Eani AlqaSodi [which is evidenily a mistranscription; the right reading being gayora saAjiEi A^aYo jaAy^irFA Eani AlqaSodi , or the like]. (TA.) ― -b2- [Hence,] A face justly proportioned; [ symmetrical; ] well, or beautifully, formed. (K.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] HamaAmapN saAjiEapN , and ↓ sajuwEN , (K,) without p , (TA,) [ A pigeon continuing its cry uninterruptedly in one uniform way or manner; or calling, and prolonging its voice or cry, modulating it sweetly: or cooing: (see 1:) or] reiterating its voice or cry: pl. [of the former or of both] suj~aEN and [of the former] sawaAjiEu . (K.) ― -b4- And naAqapN saAjiEN A she-camel prolonging her yearning cry in one uniform manner: (TA:) or quavering, and prolonging her voice, [in the copies of the K muToribap , but correctly muTar~ibap ,] in her yearning cry: (K:) or tall; (AA, K;) but Az says, I have not heard this on any authority beside that of AA. (TA.) ― -b5- [And hence,] saAjiEN also signifies (tropical:) [ A rhyming-proser, or rhyming-prosaist; ] one who speaks, or utters, [or composes, ] sajoE : and in like manner, [↓ saj~aAEN (mentioned by Golius, and by Freytag as on the authority of the K, in no copy of which do I find it,) meaning one who speaks, or utters, or composes, sajoE much: and] ↓ saj~aAEapN [meaning one who does so very much: the three epithets being similar to raAjizN and raj~aAzN and raj~aAzapN ]. (K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (M,) or biyadihi , (K,) [aor. yasoduw ,] inf. n. sadowN , (S, M, K,) He stretched forth (S, M, K) his arms or hands, or, as when said of a camel, his fore legs, (M,) or his arm or hand, or his fore leg, (S, K, TA,) A_ilayohi [ towards him or it ], (CK,) or naHowa Al$~aYo'i [ towards the thing ], like as do camels ( kamaA tasoduw AlA_ibilu ) in their going along; (TA;) as also ↓ AstdY , (M, K, TA,) in [some of] the copies of the K AsdY , but the former is the right. (TA.) You say of a man, sadaA , aor. yasoduw , He stretched forth his arm, or hand, towards a thing: and of a camel, sadaA , inf. n. sadowN , he stretched forth his fore leg in going along: (Msb:) or of a she-camel, sadato , (S, K,) aor. tasoduw , inf. n. sadowN , (S,) she went with wide steps; (K;) or she stretched forth her arms in going along, and went with wide steps: and maA A^aHosana sadowa rijolayohaA waA^atowa yadayohaA [ How good, or beautiful, is her stretching forth of her hind legs, and her returning of her fore legs in her going! ]. (S.) See also sataY . ― -b2- sadaA , (M,) or yasoduw , (S,) ka*aA ↓ sadowa , (S, M,) He went, (M,) or he goes, (S,) towards, or in the direction of, such a thing; (S, M;) said of a man. (S.) ― -b3- sadowN also signifies The going at random, heedlessly, or in a headlong manner, without consideration, or without any certain aim, or object, not obeying a guide to the right course, in journeying; (S, M;) said in relation to camels and horses. (M.) ― -b4- Hence, (M,) sadaA biAljawoz , (K,) aor. yasoduw , (TA,) inf. n. sadowN , (M, TA,) He (a boy, or child,) played with walnuts, (M, K, TA,) throwing them into a hole; (TA;) a dial. var. of zadaA ; (K;) or, accord. to the T, the latter is of the dial. of children; (TA;) as also ↓ AstdY , (M, K, TA,) in [some of] the copies of the K, erroneously, AsdY . (TA.) See also midoHaApN , in art. dHw . -A2- See also 5. -A3- sadiyati AalA^aroDu The land was, or became, moistened by much dew, (S, Msb,) either from the sky or from the ground. (S.) And sadiyati All~ayolapu The night was, or became, moist with much dew. (M, * TA.) ― -b2- sadiYa Albusoru , (S, K,) or AlbalaHu , (M,) inf. n. sadFY ; (TA;) and ↓ A^asodaY ; (M;) The dates in the state in which they are termed blH , or blH , [see these words,] were, or became, lax in their vafaAriyq [or bases, so as to be easily detached therefrom], (S, M, K,) and moist. (M.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, Msb, K,) and AstAhu ; (S;) as also ↓ sd~Ahu , (K,) inf. n. tasodiyapN ; (TA;) and ↓ tsd~Ahu ; (K;) He set, or disposed, the warp ( Als~adaY ) of the garment, or piece of cloth; (S, * Msb, K, * TA;) he made a warp ( sadFY ) in the garment, or piece of cloth: (Har p. 241:) or ↓ sd~Ahu means he did so for another; and ↓ tsd~Ahu , he did so for himself. (M, TA.) [Golius explains ↓ sd~Y as signifying also “ Oblivit telam viscosiore aquâ, ut cui mistus fuerit panis, quod fit roboris conciliandi ergo; ” as on the authority of the KL; in my copy of which I find only its inf. n., tasodiyapN , expl. as meaning the weaver's making a warp in a garment, or piece of cloth ( tAr drjAmh krdn jwlAh ): and Freytag adds, as a signification assigned to the same verb by Jac. Schultens, “ Cirris s. fimbriis ornavit vestem. ”] ― -b2- [Hence,] one says, AlA^umuwra wayuniyruhaA ↓ huwa yusad~iY (A in art. nyr ) or yusodiY (TA in that art.) [meaning (assumed tropical:) He commences things, or affairs, and completes them ]. And A^aloHimo maA A^asodayota (assumed tropical:) Complete what thou hast commenced (S and K in art. lHm ) of beneficence. (S in that art.) ― -b3- Hence also, AsdY bayonahumo HadiyvFA i. q. nasajahu [i. e. (tropical:) He wove, or composed, or he forged, a discourse between them ]. (M, TA.) ― -b4- And AsdY bayonahumaA i. q. A^aSolaHa [i. e. (assumed tropical:) He effected a rectification of affairs, an agreement, a harmony, or a reconciliation, between them two ]. (AA, Az, K.) ― -b5- And AsdY A_ilayohi (assumed tropical:) He did a benefit to him; as also ↓ sd~Y , inf. n. tasodiyapN : (K:) or AsdY A_ilayohi sadFY , and Ealayohi ↓ sd~Ahu , (M, TA, [thus in the latter case, Elyh , not Alyh ,]) or AsdY A_ilayohi maEozuwfFA , (Msb,) he did to him, or conferred upon him, a benefit, benefaction, favour, or the like: (M, * Msb, TA:) [app. from AsdY Alv~awoba , and sd~Ahu ; and accordingly mentioned in the M in art. sdY : or] it is from sdY [or rather sadaA , inf. n. sadowN ,] as meaning “ he (a camel) put forward his fore legs in going along; ” for he of whom one says A^asodaAka xayorFA [ he did to thee good, like A^asodaY A_ilayoka xayorFA ,] is as though he stretched forth to the his arm, or hand, therewith, advancing: (Ham p. 696:) you say, AsdY niEomapF , meaning AiSoTanoE [i. e. he did a benefit, &c.]. (Idem p. 759.) ― -b6- You say also, Talabotu A^amorFA faA^asodayotuhu i. e. (assumed tropical:) [ I sought a thing, and ] I attained it, or obtained it: [as though meaning I stretched forth my hand to it and reached it:] if you do not attain it, or obtain it, you say, A^aEomasotuhu : (S:) or A_isodaA='N signifies the attaining quickly. (KL. [There expl. by the words zwd dryAftn : for which Golius seems to have found in his copy zwd rftn ; for he has assigned to AsdY , as on the authority of the KL, the meaning of cito incessit. ]) -A2- AsdAhu also signifies He left, let alone, or neglected, him, or it: (K:) he left him to himself, uncontrolled, (M, Msb,) neither commanded nor forbidden. (M.) And you say, A^asodayotu A_ibiliY , (AZ, T, S,) inf. n. A_isodaA='N , (AZ, T,) I left my camels to pasture by themselves. (AZ, T, S.) -A3- AsdY AlbalaHu : see 1, last sentence. ― -b2- AsdY Aln~axolu The palm-trees had dates such as are termed sadK . (As, T, S, K.)

definition: of a garment, or piece of cloth, (S, M, K, &c.
sourceDefinition: of a garment, or piece of cloth, (S, M, K, &c.,) The warp; (MA, KL;) contr. of luHomapN ; (S, M, Msb;) i. e. (Msb [in the M “ and it is said to mean ”]) the portion [or threads ] thereof extended longitudinally (M, * Msb, K *) in the weaving: (Msb:) and it is said to mean the lower, or lowest, part thereof: (M: [but this is a strange explanation, which I do not find elsewhere:]) it is [said to be] from Als~adowu [inf. n. of sadaA ] signifying “ the stretching forth the arm, or hand, or the fore leg, towards a thing: ” (Har p. 241: [but it is mentioned in the M as belonging to art. sdY ; and its dual, mentioned below, requires its being so:]) and ↓ A^asodiY~N , (M, K,) also [and more commonly] written ↓ A^usodiY~N , (K,) signifies the same; (M, K;) as also ↓ sadaApN ; (S, K;) or this last is the n. un. of sadFY , (M, TA,) having a more special signification, (Msb, TA,) [as though meaning a warp, or a sort of warp; or the luHomapN may be affixed for the purpose of assimilating the word to its contr. sadFY , with which it is often coupled:] the dual [of sadFY ] is sadayaAni : (S, Msb, TA:) and the pl. is A^asodiyapN (accord. to the S) or A^asodaA='N . (Msb.) ↓ maA A^anota biluHomapK walaA sadaApK [lit. Thou art neither a woof nor a warp ] is said to him who neither harms nor profits. (TA. [See also satFY .]) ― -b2- Hence, as being likened thereto, (M, [see 2, second sentence,]) (tropical:) Honey in its comb; syn. $uhodN or $ahodN . (M, K, TA.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) A benefit, benefaction, favour, or the like. (S, M, K, TA. [See also the next two sentences.]) ― -b4- The nightdew; (S, M, Msb, K;) by means of which seedproduce lives: (S, * Msb:) or, as some say, sadFY and nadFY are syn. [and both applied to dew in an absolute sense ]: and the pl. is A^asodaA='N . (M.) ― -b5- And (tropical:) Liberality, bounty, munificence, or generosity; as being likened thereto; and so nadFY . (S in art. ndw and ndY .) [See an ex. in a verse cited voce riqobapN .] -A2- Green dates, (M, K,) with their $amaAriyx [or fruit-stalks ]; (M;) as also ↓ sadaA='N ; (M, K;) of the dial of El-Yemen: n. un. ↓ sadaApN and ↓ sadaA='apN , (M, TA,) on the authority of AA, and of Sh also, who says that they are of the dial. of El-Medeeneh. (TA.) [See also the last sentence of the next paragraph: and see sayaAbN .] -A3- Also sometimes used in the sense of sudFY . (S, K.) See this latter word.

(O, Msb, K.)

Samata : (Lth, Msb, TA:) or sakata is said of him who has the power, or faculty, of speech, but abstains from making use of it; whereas Samata is sometimes said of that which has not the power, or faculty, of speech: (Er-Rághib, MF, TA:) or sakata , aor. , inf. n. sukuwtN and sakotN , signifies he (a man) ceased, or stopped, speaking; and sakata , aor. , inf. n. sakotN , (assumed tropical:) he (a man) was, or became, still, or quiet; syn. sakana : (Zj, TA:) [it is said that] ↓ Askt , also, is syn. with Samata , like sakata ; (Msb;) accord. to AZ, one says of a man, Samata and A^aSamata and sakata and ↓ A^asokata : (TA:) or, as some say, ↓ Askt signifies he was, or became, silent, or he spoke not; and he ceased [ from speech ], or broke off [ therefrom ], or became cut short [ therein ]: (Msb:) or sakata signifies he was, or became, silent intentionally; and ↓ Askt , he was, or became, silent by reason of thought or disease or fear: (TA:) or you say takal~ama vum~a sakata without A [when you mean he spoke and then became silent, i. e., intentionally ]; (S) but you say ↓ Askt when you mean his speech became broken off, or cut short, and so he spoke not. (S, K.) It is said in a prov., sakata A^alofFA wnaTaqa xalofFA He held his tongue from a thousand words ( sakata Eano A^alofi kalimapK ), and then uttered what was wrong. (ISk, S and Msb in art. xlf .) And you say [of the quiescent h that is sometimes added at the end of a word, after a vowel or a letter of prolongation, as in lamo yaroDaho and waA zayodaAho ], h`*ihi haA='u Als~akoti [ This is the hA' of pausation ]. (A, TA.) One says also, of a she-camel, sakatato , inf. n. sukuwtN , meaning She uttered not the [ grumbling ] cry termed rugaA=' when the saddle was put upon her. (TA. [See also 4.]) You say also, sakata AlHar~u , meaning (assumed tropical:) The heat became vehement, or intense, the wind being still. definition: A single state of silence, muteness, or speechlessness.
sourceDefinition: A single state of silence, muteness, or speechlessness. (Msb.) One says, lilojubolaY SaroxapN vum~a sakotapN [ To the pregnant woman is attributable a vehement cry, then a silence ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- In prayer, A silence [or pause ] after the commencement; [i. e. after what precedes the first recitation of the Opening Chapter of the Kur-án; ] which is approved: and, in like manner, after the ending of the recitation of the Opening Chapter of the Kur-án. (T, TA.) ― -b3- See also sakotN . ― -b4- Also A certain disease [ by which a person loses his powers of speech and motion ], (S, K, TA,) well known among the physicians; (TA;) [i. e. apoplexy; thus called in the present day:] accord. to some, the word in this sense should be written ↓ sikotapN , because it denotes a mode [ of silence or stillness ]; but this is incorrect, being at variance with the authority of transmission. (TA.) ― -b5- See also the next paragraph: -A2- and see sik~iytN .

definition: Constant, or continual, silence.
sourceDefinition: Constant, or continual, silence. (Msb.) Hence, by way of comparison, one says, AlA_ifoHaAmu sukaAtN [as though meaning The state of being silenced in a dispute, &c., is a state of constant, or continual, silence: but it seems to mean, more probably, AlAfHAm (as an act. inf. n.) is an act that silences; agreeably with what here follows]. (Msb.) ― -b2- ramaAhu bisukaAtK (AZ, M, K) and ↓ sukaAtapK , (AZ, S, M, A, K,) to which latter is generally added waSumaAtapK , (M, TA,) He (a man, S, M, and God, TA) smote him, or afflicted him, with a thing that silenced him; (S, A, K;) thought by ISd to mean, with anxiety, or grief, that silenced him, or a thing in consequence of which he became silent: not expl. by AZ. (TA.) ― -b3- [In like manner] one says also, ↓ ramaAhu biAlmusokitaAti [ He smote him, or afflicted him, with the words, or acts, that silenced him ]. (T in art. rm , from Aboo-Málik.) And bihi sukaAtN [ He has in him that which makes him silent ]: said of one long silent in consequence of disease (A, TA) or of some evil in him. (TA.) And A^aSaAba sukaAtFA He met with, or experienced, a disease that prevented him from speaking. (TA.) ― -b4- huwaEalaY sukaAti AlA^amori He is at the point of accomplishing the affair. (K.) And kunotu EalaY sukaAti h`*ihi AlHaAjapi I was at the point of attaining this want, or needful affair. (S.) ― -b5- Hay~apN sukaAtN (tropical:) A serpent that bites before one has knowledge of it; (S, A, K, TA;) as also ↓ sakuwtN . (TA.)

sourceDefinition: The part that faces one, of a mountain, and rises from ( Ean ) the safoH [i. e. base, or foot ]; (S, K;) the acclivity, or rising part, in the face, or front, [or side, ] of a mountain or a valley: (T, M, A:) or a rising, or an elevated, portion of ground: (Mgh:) pl. A^asonaAdN , (M, A,) [properly a pl. of pauc., but] the only pl. form. (M.) ― -b2- A thing, such as a wall &c., against, or upon, which one leans, rests, or stays himself: (Mgh, Msb:) and ↓ misonadN and ↓ musonadN [the latter in the TA said to be with fet-h, but this is evidently a mistake, occasioned by a copyist's writing wyftH for wyDm~ ,] signify [the same,] a thing against, or upon, which one leans, rests, or stays himself; [and the former of these two particularly signifies a cushion, or pillow, and more particularly a large cushion or pillow, against which one leans; as expl. by Golius on the authority of Meyd;] pl. masaAnidu . (L, Msb.) ― -b3- Applied to a man, i. q. muEotamadN [meaning (tropical:) A person upon whom one leans, rests, stays himself, or relies ]; (S;) a man's muEotamad [i. e. sourceDefinition: [pass. part. n. of 4, Made to lean, rest, &c., against, or upon, a thing: and stayed, propped, or supported; or set up. ― -b2- Hence used in the sense of misonadN , as being a thing set up]: see sanadN . ― -b3- Also (tropical:) A tradition ( HadiyvN ) traced up, or ascribed, or attributed, to the author thereof, (T, L, K, TA,) [ rested on his authority by the mention of him, (see 4,) or] by the mention, uninterruptedly, in ascending order, of the persons by whom it has been transmitted, up to the Prophet; (T, L, KT;) [or by the mention of him who has related it from the Prophet when only one has intervened; ] opposed to murosalN and munoqiTiEN ; (T, L;) or it may be mnqTE , i. e. interrupted in the mention of the persons by whom it has been transmitted: (KT:) pl. masaAnidu , (K,) agreeably with analogy, (TA,) and masaAniydu , (Esh-Sháfi'ee, K,) which latter has Y added to render the sound of the kesreh more full; or, accord. to some, it is a dial. var.; and accord. to some, agreeable with analogy. (TA.) ― -b4- And i. q. daEiY~N [as meaning (assumed tropical:) One who claims as his father a person who is not his father; or an adopted son; or one whose origin, or lineage, or parentage, is suspected ]; (S, M, L, K;) as also ↓ saniydN ; (M, L, K; [see an ex. in a verse cited voce A^asar~u ;]) opposed to kariymN . (L.) ― -b5- Almusonadu , accord. to Sb, signifies (assumed tropical:) The first portion [i. e. the subject ] of a proposition; and Almusonadu A_ilayohi , (assumed tropical:) the second portion [i. e. the attribute, or predicate, ] thereof: (M, L:) of, accord. to Kh, a proposition consists of a ↓ sanad and a musonad A_ilayoh ; and in the phrase Eabodu A@ll~`hi rajulN SaAliHN , [for ex.,] Ebd All~`h is a snd , and rjl SAlH is a msnd Alyh : (O, L:) [but accord. to other authors, and general modern usage, and agreeably with the proper meanings of the terms, Almusonadu (meaning the attributed) signifies the attribute, or predicate; and Almusonadu A_ilayohi , (meaning that to which a thing or an accident is attributed) signifies the subject. ] ― -b6- Also The Himyeree, or Himyeritic, character of writing; the character of Himyer; (S, M, A, O, K;) differing from the modern Arabic character: (S, O:) they used to write it commonly in the days of their rule; and AHát says that it continued in use among them in El-Yemen in his day [i. e. in the latter half of the second century of the Flight and the former half of the third century]: (M, TA:) Abu-l-'Abbás says, Almusonadu was the language of the sons of Seth; (O, TA;) [i. e. the language written in the character so called;] and the like is said in the “ Sirr es-Siná'ah ” of IJ. (TA.) [See also De Sacy's Chrest. Ar., sec. ed., vol. ii., p. 122 of the Ar. text, and 311 of the transl.] ― -b7- And i. q. Ald~ahoru [i. e. Time, from the beginning of the world to its end; or time absolutely; or a long time; or a long unlimited time; or time without end; &c.]. (S, M, A, K.) So in the saying, laA A^afoEaluhu A=xira Almusonadi [ I will not do it to the end of time ]. (A, TA.) One says also, laA A=tiyhi yada Almusonadi , meaning [ I will not do it, or I will not come to him or it, ] ever. (IAar, TA.)

definition: (tropical:) They two went forth aiding, or assisting, each other;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) They two went forth aiding, or assisting, each other; (A, * L, TA;) as though each of them leaned, or stayed himself, upon the other, and aided himself by him. (L, TA.) The latter word is used, in this sense, of two men going on a hostile, or hostile and plundering, expedition: and of two wolves attacking a person. (A.) And one says, xarajuwA mutasaAnidiyna , meaning (tropical:) They went forth under sundry, or different, banners, or standards, (S, A, M, L, K, *) every party by itself, (A, L,) the sons of one father under one [ separate ] banner, (L,) not all under the banner of one commander. (S, L. K.)

definition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. yasiybu , (S, A,) inf. n. sayobN , (S, M, A, K,) It ran; (S, M, A, * Mgh, Msb, K;) said of water: (S, M, A, Msb:) and ↓ AnsAb , likewise said of water, it ran of itself. (Msb.) ― -b2- [Hence,] sAbt AlHay~apu , (M,) aor. as above; (M, A;) and ↓ AnsAbt ; (S, M, A, Msb;) (tropical:) The serpent ran: (S, A, * Msb:) or went along (M, TA) in a uniform, or continuous, course, (M,) or quickly. (TA.) sAb and ↓ AnsAb both signify (assumed tropical:) He, or it, walked, or went along, quickly: (K, TA:) [or] so the former verb. (M.) It is said in a trad., respecting a man who drank from the mouth of a skin, fiY baTonihi Hay~apN ↓ AinosaAbato (tropical:) A serpent entered and ran into his belly with the running of the water: wherefore it was forbidden to drink from the mouth of a skin. (TA.) El-Hareeree, in [his first Makámeh, entitled] the San'áneeyeh, [p. 20,] uses the phrase, fiyhaA EalaY garaArapK ↓ AnsAb , meaning He entered into it as the serpent enters into its lurking place. (TA.) And you say of a viper, sAb and ↓ AnsAb , meaning (tropical:) It came forth from its lurkingplace. (TA.) And naHowakumo ↓ AnsAb (assumed tropical:) He returned towards you. (S.) ― -b3- sAb , (Mgh, Msb,) aor. as above, inf. n. sayabaAnN , said of a horse and the like, (assumed tropical:) He went away at random: (Msb:) or (assumed tropical:) he [app. a horse or the like] went any, or every, way: (Mgh:) or sAbt Ald~aAb~apu (tropical:) The beast was left alone, or by itself, to pasture, without a pastor. (S, * A, TA.) ― -b4- And sAb fiY manoTiqihi (tropical:) He took every way [or roved at large ] in his speech: (TA:) or he dilated, or was profuse, without consideration, in his speech. (A, TA.) And sAb fiY AlkalaAmi (tropical:) He entered into talk, or discourse, with loquacity, or irrationality. (TA.) It is said in a trad., A_in~a AlHiylapa biAlmanoTiqi A^abolagu mina Als~uyuwbi fiY Alkalimi , meaning (tropical:) [ Verily art, or skill, in speech is more eloquent, or effective, ] than what is loose, or unrestrained, [or rambling, ] in words; i. e. elegance of speech, with paucity, [ is more eloquent, or effective, ] than profusion. (L, TA. [ Als~uyuwb is here an inf. n.])

(L, TA.) It is said in a trad. respecting a prayer for rain, waA@joEalohu sayobFA naAfiEFA (tropical:) And make Thou it to be a beneficial gift: or the meaning in this instance may be, a flowing rain. (TA.) And one says, faADa sayobuhu EalaY Aln~aAsi (tropical:) His gifts flowed abundantly upon the people. (A, TA.) [See also an ex. in a verse cited voce jub~aA^N .] ― -b3- Also i. q. rikaAzN (tropical:) [i. e. Metal, or mineral; or pieces of gold or silver, that are extracted from the earth; or any metals or other minerals; or buried treasure of the people of the Time of Ignorance ]: (A, Msb:) or so suyuwbN ; (A 'Obeyd, S, M, Mgh, K;) which is the pl.: (A, Msb:) the latter signifies, accord. to Th, metals, or minerals: (M, TA:) accord. to Aboo-Sa'eed, veins of gold and of silver, that come into existence, and appear, in the mines: so called because of their running ( liA@nosiyaAbihaA ) in the earth: accord to Z, treasure buried in the Time of Ignorance: or metal, or mineral: (TA:) because of the gift of God, (M, Z, Mgh, TA,) to him who finds it. (Z, TA.) The Prophet said, (Mgh, TA,) fiY Als~uyuwbi Alxumosu , i. e. In the case of rikaAz , the fifth part [is for the government-treasury]. (A, Mgh, TA.) -A2- Also The hair of the tail of a horse. (M, K.) -A3- And A pole with which a ship or boat is propelled. (M, K.)

definition: (tropical:) Any beast that is left to pasture where it will, without a pastor: (M, A, K: *) pl.
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) Any beast that is left to pasture where it will, without a pastor: (M, A, K: *) pl. sawaAy^ibu and suy~abN . (A.) (assumed tropical:) A camel that has lived until his offspring have had offspring, and is therefore set at liberty, and not ridden, (M, K,) nor laden with a burden. (M.) In the Kur v. 102, (TA,) (assumed tropical:) A she-camel that was set at liberty to pasture where it would, (S, Mgh, Msb, K,) in the Time of Ignorance, (S, K,) on account of a vow (S, Mgh, Msb, K) and the like: (S, K:) or the mother of a baHiyrap ; (S, Mgh; [in the Msb, said to be a baHiyrap (itself); and in one place in the TA said to be a she-camel of which the dam is a baHiyrp ; but both of these explanations require consideration, as will be seen from what follows;]) or (K) a she-camel which, having brought forth females at ten successive births, was set at liberty to pasture where she would, (S, K,) and not ridden, nor was here milk drunk except by her young one or a guest, until she died, when the men and the women ate her together; and the ear of her last female young one was slit, and she was [ therefore ] called baHiyrap , and was a saAy^ibap like her mother: (S:) or a she-camel of which a man, (M, IAth, K,) in the Time of Ignorance, (M,) when he came from a far journey, (M. IAth, K,) or re- covered from a disease, (IAth, TA,) or had been saved by his beast from difficulty or trouble, (M, IAth,) or when his beast had been saved therefrom, (K,) or from war, said, hiYa saAy^ibapN ; (M, IAth, K;) i. e. she was left to pasture where she would, without a pastor, and no use was made of her back, nor was she debarred from water, nor from herbage, nor ridden: (IAth, TA:) thus it signifies in the Kur: (M:) or a she-camel from whose back a vertebra or [ some other ] bone was taken forth, (M, K,) so that she became known thereby, (M,) and which was not debarred from water nor from herbage, nor ridden, (M, K,) nor milked: (TA:) the pl. is suy~abN , like nuw~aHN pl. of naAy^iHapN , and nuw~amN pl. of naAy^imapN ; (S;) and sawaAy^ibu . (TA.) It is said in a trad., “ I saw 'Amr Ibn-Loheí dragging his intestines in the fire [of Hell]: ” and he was the first who set at liberty sawaAy^ib : the doing of which is forbidden in the Kur v. 102. (TA.) And it is related that a hostile attack was made upon a certain man of the Arabs, and he found not any [other] beast to ride, so he rode a saAy^ibap : whereupon it was said to him, “ Dost thou ride what is forbidden? ” and he replied, yarokabu AlHaraAma mano laA HalaAla lahu [He rides what is forbidden who has not what is allowed]: and this saying became a proverb. (M.) Als~aAy^ibataAni means The badanataAni [i. e. two camels, or cows or bulls, for sacrifice, ] which the Prophet brought as offerings to the House [ of God at Mekkeh ], and which one of the believers in a plurality of gods took away: they are thus called because he gave them up ( say~abahumaA ) to God. (TA.) ― -b2- Also (assumed tropical:) A slave emancipated so that the emancipator has no claim to inherit from him, (S, M, A, Mgh, Msb, K,) except, accord. to EshSháfi'ee, in the case of the slave's dying without appointing any heir, in which case his inheritance belongs to his emancipator, (TA,) [ for ] such an emancipated slave may bestow his property where [or on whom ] he pleases, (S, Mgh, Msb, TA,) agreeably with a trad.: (Mgh, TA:) [in the S, and in the Msb as on the authority of IF, it is added, that “ this is what is related to have been forbidden: ” but from what has been stated above, this appears to be a mistake; and I think that these words have been misplaced in the S and Msb, and that they relate only to the she-camel termed saAy^ibap :] a slave is thus emancipated by his owner's saying to him, A^anota saAy^ibapN . (S.) 'Omar said, Als~aAy^ibapu waAlS~adaqapu liyawomihimaA [ The sáïbeh and alms are for their day ]: i. e., for the day of resurrection; so that one may not return to the deriving of any advantage from them in the present world. (AO, Mgh, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , [aor. ,] inf. n. $ibaEN (IDrd, S, Msb, K) and $iboEN , (IDrd, Msb, TA,) which is a contraction of the former, or accord. to some it is a subst., having the signification assigned to it below, (Msb,) or it is both, (TA,) and $aboEN , (Ibn- 'Abbád, K,) He was, or became, satiated, sated, or satisfied in stomach; $ibaEN being the contr. of juwEN , (S, K,) and one of those inf. ns. [which are of a measure often] denoting natural affections or qualities [such as riwFY and simanN &c.]. (S.) You say baladN qado $abiEato ganamuhu A country of which the sheep, or goats, have become completely satiated, or satisfied, by abundance of herbage. (TA.) And $abiEotu xubozFA , and laHomFA , (S, Msb, K,) and mino xubozK , and mn laHomK , (S, K,) I was, or became, satiated, sated, or satisfied, with bread, and with flesh-meat. (S, K.) ― -b2- Hence, metaphorically, $abiEotu mino h`*aA AlA^amoi warawiytu (tropical:) I have become, or I became, disgusted [or satiated to loathing ] with this thing, or affair. (S, * TA.) ― -b3- [See also another metaphorical usage of this verb voce HuzaAnapN .] -A2- $abuEa Eaqoluhu (assumed tropical:) His intellect was, or became, full, perfect, (K,) strong, or solid. (TA.)

definition: [signifying It satiated him, sated him, or satisfied his stomach, ] is said of food and of abundance of drink.
sourceDefinition: [signifying It satiated him, sated him, or satisfied his stomach, ] is said of food and of abundance of drink. (TA.) ― -b2- A^a$obaEotuhu [ I satiated him, sated him, or satisfied his stomach; or] I fed him so that he became satiated, sated, or satisfied. (Msb.) And A^a$obaEotuhu mina AljuwEi [ I fed him so as fully to relieve him from hunger ]. (S, K.) [Hence,] A^a$obaEotu Alv~awoba (S, TA) mina AlS~ibogi (S) (tropical:) I saturated the garment, or piece of cloth, with the dye. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] A$bEhu (tropical:) He made it (namely anything, TA) full, without lack or defect, or abundant, or copious. (K, * TA.) It is said of other things beside substances; as, for instance, of blowing, and of reading or reciting, and of any expression. (TA.) You say also, saAqa fiY h`*aA AlmaEonaY faSolFA mu$obaEFA [ He carried on, respecting this idea, a full section ]. (TA.) [And A$bE HarakapF He rendered a vowel full in sound, by inserting after it its analogous letter of prolongation. And such a letter of prolongation is said to be inserted, or added, liloA_i$obaAEi to render the sound full; as in nukaAtN for nukatN , and A^anoZuwru for A^anoZuru , and maraADiyEu for maraADiEu . And A_i$obaAEFA is also used as signifying For the sake of, or by way of, pleonasm, or giving fulness of expression. ] -A2- A$bE Alr~ajulu The man's beasts were, or became, completely satiated, or satisfied, by abundance of herbage. (TA.)

definition: Satiated, sated, or satisfied in stomach;
sourceDefinition: Satiated, sated, or satisfied in stomach; (S, Msb, * K;) as also ↓ $aAbiEN , but this is allowable only in poetry: (K:) fem. of the former $aboEaY , (S, Msb, K,) and $aboEaAnapN (Sgh, K) is sometimes used: (Sgh:) the pl. of $bEAn and of $bEY is $ibaAEN and $abaAEaY . (TA.) [Hence the saying,] qawomN A_i*aA jaAEuwA kaAEuwA wataraAhumo sibaAEFA A_i*aA kaAnuwA $ibaAEFA [ A people who, when they are hungry, are fearful and cowardly, and thou seest them to be beasts of prey when they are satiated ]. (A, TA.) ― -b2- [And hence,] $aboEaY AlxaloxaAli (tropical:) A woman who fills up the anklet by reason of her fatness. (S, K, TA.) And $aboEaY Als~iwaAri (tropical:) Who fills up the bracelet by reason of fatness. (K, TA.) And $aboEaY Alwi$aAHi (tropical:) A woman large in the belly. (TA.) And $aboEaY Ald~iroEi (tropical:) A woman bulky in make: (A, O, L, TA:) in the K erroneously written $aboEaY Al*~iraAEi , and expl. as meaning bulky in the forearm. (TA.)

definition: (tropical:) One who invests himself with, and makes a boast of, more than he possesses;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) One who invests himself with, and makes a boast of, more than he possesses; who invests himself with that which he does not possess; (S, TA;) who affects goodly qualities more than he possesses; like him who feigns himself satiated, or satisfied in stomach, not being so: (TA:) or he who feigns himself satiated, or satisfied in stomach, not being so: and hence, (assumed tropical:) a lying person, who affects to be commended or praised for, or boasts of, or glories in, that which he does not possess. (Mgh.) Thus in a trad., (S, Mgh,) in which it is said, Almuta$ab~iEu bimaA laA yamoliku kalaA bisi vawobaYo zuwrK , (S, TA,) or bimaA layosa Einodahu , (Mgh,) (tropical:) [ He who invests himself with, and makes a boast of, more than he possesses, &c., is like the wearer of two garments of falsity: or] accord. to A'Obeyd, it means [that such is like ] the hypocrite who wears the garments of the devotees in order that he may be thought to be a devotee, not being so: or, as some say, the person who wears a shirt to the sleeves of which he attaches two other sleeves in order to make it appear that he is wearing two shirts: or [ the wearer of the garments of the false witness; for] it is said that there used to be in the tribe the man of goodly exterior, and when false witness was needed, he bore [such] witness, and was not rejected, because of the goodliness of his apparel. (Mgh.) [See also art. zwr , in which this trad, is cited with a small variation.]
