definition: , (Mgh, TA,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (Mgh, TA,) aor. [and ], inf. n. $axobN , said of milk, (Mgh,) and of anything, It flowed. (Mgh, TA.) And $axabotuhu I made it to flow. (Mgh.) You say, $axaba All~abanu , aor. and , (S, O, CK,) inf. n. $axobN , (S, O,) The milk flowed in an extended stream from the udder when milked; (S, O, CK;) and (assumed tropical:) in like manner one says of blood: (O:) or $axaba All~abana , aor. and , he made the milk to flow in a continuous stream from the udder (K accord. to the TA [and accord. to the context in the K, in which it is immediately added faA@no$axaba , showing that ↓ An$xb has the former of these two significations as quasi-pass. of $axaba , and the like is said in the A,]) between the vessel and the teat. (TA.) Hence, i. e. from $axaba All~abanu , the saying of ElKumeyt, wawaHowaHa fiY HiDoni AlfataApi DajiyEuhaA walamo yaku fiY Aln~ukodi AlmaqaAliyti ma$oxabu [ And he who lay upon his side with her, or her bedfellow, breathed audibly, by reason of the cold, in the bosom of the young woman, and there was not, among the she-camels that had no young ones living, and that should therefore abound with milk, because not suckling, any flowing of milk in a continuous, or an extended, stream, or any time, or place, thereof, for ma$oxabN may be, agreeably with a general rule, an inf. n. or a n. of time or of place]. (S.) And some expl. $axobN as signifying The sounding, or sound, of milk when it is being drawn from the udder. (TA.) One says also, $axabato A^awodaAju Alqatiyli damFA i. e. (tropical:) [ The external jugular veins of the slain person ] streamed, or flowed with blood: (Msb, TA: * [and the like is said in the Mgh:]) and $axabotuhu A^anaA (assumed tropical:) [ I made it to stream, or flow ]: the verb being intrans. and trans. (Msb.) And huwa ya$oxubu damFA (assumed tropical:) He, or it, flows [or streams ] with blood; the last word being in the accus. case as a specificative: and be, or it, pours forth, or makes to flow [or stream ], blood; the last word, when this is the meaning, being in the accus. case as an objective complement: but the former is that which is commonly known. (Mgh.) And $axabato yadaAhu Hat~aY maAta (assumed tropical:) [ His hands flowed, or streamed, with blood, until he died: or poured forth blood, &c.]: said, in a trad., of one whose knuckles, or finger-joints, were cut. (TA.) ↓ An$xb , also, is said of blood [as meaning (assumed tropical:) It flowed, or streamed ]. (TA.) And damFA ↓ An$xb , said of a vein, means (assumed tropical:) It flowed, or streamed, with blood. (S, K, TA.) And it is said in a trad. respecting the HawoD [or pool (of the Apostle)], ya$oxuabu fiyhi miyzaAbaAni mina Aljan~api (assumed tropical:) [ Two spouts will pour forth into it from Paradise ]. (TA.) And one says, $axabotu All~iqaAHa I milked the milch camels. (A, TA.) ― -b2- And mar~a ya$oxabu fiY AlA^aroDi (assumed tropical:) He went, or passed by, (O,) or ran, (El-Fáïk, TA,) swiftly [ in the land, or upon the ground ]. (El-Fáïk, O, TA.)

definition: Milk coming forth, (A,) or milk that has come forth, (K,) from the udder, (A, K,) when drawn therefrom;
sourceDefinition: Milk coming forth, (A,) or milk that has come forth, (K,) from the udder, (A, K,) when drawn therefrom; (TA;) and so ↓ $axobN ; (A, K;) which is also an inf. n.; (TA;) or this latter is an inf. n., (S, O,) and the former [is a subst. properly so called, and] signifies an extended stream of milk, (S, A, O,) like a thread, or string, (A,) when it is drawn from the udder; (S, A, O;) of the measure fuEolN in the sense of the measure mafoEuwlN : (A:) or the milk that comes forth from beneath the hand of the milker at each squeeze of the udder of the ewe or she-goat. (TA.) It is said in a prov., $uxobN fiY AlA_inaA='i wa$uxobN fiY AlA^aroDi , (S, Meyd, A, O,) i. e. One extended stream of milk from the udder into the vessel, and one &c. upon the ground: (Meyd:) applied to him who hits the mark one time and misses another time (S, Meyd, A, O) in what he says; or says right one time and wrong another time. (Meyd.) And in another prov., $uxobN TamaHa An extended stream of milk from the udder that has fallen upon the ground so as to be unprofitable; for such is the meaning of TamaHa in this case: applied to a man who has made a slip, or mistake: or it means a good hap that has escaped one's opportunity to avail himself of it. (Meyd.) See also the next paragraph.

definition: A place in which water flows from a [ stony tract such as is termed ] Har~ap to a soft, or plain, tract;
sourceDefinition: A place in which water flows from a [ stony tract such as is termed ] Har~ap to a soft, or plain, tract; (S, K;) as also ↓ $arojapN : (TA:) or the latter signifies [simply] a place in which water flows; and some elide the p , saying $arojN : (Msb:) pl. $iraAjN (S, Mgh, Msb, K, expl. in the Mgh agreeably with the former explanation above, and said in the Msb to be pl. of $arojapN ,) and $uruwjN . (S, K.) -A2- Also A party, or distinct body or class [of men]. (S, K.) One says, A^aSobaHuwA fiY h`*aA AlA^amori $arojayoni i. e. [ They became, in this affair, ] two parties. (S.) And it is said in a trad., A^aSobaHa Aln~aAsu $arojayoni fiY Als~afari [ The people, or men, became two parties in the journey ]; meaning, half of them fasting, and half of them breaking the fast. (TA.) ― -b2- And The like of another; (S, K;) as also ↓ $ariyjN : (O, K:) the latter from the same word as meaning “ a piece of wood [or a branch] that is split into two halves; ” each of which is the $ryj of the other. (O.) One says, h`*aA $aroju h`*aA This is the like of this. (S.) ― -b3- And A sort, or species. (S, K.) One says, humaA $arojN waAHidN They two are one sort, or species. (S.) ― -b4- And $arojaAni Any two different colours: (S:) [and] ↓ $ariyjaAni signifies [the same, i. e.] two different colours (K, TA) of anything; or, accord. to IAar, two mixed colours, not black and white: (TA:) and ↓ this latter, also, the two lines of the nayraAni [or two ornamental borders ] of a [ garment of the kind called ] burod , (O, K,) one of which is A^axoDar [here meaning of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour ], and the other white or red. (O.) ― -b5- And Al$~aroju , like falos [in measure, not to be confounded with Al$~araju ], signifies The [ perinæum, or] part between the anus and the testicles. (IKtt, TA.)

sourceDefinition: A branch, or rod, that is split into two halves: and ↓ $ariyjapN , a bow that is made thereof: (S, O, K:) or the former, a branch, or rod, from which are split two bows: and either of the bows thus made: or a split bow: pl. $araAy^iju : accord. to AA, a bow that is split from a branch, or rod, in two halves; also called filoqN : accord. to Lh, a bow in which is a splitting ( $aq~N , used as an inf. n.), and [ such as is ] a $iq~ , by which is meant the subst. definition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor. , (O, K, MS,) inf. n. $agolN (Msb, K) and $ugolN , (K,) the latter on the authority of Sb, (TA,) He, or it, (a man, S, or an affair, Msb,) busied him, occupied him, or employed him; (K;) i. q. A^alohaAhu [signifying as above; and particularly he, or it, busied him, &c., so as to divert him from ( Eano ) something; or diverted him from a thing by busying him, &c.]: (S and Msb and K in art. lhw , and Bd and Jel in xv. 3, &c.:) [↓ $g~lhu signifies he, or it, busied him, &c., much; i. e.] with teshdeed it denotes muchness: (Bd in xlviii. 11:) ↓ A$glhu is a good dial. var. of $agalahu ; or is rare; or bad: (K:) accord. to IDrd [and J], (O,) one should not say A^a$ogalotuhu ; (S, O;) for it is bad: (S:) accord. to IF, they scarcely ever say A^a$ogalotu , [thus in the O, but in the Msb ↓ Ai$otagala ,] but it is allowable: (O:) none of the leading lexicologists is known to have pronounced it good. (TA.) [Hence the saying, $agalato saEaAtiY jadowaAYa (see art. sEw and sEY ), or, as some relate it, $glt $iEaAbiY jdwAY (see art. $Eb ).] See another ex. voce $aAgilN . One says also $ugila bihi , (Msb, K,) meaning talah~aY [i. e. He was, or became, busied, &c., by it ], (Msb,) and bh ↓ A$tgl [meaning the same]; (Az, Msb, K;) and $ugilotu Eanoka bika*aA [ I was, or became, busied, &c., so as to be diverted from thee, by such a thing ], (S, O,) and ↓ Ai$otagalotu [in the same sense]: (S:) and Eanohu ↓ t$Agl , (TA,) which likewise signifies talah~aY [meaning as expl. above, or he busied himself, &c., so as to divert himself from him, or it ]: (TA in art. lhw , and Bd and Jel in lxxx. 10:) some disallow ↓ Ai$otagala , in the form of an active verb, but say Au$otugila , in the form of a pass. verb; but it is originally quasi-pass of A^a$ogalotuhu , like as are AiHotaraqa and Aikotahala of A^aHoraqotuhu and A^akohalotuhu ; [though why of A^a$ogalotuhu rather than of $agalotuhu , I do not see:] Az mentions the usage of its act. and pass. part. ns.: (Msb:) accord. to AHát and IDrd, one should not say ↓ Ai$otagala ; but IF mentions, as transmitted from the Arabs, Au$otugila fulaAnN biAl$~aYo'i , and the pass. part. n. (O.) ― -b2- One says also, naHonu na$ogalu Eanoka AlmarotaEa (assumed tropical:) [ We occupy the place of pasturage so as to keep it from thee ], and AlmaA='a [ the water ]; meaning, it is sufficient for us without being more than sufficient. (S in art. $fh .) And $ugila Eanoka maA EinodanaA (assumed tropical:) [ What we had was employed so as to be kept from thee ]. (JK in that art.)

definition: [ More, and most, busy &c.
sourceDefinition: [ More, and most, busy &c.]. A^a$ogalu mino *aAti Aln~iHoyayoni [ More busy than she who was the owner of the two skins of butter ] is a prov. [mentioned in the TA]: she was a woman of [the tribe of] Teym-Allah: she used to sell clarified butter, in the Time of Ignorance; and Khowwát Ibn-Jubeyr El-Ansáree came to her, demanding to buy clarified butter of her, and saw no one with her, and he bargained with her: so she untied a skin, and he looked at it: then he said to her, “ Hold thou it until I look at another: ” and she said, “ Untie thou another skin: ” and he did so, and looked at it, and said, “ I desire other than this; therefore hold thou it: ” and she did so: and when her hands were [thus] occupied, he assaulted her, and she was unable to repel the him. (Meyd.)

definition: Lustre, and fineness, or delicacy, or thinness, and coolness, and sweetness, in the teeth: (A, K:) or lustre, and fineness, or delicacy, or thinness, in the fore teeth: (TA:) or these two qualities,...
sourceDefinition: Lustre, and fineness, or delicacy, or thinness, and coolness, and sweetness, in the teeth: (A, K:) or lustre, and fineness, or delicacy, or thinness, in the fore teeth: (TA:) or these two qualities, together with coolness and sweetness, in the mouth, accord. to As, or in the teeth: (TA:) or coolness and sweetness in the teeth: or sharpness of the teeth: (S:) or sharpness of the canine teeth, like garobN , so that they appear like a saw: (K:) or white specks in the teeth: (A, K:) or the state of the teeth when they appear somewhat tinged with blackness, like the appearance of blackness in hail; guruwbN signifying the “ lustre ” of the teeth; and ZalomN , their “ whiteness that is as though there were over it a blackness: ” (ISh, TA:) Abu-l-'Abbás says, It is variously expl., as a serrated state of the teeth: and their clearness and cleanness: and their being separate, or apart, one from another: and the sweetness of their odour: (TA:) El-Jarmee says, I heard As say that this word signifies coolness of the mouth and teeth; and I said, Our companions say that it is their sharpness when they come forth; by which is meant their new, or recent, and fresh state; for when they have undergone the lapse of years, they become abraded, or worn: but he said, It is nothing but their coolness: and the saying of Dhu-r-Rummeh, wafiY All~ivaAti wafiY A^anoyaAbihaA $anabu [which should be rendered And in the gums, and in her canine teeth, is coolness ], corroborates the assertion of As; for there is no sharpness in the gum: (S, L, TA:) it is also related of As that he said, I asked Ru-beh respecting the meaning of $anabN , and he took a grain of pomegranate, and pointed to its lustre: (Mz, TA:) [and ↓ $unobapN signifies the same:] a poet says, munaS~abuhaA Hamo$N A^aHam~u yaziynuhu EawaAriDu fiyhaA $unobapN waguruwbu [ Her even set of front teeth are slender and white, side teeth in which are coolness and lustre adorning them ]. (O, TA.) ― -b2- [In the present day, it signifies The mustache. ]

definition: Of the colour termed $uhobapN ;
sourceDefinition: Of the colour termed $uhobapN ; (S, Msb, K;) as also ↓ $aAhibN , (K,) occurring in the poetry of Hudheyl: (TA:) fem. of the former $ahobaA='u : (S, Msb, K: *) and pl. $uhobN : (O:) the former epithet is applied to a horse, (S,) [contr. to an assertion of IAar, (see 4,)] and to a he-mule, (Msb,) and $ahobaA='u to a she-mule. (Mgh, Msb.) [Golius, on the authority of Meyd, explains A^a$ohabu A^adohamu , applied to a horse, as meaning Subniger, spadiceus: and A^a$ohabu A^axoDaru as meaning lucide leviterve viridis: the correct meaning of the former seems to be of a blackish, or brownish, gray: and that of the latter, of a dark dustcoloured gray: see A^adohamu and A^axoDaru .] Al$~ahobaA='u was the name of a mare belonging to El-Kattál ElBejelee. (O, K; in the CK El-Bejlee.) Applied to a she-goat, $ahobaA='u signifies Of a white colour intermixed with black: thus applied, it is like maloHaA='u applied to a ewe. (K.) Applied to a gur~ap [or blaze on a horse's forehead], it means In which are hairs differing from the whiteness [ of the blaze ]. (S.) And AlA^a$aAhibu is [a pl. formed from AlA^a$ohabu as though this were a subst.] applied to the Benu-l-Mundhir, (K,) or one of the troops of En-Noamán Ibn-El-Mundhir, consisting of the sons of his paternal uncle and his maternal uncles, and their brethren; (TA;) so called because of their comeliness, (K,) or because of the whiteness of their faces. (TA.) ― -b2- Applied to ambergris, (K, TA,) (assumed tropical:) Of an excellent colour, i. e., (TA,) inclining to whiteness. (K, TA.) And applied to an iron head or blade of an arrow or of a spear &c., (tropical:) That has been filed so that its blackness has gone: (S, A, TA:) or that has been filed lightly, so that all its blackness has not gone. (AHn, TA.) [Hence,] katiybapN $ahobaA='u (assumed tropical:) A great troop having numerous weapons; (K;) so called because of the iron; (S;) or because of the whiteness of the weapons and iron, intermixed with blackness: or a troop of which the iron [ of the weapons and armour ] is white and bright: (TA:) or, as also ↓ katiybapN $ah~aAbapN , a troop upon which is [ seen ] the whiteness of the iron [ weapons &c. ]. (T, TA. [See also katiybapN maloHaA='u , voce A^amolaHu .]) And jayo$N A^a$ohabu A strong army [app. because of its numerous weapons]. (TA.) ― -b3- A^aroDN $ahobaA='u (assumed tropical:) A land in which is no verdure, by reason of the paucity of rain. (TA.) And [hence,] sanapN $ahobaA='u (tropical:) A year of drought, or sterility, white in consequence thereof, (TA,) in which is no verdure, or in which is no rain: (K, TA:) next in degree is the bayoDaA=' ; then, the HamoraA=' , which is more severe than the bayoDaA=' ; (TA;) and then, the sawodaA=' : (TA in art. Hmr :) or a year that is white by reason of the abundance of snow and the want of herbage: (IB, TA:) or a year of drought, or sterility; because the seedproduce dries up therein, and becomes yellow: and EaAmN A^a$ohabu signifies the same. (Har p. 150.) And A^a$ohabaAni (assumed tropical:) Two white years ( EaAmaAni A^aboyaDaAni ) between which is no verdure (K, TA) of herbage. (TA.) And yawomN A^a$ohabu (tropical:) A cold day: (A, K:) or a day of cold wind; thought to be so called on account of the snow and hoar frost and hail therein: (L, TA:) or a day of hoar-frost: (Az, TA:) a day of cold wind and hoar frost; and [in like manner] the night ( All~ayolapu ) is termed $ahobaA='u . (S.) In the following verse, cited by Sb, fidFY libaniY *uholi boni $ayobaAna naAqatiY A_i*aA kaAna yawomN *uw kawaAkiba A^a$ohabu [ May my she-camel be a ransom for the sons of Dhuhl Ibn-Sheybán when there is a day of difficulties, or distresses, . . .] the meaning may be A$hb [or whitish ] by reason of the whiteness of the weapons, or by reason of the dust. (TA.) And Al$~uhobu [pl. of A^a$ohabu ], (O,) or ↓ Al$~uhubu [pl. of $ihaAbN ], (K,) [but the former, I think, is evidently the right,] (assumed tropical:) The white nights; ( All~ayaAliY AlbiyDu ;) [i. e. the thirteenth and fourteenth and fifteenth nights of the lunar month; so called because lighted by the moon throughout, (see art. byD ;)] (O;) three nights of the month; (K, TA;) because of the alteration of their colour. (TA.) ― -b4- A^a$ohabu [or A^amorN A^a$ohabu ] also signifies (assumed tropical:) A hard, or difficult, affair or case, (K, TA,) such as is disliked, or hated. (TA.) And A^a$ohabu baAzilN (assumed tropical:) A hard, or difficult, affair or case, that is beyond one's power [ of accomplishment or endurance ]: termed bAzl because the camel thus termed is one that has attained its utmost strength. (O, TA. [See also art. bzl .]) ― -b5- And AlA^a$ohabu signifies The lion. (O, K.) [And in the Deewán of Jereer, it is applied to The swine. (Freytag.)]

sourceDefinition: A written piece of paper (MA, Mgh, Msb) or of skin; (Msb;) a writing, or thing written; a book, or volume; a letter, i. e. an epistle; syn. kitaAbN ; (S, O, K;) [syn. with kitaAbN in all of these senses; in the last of them in an anecdote related in Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 721-2, and in Har p. 119, q. v.;] and a [ portion of a book, such as is termed ] kur~aAsap ; and a register; [for] in the A_inoqaAE [a title of several books, it is said that] the kur~aAsap and ↓ muSoHaf and SaHiyfap and kitaAb and dafotar are one: (MA:) pl. SuHufN (S, Mgh, O, Msb, K) and SuHofN , a contraction of the former, (TA,) and SaHaAy^ifu , (S, O, Msb, K,) like safaAy^inu pl. of safiynapN ; (Lth, O;) the first of these pls. anomalous, (Lth, Sb, O, K,) the sing. being likened to qaDiytN (Sb, O, TA) and qaliybN (Sb, TA) and ragiyfN , (O,) of which the pls. are quDubN (Sb, O, TA) and qulubN (Sb, TA) and rugufN : (O:) [or SaHiyfN may be its original, as well as regular, sing.:] see the next preceding paragraph. [ SaHiyfapN also means The record of the actions of anyone, that is kept in heaven: (see raq~N :) one says, SaHiyfanuhu sawodaA='u , meaning (assumed tropical:) The record of his actions is black; a phrase often used in the present day, in speaking of a bad man.] Mohammad [the Hanafee Imám] speaks of SuHuf not written upon; saying, faA_ino kaAnati Als~ariqapu SuHufFA layosa fiyhaA kitaAbN [ And if the stolen property be papers, or books, not having any writing upon them ]. (Mgh. [See, again, raq~N .]) ― -b2- SaHiyfapN signifies also A plank, board, or leaf, of a door; like SaHaAy^ifu [from which it is perhaps formed by transposition, or it may be tropical in this sense]: pl. SaHiyfN . (MA.) ― -b3- Also (tropical:) The external skin, or scarf-skin, of the face: (O, TA:) or as some say, the part thereof that fronts one: pl. [or rather coll. gen. n.] ↓ SaHiyfN ; or this may be used, in a verse in which it occurs, for SaHiyfap . (TA.) ― -b4- One says also SaHaAy^ifu mino $aHomK [meaning (assumed tropical:) Layers of fat ]. (A in art. nyr .)

sourceDefinition: , (S, M, O, Msb, K,) aor. , (M, TA,) inf. n. SidoqN (S, * M, O, * Msb, K, TA) and SadoqN , (M, K,) the former of which is the more chaste, (TA,) or the latter is an inf. n. and the former is a simple subst., (K,) and taSodaAqN (M) and maSoduwqapN , (O, K, TA,) which is one of the [few] inf. ns. of the measure mafoEuwlapN , (O, TA,) [or a fem. pass. part. n. used as an inf. n. like as is said of its contr. mako*uwbapN ,] he spoke, said, uttered, or told, truth, or truly, or veraciously; contr. of ka*aba : (Msb: [and in like manner it is said in the S and M and O and K that SidoqN is the contr. of ka*ibN :]) Er-Rághib says that SidoqN and ka*ibN are primarily in what is said, whether relating to the past or to the future, and [in the latter case] whether it be a promise or other than a promise; and only in what is said in the way of information: but sometimes they are in other modes of speech, such as asking a question, and commanding, and supplicating; as when one says, “ Is Zeyd in the house? ” for this implies information of his being ignorant of the state of Zeyd; and when one says, “ Make me to share with thee, or to be equal with thee, ” for this implies his requiring to be made to share with the other, or to be made equal with him; and when one says, “ Do not thou hurt me, ” for this implies that the other is hurting him: SidoqN , he says, is [by implication] the agreeing of what is said with what is conceived in the mind and with the thing told of, together; otherwise it is not complete Sidoq , but may be described either as Sidoq or sometimes as Sidoq and sometimes as ka*ib according to two different points of view; as when one says without believing it, “ Mohammad is the Apostle of God, ” for this may be termed Sidoq because what is told is such, and it may be termed ka*ib because it is at variance with what the speaker conceives in his mind. (TA.) One says, Sadaqa fiY AlHadiyvi [ He spoke truth in the information, or narration ]. (S, O, K.) And Sadaqahu i. e. He told him, or informed him, with truth, or veracity, (AHeyth, * M, Msb, *) fiY Alqawoli [ in the saying ]; for it is trans. as well as intrans. (Msb.) And Sadaqahu AlHadiyva (S, O, K, in the CK [erroneously] Sad~aqa fulAnFA AlHadiyva ) He told him with truth, or veracity, the information, or narration; for it is sometimes doubly trans. (TA.) And SadaqaniY sin~a bakorihi [ He hath told me truly the age, or as to the age, of his youthful camel; or SadaqaniY sin~u bakorihi the age of his youthful camel has spoken truly to me ]: (S, O, K:) a prov., (S, O,) expl. in art. bkr [q. v.]. (K.) And fulaAnN laA yaSoduqu A^avaruhu and A^avarahu , meaning Such a one, when asked, will not tell truly whence he comes. (M.) And Sadaqato yamiynuhu His oath was, or proved, true. (Msb in art. bt .) Sadaqotu A@ll~`ha HadiyvFA A_ino lamo A^afoEalo ka*aA is an oath of the Arabs, meaning laA Sadaqotu Alx [ May I not utter truly to God a saying, i. e. may I not speak truth to God, if I do not such a thing ]. (AHeyth, O, K.) One says also, Sadaqahu Aln~aSiyHapa , and AlA_ixaA='a , He rendered to him truly, or sincerely, good advice, and brotherly affection. (M.) And Sada quwhumu AlqitaAla (S, M, K, * TA) [ They gave them battle earnestly, not with a false show of bravery; as is implied in the S, and M, and K; i. e.] they advanced against them boldly in fight: (M, TA:) and in like manner, SadaquwA fiY AlqitaAli they advanced boldly in fight: or, accord. to Er-Rághib, the former means they gave them battle so as to fulfil their duty: and hence, in the Kur [xxxiii. 23], rijaAlN SadaquwA maA EaAhaduwA A@ll~`ha Ealayohi , Men who fulfilled the covenant that they had made with God. (TA.) And Sadaqa All~iqaA='a , inf. n. SidoqN , He was firm, or steady, in encounter, or conflict. (M, TA.) And Sadaqa Zan~iY My opinion was, or proved, true, or correct, like as one says [in the contrary case], ka*aba : (Er-Rághib, TA:) whence, in the Kur [xxxiv. 19], walaqado Sadaqa Ealayohimo A_iboliysu Zan~ahu , meaning fiY Zan~ihi [i. e. And assuredly Iblees was, or proved to be, correct in his opinion that he had formed against them ]: but some read ↓ Sad~aqa , meaning, as Fr says, Haq~aqa [i. e. Iblees proved, or found, to be true, his opinion &c.]. (TA.) And Sadaqatohu nafosuhu His soul [ told him truth; meaning,] diverted him, or hindered him, or held him back, from an undertaking, causing him to imagine himself unable to prosecute it. (TA in art. k*b .) And Sadaqa AlS~uboHu [ The dawn shone clearly ]. (S in art. sqT .) [And one says of a word or the like, yaSoduqu EalaY ka*aA , meaning It applies correctly to such a thing. ] ― -b2- Sadaqa AlwaHo$iY~u : see 2, near the end.

sourceDefinition: , (S, M, O, &c.,) inf. n. taSodiyqN , contr. of ka*~abahu . (O, * K.) [This explanation implies several meanings here following.] He attributed, or ascribed, to him truth, veracity, or the speaking truth. (Msb.) And He said to him, “ Thou hast spoken truth. ” (Msb.) He accepted, or admitted, [or assented to, or believed, ] what he said: (M:) you say, Sd~qhu fiY Hadiyvihi [ He accepted, &c., what he said in his information, or narration ]: (S:) and you say Sd~q bilisaAnihi [ He assented to the truth of what was said with his tongue ]; as well as biqalobihi [ with his heart, or mind ]. (T in art. Aamn .) He held him to be a speaker of truth. (MA.) [ He found him to be a speaker of truth. He, or it, proved him to be a speaker of truth; verified him; or confirmed the truth of what he said: see an ex. in a verse cited voce bayonN .] He found it (an opinion) to be true, or veritable. (Ksh and Bd and Jel, in xxxiv. 19.) He verified it; confirmed its truth; or proved it to be true, or veritable; i. e. an opinion [&c.]; syn. Haq~aqahu : (Ksh and Bd, ibid.:) one says, Sad~aqa Alxabara Alxuboru [ The trial, proof, or test, verified the information ]. (S in art. xbr .) See 1, near the end. In the saying in the Kur [xxxix. 34], waA@l~a*iY jaA='a biAlS~idoqi waSad~aqa bihi , [which seems to be best rendered But he who hath brought the truth and he who hath accepted it as the truth, (see ka*~aba biAlA^amori ,)] 'Alee the son of Aboo-Tálib is related to have said that by Al*Y jA=' bAlSdq is meant Mohammad; and by Al*Y Sd~q bh , Aboo-Bekr: or, as some say, Gabriel and Mohammad [are meant by the former and the latter respectively]: or by the former, Mohammad; and by the latter, [every one of] the believers: (M:) accord. to Er-Rághib, by wSd~q bh is meant and hath found, or proved, to be true ( Haq~aqa ) that which he hath brought by word, by that which he hath aimed at ( bimaA taHar~aAhu ) by deed. (TA.) ― -b2- Sd~q is also said to signify He said, “ This thing is the truth; ” like Haq~aqa . (TA in art. Hq .) ― -b3- And this verb also denotes AlmubaAlagapu fiY AlS~idoqi : thus in the saying, Sad~aqato fiyhimo ZunuwniY [ My opinions respecting them were, or proved to be, very true or correct ]. (Ksh, in xxxiv. 19.) ― -b4- Sd~q AlwaHo$iY~u , (O, K, TA,) or ↓ Sadaqa , (so in a copy of the M,) (tropical:) The wild animal ran without looking aside, when charged upon, or attacked: (M, O, K, TA:) mentioned by IDrd. (O, TA.) -A2- Sad~aqahumo He exacted from them the poor-rate. (TA. [See SadaqapN .]) ― -b2- See also 5.

sourceDefinition: He gave him (i. e. the poor, Mgh, Msb) what is termed Sadaqap , (M, Mgh, Msb,) meaning [ an alms, or] what is given for the sake of God, (M,) or what is given with the desire of obtaining a recompense from God: (M, * Mgh:) and Elyh ↓ Sad~aqa signifies the same; (M, TA;) and in this sense Sd~q is [said by some to be] used in the Kur lxxv. 31. (TA.) Hence, in the Kur [xii. 88], wataSad~aqo EalayonaA : (TA:) or this means (assumed tropical:) And do thou confer a favour upon us by giving that which is [not like the mean merchandise that we have brought, but of middling quality,] between good and bad. (M.) One says, taSad~aqotu bika*aA , meaning I gave such a thing as a Sadaqap . (Msb.) See an ex. voce $iq~N . The saying, in a trad., A_in~a A@ll~`ha taSad~aqa Ealayokumo bivuluvi A^amowaAlikumo , meaning (tropical:) [ Verily God ] hath conferred a favour [ upon you by giving you a third of your possessions to bequeath to whom ye will], if correct, is tropical. (Mgh.) ― -b2- It is said by Ibn-Es-Seed, on the authority of AZ and IJ, and mentioned by IAmb, that tSd~q signifies also He asked, or begged, for what is termed Sadaqap [or alms ]: but Fr and As and others disallow the beggar's being called mutaSad~iq : (Az, TA:) IKt says that the verb is improperly used in this sense by the vulgar: (Msb:) [and accord. to J and Sgh,] one says, mararotu birajulK yasoA^alu , and one should not say yataSad~aqu . (S, O.)

It is said by Ibn-Es-Seed, on the authority of AZ and IJ, and mentioned by IAmb, that tSd~q signifies also He asked, or begged, for what is termed Sadaqap [or alms ]: but Fr and As and others disallow the beggar's being called mutaSad~iq : (Az, TA:) IKt says that the verb is improperly used in this sense by the vulgar: (Msb:) [and accord. to J and Sgh,] one says, mararotu birajulK yasoA^alu , and one should not say yataSad~aqu . (S, O.)

sourceDefinition: is an inf. n. of Sadaqa [q. v.]: (M, K:) ― -b2- and is used as an epithet, applied to a man &c.: (S, M, O, K, TA:) [and] ↓ SidoqN [also, if not a mistranscription for SadoqN ,] is an inf. n. used as an epithet, applied to a man and to a woman: (so in a copy of the M and in the TA:) [it is said that] the former signifies Hard, (S, M, O, Msb,) applied to a spear, (S, M, O,) and to other things: (M:) or even, or straight; (S, O;) or it signifies thus also, applied to a spear, and to a sword: (M:) or hard and even or straight, applied to a spear, (K, TA,) and to a man, (K,) or to the latter as meaning hard: or, as IB says, on the authority of IDrst, it is not from hardness, but means combining those qualities that are commended; and it is applied to a spear as meaning long and pliant and hard, and the like; and to a man, and to a woman likewise [without p , but see what follows], as meaning true in hardness and strength and goodness; for, IDrst says, if it meant hard, one would say HajarN SadoqN and HadiydN SadoqN , which one does not: (TA:) and, applied to anything, (O, K, TA,) it means complete, or perfect, (Kh, O, K, TA,) thus applied to a man, (TA,) such as is commended; (O;) fem. with p , (O, K, TA,) applied to a woman: (O:) the pl. is SudoqN , applied to a company of men, (S, O, K,) and SuduqN (K) and Sadoquwna , so applied, and SadoqaAtN applied to women: (O, K:) and Ru-beh says, describing asses, maqo*uw*apu AlA=*aAni SadoqaAtu AlHadaqo meaning [ Rounded, as though pared, in the ears, ] penetrating in the eyes; (O, TA;) which is [said to be] tropical. (TA.) SadoqN signifies also Firm, or steady, in encounter, or conflict: (M:) or one says Sadoqu All~iqaA='i , applying this epithet to a man, (S, O, K, TA,) meaning thus: (TA:) and Sadoqu Aln~aZari [ firm, or steady, in look ]. (S, O, K, TA. [Said in the TA to be tropical.])

sourceDefinition: is an inf. n. of Sadaqa [q. v.]: (M, K, &c.:) or a simple subst., (K,) signifying [ Truth; veracity; or] agreement of what is said with what is conceived in the mind and with the thing told of, together; otherwise it is not complete Sidoq , as expl. above in the first paragraph of this art. (Er-Rághib, TA.) ― -b2- It is also syn. with $id~apN [meaning Hardness; firmness, compactness, or soundness; strength, power, or force; vigour, robustness, sturdiness, or hardiness; and courage, bravery, or firmness of heart ]: (K, TA: [in the latter of which it is said to be tropical; but this is evidently not the case accord. to the O, in which it is said that it radically denotes quw~apN (i. e. strength, force, &c.,) in a saying &c.: in the K it is implied by the context that it is syn. with $id~ap when used as the complement of a prefixed n. in instances mentioned in what here follows: but Sgh says, more correctly,]) a noun signifying anything to which goodness is attributed is prefixed to Sidoq , governing it in the gen. case; so that one says (O) rajulu SidoqK (Sb, M, O, K) [ A man of good nature or disposition or character &c.], contr. of rajulu sawo'K ; (Sb, M;) and Sadiyqu SidoqK [ a friend of good nature &c.]; (O, K;) and likewise AimoraA^apu SidoqK [ a woman of good nature &c.]; (K;) and in like manner also HimaAru SidoqK [ an ass of a good kind ]; (Sb, M, K;) and vawobu SidoqK [ a garment, or piece of cloth, of good quality ]. (Sb, M.) The saying in the Kur [x. 93], (O,) walaqado baw~aA^onaA baniY AisoraAy^iyla mubaw~aA^a SidoqK means And verily we assigned to the Children of Israel a good place of abode. (O, K.) ― -b3- See also SadoqN .

definition: [ An alms; i. e.] a gift (S, M, Mgh, O, Msb, K) to the poor (S, O, Msb) for the sake of God, (M, K,) or to obtain a recompense from God; (M, * Mgh, K; *) a portion which a man gives forth from his...
sourceDefinition: [ An alms; i. e.] a gift (S, M, Mgh, O, Msb, K) to the poor (S, O, Msb) for the sake of God, (M, K,) or to obtain a recompense from God; (M, * Mgh, K; *) a portion which a man gives forth from his property by way of propitiation, [ to obtain the favour of God, ] like zakaApN , except that the former is primarily applied to such as as is supererogatory, and the latter to such as is obligatory: but it is said to be applied to such as is obligatory [i. e. to the zakaAp , q. v., meaning the poor-rate, which is the portion, or amount, of property, that is given therefrom, as the due of God, by its possessor, to the poor, according to a fixed rate, ] when the person who does so aims at conformity with the truth in his deed: (Er-Rághib, TA:) [in this latter sense, which is indicated in the S and O &c., and more plainly in the M, it is very frequently used:] and thus it is used in the Kur ix. 104, and in like manner its pl. in ix. 60: (Er-Rághib, TA:) the pl. is SadaqaAtN . (S, M, O, Msb.) It is said in a trad., laA Sadaqapa fiY AlA_ibili AljaAr~api [ There is no poorrate in the case of working camels ], because they are the riding-camels of the people; for the poorrate is in the case of pasturing camels, exclusively of the working. (S in art. jr .) ― -b2- See also SadaAqN .

sourceDefinition: One who speaks, says, utters, or tells, truth, or truly, or veraciously, much, or often: (Mgh, O, K:) [or rather having the quality of speaking, saying, uttering, or telling, truth, or truly, or veraciously, in a very high, or very eminent, degree; for] it has a more intensive signification than SaduwqN [q. v.]: (TA:) or i. q. muSad~iqN [which may have the latter of the two meanings expl. above, or may mean one who accepts, or admits, the truth of what is said, or who verifies, &c.: or muSad~iq in a high, or an eminent, degree; for it is added that] the fem. as used in the Kur v. 79 means superlative in AlS~idoq and Alt~aSodiyq ; as a possessive epithet, i. e. *aAtu taSodiyqK : (M:) or it signifies daAy^imu Alt~aSodiyqi [i. e. always muSad~iq in one or another or all of the senses assigned to this word above: it may be correctly rendered eminently, or always, veracious: and eminently, or always, accepting, or confirming, the truth ]: and it may mean one who verifies his saying by deed, or act: (S:) it is said in the “ Mufradát ” [of Er-Rághib] that it has the first of the meanings expl. in this paragraph: or rather means, one who never lies: or rather, one by whom lying cannot be practised because of his habitual veracity: or rather, one who is true in his saying and his belief, and who confirms his truth by his deed, or acting. definition: The small star cleaving to the middle one of [ those called ] banaAtu naEo$K AlkuboraY [ which compose the tail of Ursa Major ];
sourceDefinition: The small star cleaving to the middle one of [ those called ] banaAtu naEo$K AlkuboraY [ which compose the tail of Ursa Major ]; (Kr, M, TA;) [i. e. the star called Als~uhaA , q. v.; for] it is said that the first of bnAt nE$ AlkbrY , that is at the extremity thereof, is named AlqaAy^idu ; and the second is AlEanaAqu , and by the side of it is a small star named Als~uhaA and AlS~ayodaqu ; and the third is AlHawaru : (O:) or, accord. to AA, (O, TA,) the pole-star ( AlquTobu ). (O, K, TA. [But this is strange; and the more so as it is added in the K that it is expl. in art. qwd ; for the explanation in that art. (though not free from obvious mistakes) identifies AlS~ayodaqu with Als~uhaA .]) ― -b2- And, (K,) accord. to Sh, (O, TA,) it signifies AlA^amiynu [ The trusted, trusted in, or confided in, &c.]. (O, K. [But it is added in the O that Sh cites a verse of Umeiyeh Ibn-Abi- s-Salt in which AlA^amiynu is applied as an epithet to the star called AlSaydq .]) ― -b3- And, (K,) accord. to some, as AA says, (O,) it signifies The king. (O, K.)

sourceDefinition: , (JK, S, M, O,) with fet-h, (S,) or ↓ *uw miSodaqK like minobar , (K,) applied to a man, (JK, M,) [i. e.] applied to a courageous man, (S, O, K,) means AlHamolapi ↓ SaAdiqu [ Earnest, not making a false show of bravery, in the charge, or assault ]; (JK, S, M, O, K;) or courageous [ in the charge, or assault ]: (JK:) maSaAdiqu , occurring in a verse of Aboo-Dhu-eyb, may be for *awuw maSaAdiqa ; or it may be an anomalous pl. of SidoqN [used as an epithet], like malaAmiHu and ma$aAbihu [pls. of lamoHapN and $abahN ]. (M.) Also, (S, M, O, K,) applied to a horse, (M,) [i. e.] applied to a fleet and excellent horse, (S, O,) in like manner, (M,) meaning AljaroYi ↓ SaAdiqu [ Earnest in running ]; (S, O, K;) as though fulfilling his promise of running: (S, O: [said in the TA to be tropical:]) Khufáf Ibn-Nudbeh says, A_i*aA maA A@sotaHam~ato A^aroDuhu mino samaAy^ihi jaraY wahowa mawoduwEN wawaAEidu maSodaqi meaning When his hoofs are wetted with the sweat of his upper parts, he runs, being left to himself, not beaten nor chidden, and a fulfiller of his promise to do his utmost. (S, O.) And sometimes it is applied to an opinion, in like manner [as meaning True, or sincere ]. (M.) ― -b2- maSodaqN also signifies Hardness. (Th, M.) ― -b3- Also i. q. Had~N [as meaning The edge of a sword]: (TA:) [in a copy of the M written jid~ , which I think an evident mistake; for it is added,] and it is said to have this meaning in a verse of Dureyd Ibn-Es- Simmeh [relating to a sword]. (M, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (inf. n. taSoliybN , TA,) He, or it, rendered it, or him, hard, firm, rigid, stiff, tough, strong, robust, sturdy, or hardy. (S, M, K, TA.) El-Aashà says, mino saraApi AlhijaAni Sal~abahaA AlEu D~u wariEoYu AlHimaY waTuwlu AlHiyaAli (S, TA) i. e. [ Than the back of the excellent she-camel ] which the provender of cities, such as [the trefoil called] qat~ , and date-stones, and the pasture of El-Himè, meaning Himè Dareeyeh, the place of pasture of the camels of the kings, and the being long without conceiving, (TA,) have rendered hard, or firm, or strong. (S, TA.) ― -b2- [Hence] one says, Sl~b Aln~abiy*a biHab~i Ald~aA*iY~i (assumed tropical:) [ He made the beverage termed nby* to become strong by means of the grain called Hb~ AldA*Y~ ]. (Mgh in art. dw* .) -A2- Sal~aba Alr~uTabu , (AA, S, K,) inf. n. taSoliybN , (AA, TA,) The ripe dates became dry: (AA, S, K:) and Sal~abati Alt~amorapu the date became dry. (M, L.) ― -b2- [Hence, perhaps, Sal~aba is said in the K to be syn. with Saluba :] see 1, first sentence. -A3- See also 1, latter half, in two places. ― -b2- Sl~b said of a monk, (M,) or Sl~bwA (K, TA) said of monks, (TA,) He, (M,) or they, (K, TA,) made, or took, (M, K, TA,) for himself, (M,) or for themselves, (K, TA,) a Saliyb [or cross ], (M, K, TA,) in his church, (M,) or in their churches. (TA.) ― -b3- Alt~aSoliybu also signifies [ The making the sign of the cross. And] The figuring of a cross [or crosses ] upon a garment; (T, Mgh, TA;) and hence, the figure thereof; the inf. n. being thus used as a subst. properly so termed; (Mgh;) as in a trad. where it is said of the Prophet, qaDaba Alt~aSoliyba ; meaning qaTaEa mawoDiEa Alt~aSoliybi minohu [ He cut off the place of the figuring of the cross, or crosses, from it ]. (T, Mgh, TA.) And Sal~aba bayona Eayonayohi occurs in a trad., meaning He made a mark like the cross between his eyes by a blow. (TA.) ― -b4- Also A particular mode of wearing, or disposing, the [ muffler called ] ximaAr , (M, K,) for a woman. (K.) One says of a woman, Sal~abato ximaArahaA [ She disposed her muffler cross-wise ]. (TA.) And a man's praying fiY taSoliybi AlEimaAmapi [ with the turban disposed cross-wise ] is disapproved: he should wind it so that one part [or fold] thereof is above [not across] another. (TA.)

definition: Hard, firm, rigid, stiff, tough, strong, robust, sturdy, or hardy;
sourceDefinition: Hard, firm, rigid, stiff, tough, strong, robust, sturdy, or hardy; syn. $adiydN ; (S, A, Msb, * K;) contr. of lay~inN ; (M, TA;) as also ↓ SaliybN and ↓ Sul~abN (S, M, A, K) and ↓ SalabN : (M:) pl. of the first or second, [accord. to analogy of the latter, and also of the last,] SilaAbN . (M, A.) ― -b2- [Hence,] SulobN and ↓ SalabN , (K,) or makaAnN SulobN and ↓ SalabN , (M,) A rugged, stony place: (M, K; *) or SulobN signifies a rugged, extending place, of the earth or ground; and ↓ SalabN , a hard part of the earth or ground: (S:) or this last, a tract of rugged depressed land stretching along between two hills: (Sh, TA:) or the acclivities of hills; and its pl. is A^aSolaAbN : (TA:) or A^aSolaAbN signifies hard, extending, [ tracts of] ground: (As, TA:) or hard and elevated [ tracts of] ground: (IAar, TA:) and makaAnN SulobN , a rugged, hard place: (Msb:) the pl. (of SulobN , S) is SilabapN . (S, M, K.) One says of land that has not been sown for a long time, ↓ A_in~ahaA A^aSolaAbN muno*u A^aEowaAmK (tropical:) [ Verily it has been hard by lying waste for years ]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] huwa Sulobu AlmaEaAjimi (tropical:) [lit. He is hard, &c., in respect of the places of biting; meaning he is strong, or resisting, or indomitable, of spirit; ( Eaziyzu Aln~afosi ;) thus Sulobu AlmaEojami is expl. in the S and K in art. Ejm ]: and Sulobu AlEuwdi (tropical:) [which means the same]. (A, TA.) And Sulobu AlEaSaA and AlEaSaA ↓ Saliybu , applied to a tender of camels; [lit. Hard, &c., in respect of the staff; ] meaning (assumed tropical:) hard, severe, or rigorous, in his treatment of the camels: Er-Rá'ee says, AlEaSaA baAdiY AlEuruwqi taraY lahu ↓ Saliyobu EalayohaA A_i*aA maA A^ajodaba Aln~aAsu A_iSobaEaA [ Hard, &c., having the veins of his limbs appearing: thou wilt see him to have a finger pointing at them, i. e. his camels, because of their good condition, when the people are afflicted with drought ]. (M, TA. But in the S, in art. SbE , we find DaEiyf in this verse instead of Saliyb .) ― -b4- And [in like manner] huwa SulobN fiY diynihi and ↓ Sul~abN (tropical:) [ He is hard, firm, or strong, in his religion ]. (A, TA.) ― -b5- And jaroYN SulobN (Lth, TA) or ↓ SaliybN (M, L, TA) (tropical:) A hard, or vehement, running. (Lth, M, L, TA.) ― -b6- And SahiylN SulobN (assumed tropical:) A vehement neighing. (Lth, TA.) And SawotN ↓ SaliybN (tropical:) A vehement sound or cry or voice. (M, L, TA.) -A2- Also, (S, M, A, Msb, K,) and ↓ SulubN (Msb, TA) and ↓ SalabN (S, M, A, K) and ↓ SaAlibN , (IAth, L, K,) which last is rarely used, (IAth, TA,) and is said to occur only in one instance, in poetry, but another instance of it in poetry is cited, (TA,) The back-bone; i. e. the bone extending from the kaAhil [or base of the neck ] to the Eajob [or rump bone ]; (M, A, K;) the bone upon which the neck is set, extending to the root of the tail [ in a beast ], and in a man to the EuSoEuS [or os coccygis ]: (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or a portion of the back: (S:) and any portion of the back containing vertebræ: (S, Msb, TA:) [and particularly the lumbar portion; the lions: ] and the back [absolutely]; as is said in an explanation of a verse of 'Adee Ibn-Zeyd cited in what follows: (M, TA:) pl. [of mult.] SilabapN and [of pauc.] A^aSolubN and A^aSolaAbN , (M, K,) each of which two is used in poetry in a sing. sense, as though every part of the Sulob were regarded as a Sulob in itself, and SilobapN , (M, TA,) of which last ISd says, [but this I do not find in the M,] I do not think it to be of established authority, unless it be a contraction of SilabapN . (TA.) Lh mentions, as a phrase of the Arabs, h`w^ulaA='i A^abonaA='u Silabatihimo [ These are the sons of their loins: because the sperma of the man is held to proceed from the Sulob of the man, as is said in the Ksh &c. in lxxxvi. 7]. (M. [See also a similar phrase in the Kr iv. 27.]) ― -b2- [Hence SulobN is used as signifying The middle of a page, as distinguished from the haAmi$ (or margin): and in like manner, of other things.] ― -b3- [Hence, likewise,] SulobN signifies also HasabN [meaning (assumed tropical:) Rank or quality, &c.]: (AA, S, M, K:) and power, or strength. (M, K.) A poet says, (M,) namely, 'Adee Ibn-Zeyd, (S, TA,) A_ijola A^an~a A@ll~`ha qado faD~alakumo fawoqa maA A^aHokiY biSulobK waA_izaAro (assumed tropical:) [ Because God hath made you to have excellence above what I can relate, in rank or quality, or in power, and abstinence from unlawful things ]: (S, M, TA:) AA says that Sulob here signifies Hasab ; (S;) and A_izaAr here signifies EafaAf : (S, M, TA:) but some expl. Sulob here by both Hasab and quw~ap : and some relate the latter hemistich otherwise, i. e. fawoqa mano A^aHokaA^a SulobFA biA_izaAro meaning above such as binds the back with an izár. (M, TA.) And it is said in a trad., A_in~a AlmugaAliba Suloba A@ll~`hi magoluwbN , meaning (assumed tropical:) [ Verily he who strives to overcome ] the power of God [ is overcome ]. (TA.) ― -b4- Also Coitus ( jimaAE ): because the sperma [of the man] issues from the part so called. (TA.)

(M, A.) ― -b2- [Hence,] SulobN and ↓ SalabN , (K,) or makaAnN SulobN and ↓ SalabN , (M,) A rugged, stony place: (M, K; *) or SulobN signifies a rugged, extending place, of the earth or ground; and ↓ SalabN , a hard part of the earth or ground: (S:) or this last, a tract of rugged depressed land stretching along between two hills: (Sh, TA:) or the acclivities of hills; and its pl. is A^aSolaAbN : (TA:) or A^aSolaAbN signifies hard, extending, [ tracts of] ground: (As, TA:) or hard and elevated [ tracts of] ground: (IAar, TA:) and makaAnN SulobN , a rugged, hard place: (Msb:) the pl. (of SulobN , S) is SilabapN . (S, M, K.) One says of land that has not been sown for a long time, ↓ A_in~ahaA A^aSolaAbN muno*u A^aEowaAmK (tropical:) [ Verily it has been hard by lying waste for years ]. (A, TA.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] huwa Sulobu AlmaEaAjimi (tropical:) [lit. He is hard, &c., in respect of the places of biting; meaning he is strong, or resisting, or indomitable, of spirit; ( Eaziyzu Aln~afosi ;) thus Sulobu AlmaEojami is expl. in the S and K in art. Ejm ]: and Sulobu AlEuwdi (tropical:) [which means the same]. (A, TA.) And Sulobu AlEaSaA and AlEaSaA ↓ Saliybu , applied to a tender of camels; [lit. Hard, &c., in respect of the staff; ] meaning (assumed tropical:) hard, severe, or rigorous, in his treatment of the camels: Er-Rá'ee says, AlEaSaA baAdiY AlEuruwqi taraY lahu ↓ Saliyobu EalayohaA A_i*aA maA A^ajodaba Aln~aAsu A_iSobaEaA [ Hard, &c., having the veins of his limbs appearing: thou wilt see him to have a finger pointing at them, i. e. his camels, because of their good condition, when the people are afflicted with drought ]. (M, TA. But in the S, in art. SbE , we find DaEiyf in this verse instead of Saliyb .) ― -b4- And [in like manner] huwa SulobN fiY diynihi and ↓ Sul~abN (tropical:) [ He is hard, firm, or strong, in his religion ]. (A, TA.) ― -b5- And jaroYN SulobN (Lth, TA) or ↓ SaliybN (M, L, TA) (tropical:) A hard, or vehement, running. (Lth, M, L, TA.) ― -b6- And SahiylN SulobN (assumed tropical:) A vehement neighing. (Lth, TA.) And SawotN ↓ SaliybN (tropical:) A vehement sound or cry or voice. (M, L, TA.) -A2- Also, (S, M, A, Msb, K,) and ↓ SulubN (Msb, TA) and ↓ SalabN (S, M, A, K) and ↓ SaAlibN , (IAth, L, K,) which last is rarely used, (IAth, TA,) and is said to occur only in one instance, in poetry, but another instance of it in poetry is cited, (TA,) The back-bone; i. e. the bone extending from the kaAhil [or base of the neck ] to the Eajob [or rump bone ]; (M, A, K;) the bone upon which the neck is set, extending to the root of the tail [ in a beast ], and in a man to the EuSoEuS [or os coccygis ]: (Zj in his “ Khalk el-Insán: ”) or a portion of the back: (S:) and any portion of the back containing vertebræ: (S, Msb, TA:) [and particularly the lumbar portion; the lions: ] and the back [absolutely]; as is said in an explanation of a verse of 'Adee Ibn-Zeyd cited in what follows: (M, TA:) pl. [of mult.] SilabapN and [of pauc.] A^aSolubN and A^aSolaAbN , (M, K,) each of which two is used in poetry in a sing. sense, as though every part of the Sulob were regarded as a Sulob in itself, and SilobapN , (M, TA,) of which last ISd says, [but this I do not find in the M,] I do not think it to be of established authority, unless it be a contraction of SilabapN . (TA.) Lh mentions, as a phrase of the Arabs, h`w^ulaA='i A^abonaA='u Silabatihimo [ These are the sons of their loins: because the sperma of the man is held to proceed from the Sulob of the man, as is said in the Ksh &c. in lxxxvi. 7]. (M. [See also a similar phrase in the Kr iv. 27.]) ― -b2- [Hence SulobN is used as signifying The middle of a page, as distinguished from the haAmi$ (or margin): and in like manner, of other things.] ― -b3- [Hence, likewise,] SulobN signifies also HasabN [meaning (assumed tropical:) Rank or quality, &c.]: (AA, S, M, K:) and power, or strength. (M, K.) A poet says, (M,) namely, 'Adee Ibn-Zeyd, (S, TA,) A_ijola A^an~a A@ll~`ha qado faD~alakumo fawoqa maA A^aHokiY biSulobK waA_izaAro (assumed tropical:) [ Because God hath made you to have excellence above what I can relate, in rank or quality, or in power, and abstinence from unlawful things ]: (S, M, TA:) AA says that Sulob here signifies Hasab ; (S;) and A_izaAr here signifies EafaAf : (S, M, TA:) but some expl. Sulob here by both Hasab and quw~ap : and some relate the latter hemistich otherwise, i. e. fawoqa mano A^aHokaA^a SulobFA biA_izaAro meaning above such as binds the back with an izár. (M, TA.) definition: A hot fever; contr. of naAfiDN [which means “ attended with shivering, or trembling ”]: (S:) or a fever not such as is termed naAfiDN : (M:) or a fever attended with vehement heat, and not attended...
sourceDefinition: A hot fever; contr. of naAfiDN [which means “ attended with shivering, or trembling ”]: (S:) or a fever not such as is termed naAfiDN : (M:) or a fever attended with vehement heat, and not attended with cold: (TA:) or a fever attended with tremour (A, K, TA) and quivering of the skin: (TA:) or a continual fever: (Msb:) or a fever attended with SudaAE [or headache ]: (Ham p. 345:) it is said by Ibn-Buzurj to be from the SudaAE : (L, TA:) it is masc. and fem.: one says, A^axa*atohu AlHum~aY biSaAlibK [which may be rendered Fever with burning heat, &c., seized him ] and A^axa*atohu Hum~aY SaAlibN [virtually meaning the same]; the former of which is the more chaste: and one seldom or never makes one of the two nouns to govern the other in the gen. case: (M, TA:) or, accord. to Fr, they said Hum~aY SaAlibN and Hum~aY SaAlibK and SaAlibu Hum~aY . (MF, TA.) SaAlibiY A^a$ad~u mino naAfiDika [ My burning fever, or continual fever, &c., is more severe than thy fever attended with shivering ] is a prov., (Meyd, TA,) applied to two things, or events, of which one is more severe than the other. (Meyd.) -A2- See also SulobN , in the middle of the paragraph.

definition: , applied to hair, (A, TA,) [and to camel's fur or hair,] and to a man, (S,) and to a camel, (A,) or to a male [of mankind and of camels], (Mgh, Msb,) fem.
sourceDefinition: , applied to hair, (A, TA,) [and to camel's fur or hair,] and to a man, (S,) and to a camel, (A,) or to a male [of mankind and of camels], (Mgh, Msb,) fem. SahobaA='u : (A, Mgh, Msb:) pl. SuhobN : (S, A, Msb, K:) Of the colour termed Suhobap [expl. above]: (S, A, Mgh, Msb:) as some say, (TA,) applied to hair, it means having redness intermixed with its whiteness: (K, TA:) accord. to As, it is nearly the same as A^aSobaHu : (TA:) applied to a camel, having redness intermixed with his whiteness, the upper part of the fur being red, and the inner parts white: (S:) or not having the inner parts [ of the fur ] intensely white, the flanks and sides having somewhat of whiteness; the AShb being less white than what is termed A=damu , having a dusky hue in the upper parts and a whiteness in the lower parts: (T, TA:) or not intensely white: (K:) or, accord. to IAar, white: and he says that the Suhob and A^udom were called by the Arabs “ the Kureysh of camels, ” i. e. the most noble, and the best, as Kureysh were considered by them the best of them; also, that Suhobap was said to be the most famous and the best of colours, and that a she-camel of that colour was said to be the most swift of all: [see also A^aHomaru as applied to a camel:] but accord. to As, A=damu applied to a camel signifies white; and A^aSohabu , white intermixed with redness: (TA:) [see also SuhaAbiY~N :] the dim. is ↓ A^uSayohibu . (Msb.) ― -b2- Suhobu Als~ibaAli [lit. Persons red, or reddish, &c., in respect of the mustaches, &c.,] is a designation of (tropical:) enemies; and is applied to them even if not really Suhobu Als~ibaAli : (As, S, A, * L, K:) originally applied to the Greeks ( Alr~uwm ), because redness of the hair was [common] among them, and they were enemies of the Arabs: (S, L, TA:) applied to others, it designates them as being as great enemies as the Greeks. (TA.) ― -b3- AlA^aSohabu is an appellation of The lion: (K:) because of his colour. (TA.) ― -b4- And [for the same reason] A^aSohabu is a designation of The male ostrich. (L, TA.) ― -b5- Hence also (S, TA) AlS~ahobaA='u signifies Wine: (S, K:) or wine expressed from white grapes: (K:) used in this sense as a proper name: (AHn, K:) but also used without the article Al ; being originally an epithet. (TA.) ― -b6- yawomN A^aSohabu (tropical:) A cold day: (K:) or a day intensely cold. (A, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, IB, O,) or ↓ SiySapN , (K,) thus in all the copies of the K, but it is a mistake, or a contracted form, (TA,) The weaver's [ implement called ] $awokap , with which he makes the warp and the woof even: (S, IB, K:) but IB says that its last radical letter is Y , not S ; so that it should be mentioned among the class of infirm words: (TA;) pl. SayaASK . (S.) ― -b2- Hence, (S,) The spur of the cock. (S, K.) ― -b3- [Hence also,] The horn of the bull or cow, and of the gazelle: (K:) pl. as above, (TA,) signifying the horns of bulls or cows; which were sometimes fixed upon spears, instead of the iron heads: (S:) and to such horns, called by this name, conflict and faction, or sedition, ( fitonap ,) is likened in a trad., because of its grievousness: some say that the sing. is SiySapN , [as in the K,] contracted. (TA.) ― -b4- And hence, (TA,) A wooden pin, or peg, with which dates are plucked out [ when they are compacted in a mass, closely adhering together, in the receptacle of woven palm-leaves, or the like, in which they are packed ]: (K:) likened to the horn of a bull or cow: in this sense, the word is written SiySapN : and a certain poet changes it to SiySaj~ . (TA.) ― -b5- [Hence also,] Anything with which one defends himself: pl. as above, (K,) [in the CK erroneously written SayaASiY , as though it had the article Al prefixed to it, or were itself prefixed to another noun, for otherwise it is written and pronounced] with the [final] Y elided. (TA.) ― -b6- [Hence also,] A fortress: (K:) pl. in this sense as above. (S, TA.) ― -b7- [Hence also,] A pastor who manages [ and protects ] well his herds or flocks: (AA, K:) in this sense also written SiySapN . (AA, as in the TA.)

sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) aor. , (K,) inf. n. DabovN , (S,) He grasped, seized, or laid hold upon, him, or it, with his hand; as also ↓ ADTbv : (S, K:) or, accord. to an explanation of the inf. n. by Ibn-Es-Seed, he did so with the utmost vehemence, or strength: (TA:) or he grasped, seized, or laid hold upon, and took, him, or it: (Sh, TA:) or Dabava Ealayohi has the first of these meanings; (A, L;) as also Dabavahu : (A:) and Dabava bihi signifies he seized him violently, or laid violent hands upon him. (A, TA.) ― -b2- Also, i. e. Dabava bihi , aor. and inf. n. as above, He applied his hand to it, namely, a thing that he was making, or doing, diligently, earnestly, or with painstaking. (TA.) ― -b3- And Dabavahu He beat, struck, or smote, him, namely, a man. (K.) ― -b4- And He felt, for the purpose of testing, him, or it, with his hand. (TA.) One says, of a she-camel, tuDobavu , meaning She is felt with the hand, when one doubts of her fatness. (S, A, K.)

DaroHN , (S, A, O, L,) He removed it from its place; put it away or aside; pushed, or thrust, it away: (S, A, * O, L, K:) he took it, and threw it away or aside: (L:) he pushed it, or thrust it, away with his foot: (Expos. of the “ Amálee ” of El- Kálee:) [and] DaraHa biAl$~aYo'i [if not a mistranscription for DrH Al$~aYo'a ] He threw [ from him ] the thing; and put it away or aside: and DaraHa Eanohu Alv~awoba He cast off from him the garment. (A.) See also 4. [And see 8.] [Hence] DaraHotu Ean~iY $ahaAdapa Alqawomi (tropical:) I invalidated the testimony of the people or party, or annulled its claim to credibility, ( jaraHotuhaA ,) and cast it from me, or rejected it: (S, A, O, K: *) said by one against whom false witness has been borne, and who has shown its falseness. (A.) ― -b2- And DaraHati Ald~aAb~apu birijolihaA , (S, O, K,) aor. , (K, * TA,) inf. n. definition: A hawk, (S, A, O, K,) and a vulture, (A,) having long wings;
sourceDefinition: A hawk, (S, A, O, K,) and a vulture, (A,) having long wings; (S, A, O, K;) as also ↓ maDoraHN ; (O, K;) but the former is the more common: a hawk of this description is of an excellent kind: (TA:) and to the wings of the vulture of this sort is likened the extremity of the tail of a she-camel with the coarse hairs that are upon it: (Kf, TA:) or white, applied to a hawk and to a vulture; (A;) or thus, applied to a vulture; and sometimes, so applied, black: (Ham p. 95:) or a vulture intensely red [or brown ]: (AHát, O:) [and a hawk in which is redness; otherwise it is not thus called: (so in the Deewán of Jereer, accord. to Freytag:)] or i. q. A^ajodalN and SaqorN and qaTaAmiY~N : (A'Obeyd, TA:) [it is mentioned in the K again in art. mDrH ; for,] accord. to some, the m is radical: (TA in art. mDrH :) or, applied to a hawk, it means that darts down sideways; or that thrusts the prey. (Ham ubi suprà.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (tropical:) A chief, (S, A, O, K,) such as is generous, or noble, (K,) or of ancient (A, O) and generous (O) origin. (A, O.) ― -b3- Also White as an epithet applied to anything. (K.) ― -b4- And (tropical:) Tall, or long. (K, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , of the measure faEolalN , or, as some say, faEoyalN ; if of the latter, [said to be] the only instance of this measure in the language; DahoyadN being a foreign proper name; (TA;) or, maroyamu being a foreign proper name; (TA;) or, accord. to Sb, the hemzeh in DahoyaA^N , which is with tenween, is augmentative, because it is syn. with DahoyaA='u , which is with the long A and imperfectly decl., for the Y cannot be augmentative and the hemzeh radical in the latter; (MF and TA in art. DhY ;) [a word like DahoyFA and DahoyaA='u (which see in art. DhY ) in most, or a some seem to say in all, of its meanings;] A certain tree, resembling the sayaAl , (AZ, O, K,) each of which has its fruit in a sinofap [or pod ]; it has weak thorns, and grows in the valleys and on the mountains: (AZ, O:) Ed-Deenawaree [i. e. AHn] says, on the authority of some one or more of the Arabs of the desert, of El-Azd, that the DhyA^ is a great tree of the kind called EiDaAh , having a baramap [q. v.] and a pod ( Eul~~afap ) [ which succeeds the baramap ], and many thorns; its pods ( Eul~af ) are intensely red, and its leaves are like those of the [ species of acacia called ] samur . (O.) -A2- Also A woman that does not menstruate: and that has neither milk nor breast: as also ↓ DahoyaA^apN : (K:) or the latter is an epithet applied to a woman in these two senses: (O: [in which the former word, without p , is not mentioned:]) Seer says, in his Expos. of “ the Book ” of Sb, that DahoyaA^N , like DahoyaA='u [which belongs to art. DhY ], is a subst. as well as an epithet, signifying a woman whose breast has not grown forth: and one who has not menstruated: ― -b2- and also (assumed tropical:) A land that has not given growth to anything: (MF, TA:) or ↓ DahoyaA^apN signifies as above: and also (assumed tropical:) a desert ( falaApN ) having in it no water: (O, K, TA:) or that does not give growth to anything; app. because it has no water. (TA.) [Accord. to those who hold the Y to be augmentative,] a woman is thus termed because she resembles men ( liA^an~ahaA DaAhaA^ati Alr~ijaAla ). (O, TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. TaA^oTaA^apN , He lowered, or depressed, a thing. (TA.) You say, TA^TA^ raA^osahu He lowered his head; (S, K, TA;) and so ↓ taTaA^oTaA^a , alone. (TA.) And TA^TA^ Eani Al$~aYo'i He lowered his head from the thing. (TA.) And lahumo taTaA^uTuw^a Ald~ulaApi ↓ taTaA^oTaA^otu , (S, TA,) occurring in a trad. of 'Othmán, (TA,) I stooped, or lowered myself, [or bent myself down, ] to them, like as do the drawers of water with the bucket. (S, TA.) And lahaA tuxoTiy^oka ↓ taTaA^oTaA^o , a prov., (Meyd, TA,) meaning Stoop thy head to it, i. e. to an accident, or a calamity, and it will [ miss thee, or] pass by thee: applied in relation to the abstaining from exposing oneself to evil. (Meyd.) And TaA^oTaA^ato sitorahaA (tropical:) She (a woman) lowered her veil, or curtain. (TA.) And TA^TA^ yadahu biAlEinaAni He lowered his hand with the rein, for the purpose of [ the horse's ] running and hastening. (K, * TA.) And [hence, perhaps,] TA^TA^ farasahu He struck his horse with his thighs, to make him go quickly. (K, * TA.) And TA^TA^ mino fulaAnK (assumed tropical:) He lowered the reputation, or estimation, or dignity, of such a one. (TA.) ― -b2- He hastened, or was quick. (TA.) You say, TA^TA^ fiY maAlihi He hastened, and exceeded the usual bounds, in the expenditure of his property. (A, K, TA.) And TA^TA^ fiY qatolihimo He hastened, and exceeded the usual bounds, in their slaughter. (TA.) ― -b3- And He filled up a hollow, or cavity, dug in the ground. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. TaroTabapN , He (the milker) called the goats, [app. by making a sound with the lips; for,] accord. to AZ, TaroTabapN is with the lips: (S:) he called the goats: (IKtt, TA:) and TaroTaba biAln~aEojapi he called the ewe: (AZ, TA:) [and Freytag says, on the authority of the “ Kitáb el-Addád, ” that TaroTaba signifies also he drove away sheep from himself:] the inf. n. signifies the milker's making a sound to the goats with his lips, (ISd, K, TA,) to quiet them, or appease them: (ISd, TA:) and the calling sheep or goats to be milked, (K, TA,) as some say, with the lips: (TA:) also the calling of asses: (Az, TA:) and, accord. to some, the whistling with the lips to sheep. (TA.) ― -b2- yuTaroTibu $uEayoraAtK lahu , occurring in a trad., means Putting in motion his mustache [lit. some small hairs that he had ] in his speech: or, as some say, blowing with his lips into his mustache by reason of rage and pride. (O.) ― -b3- And TaroTabapN signifies also The agitation, or commotion, of water in the belly (IKtt, K, TA) and in a skin. (IKtt, TA.) ― -b4- And The act of fleeing. (IKtt, TA.)

definition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor.
sourceDefinition: , (S, O, Msb, K,) aor. [notwithstanding the faucial letter], (Msb, JM, TA,) inf. n. TuluwEN and maTolaEN and maToliEN , (S, O, Msb, K,) the second and third both used as inf. ns., and also as ns. of place [and of time], (S, O, K,) but the former of them is preferable on the ground of analogy as an inf. n., and the latter as a n. of place (Fr, O) or of time, (Zj, O,) The sun rose, (MA,) or appeared; (K;) and in like manner TalaEa is said of the moon, (TA,) and of a star, or an asterism; (S, O, K;) and so ↓ AiT~alaEa ; (K;) [and ↓ A^aTolaEa , for] A^aTolaEati Alv~uray~aA means TalaEat [i. e. The Pleiades rose ], as in a verse of El-Kumeyt [in which, however, the verb may, consistently with the metre, be a mistranscription for AT~alaEat ]; (IB, TA); and A^aTolaEa is syn. with TalaEa in the saying of Ru-beh, kaA^an~ahu kawokabu gayomK A^aTolaEaA [ As though it, or he, were a star in the midst of clouds, that had risen ]. (TA.) One says also, A=tiyka kul~a yawomK TalaEatohu Al$~amosu , meaning TalaEato fiyhi [i. e. I will come to thee every day in which the sun rises ]: and it is said in a prayer, TalaEati Al$~amosu walaA taToluEu binafosi A^aHadK min~aA [meaning The sun has risen, and may it not have risen with the soul of any one of us ]; i. e., may not any one of us have died with its rising: the future being put in the place of the preterite. (TA.) ― -b2- And TalaEa is said of anything that appears to one from the upper part [of a thing, or that comes up out of a thing and appears]. (Mgh, Msb.) It is said in the Ksh that AlT~uluwEu signifies The appearing by rising, or by becoming elevated. (TA.) One says, TalaEato sin~u AlS~abiY~i (tropical:) The tooth of the child showed its point. (K, TA.) And TalaEa Alz~aroEu , [aor. ,] inf. n. TuluwEN , (tropical:) The seed-produce began to come up, and showed its sprouting forth: (T, TA:) and Alz~aroEu ↓ A^aTolaEa (tropical:) The seed-produce appeared: (TA:) and nabotu AlA^aroDi ↓ A^aTolaEa (assumed tropical:) The plants, or herbage, of the earth, or land, came forth: (Mgh:) and Al$~ajaru ↓ A^aTolaEa (tropical:) The trees put forth their leaves. (TA.) And TalaEa Aln~axolu , (O, K,) aor. , inf. n. TuluwEN ; (TA;) and (O, K) ↓ A^aTolaEa ; (Zj, S, Mgh, O, K;) or A^aTolaEati Aln~axolapu ; (Msb;) (assumed tropical:) The palm-trees, or -tree, put forth the TaloE [q. v.]; (Zj, S, Mgh, O, Msb, K;) as also ↓ Tl~E , (L, K, TA,) inf. n. taToliyEN . (L, TA. [These verbs, in this sense, are app. derived from the subst. TaloEN ; but this is obviously from TalaEa .]) ― -b3- One says also, malaA^otu lahu AlqadaHa Hat~aY yakaAda yaToluEu mino nawaAHiyhi [ I filled for him the drinking-vessel until it nearly overflowed from its sides ]. (TA.) And AlmaA='u fiY AlA_inaA='i ↓ taTal~aEa (assumed tropical:) The water in the vessel poured forth [or overflowed ] from its sides. (TA.) ― -b4- And TalaEa Aljabala , (Mgh, Msb, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. TuluwEN , (Msb, TA,) (tropical:) He ascended upon the mountain; (Mgh, Msb, K, TA;) the prep. [ EalaY ] being suppressed; (Mgh;) as also TaliEa , with kesr; (K;) and Aljabala ↓ AiT~alaEa signifies the same as TalaEahu : (TA: [see also muDoTaliEN , in art. DlE :]) accord. to ISk, one says, TaliEotu Aljabala , with kesr, meaning (assumed tropical:) I ascended upon the mountain; (S, O;) but others say, TalaEotu , with fet-h. (O.) And (tropical:) He ascended the mountain: (TA:) [or] TalaEotu fiY Aljabali means (assumed tropical:) I ascended the mountain. (Msb. [See also another explanation of this latter phrase in what follows.]) ― -b5- And TalaEa EalayonaA , aor. and ; and ↓ AiT~alaEa ; (assumed tropical:) He (a man) came to us; (K;) and came upon us suddenly, or at unawares: (TA:) and TalaEa Eanohumo he became absent, or absented himself, or departed, from them: (K:) or TalaEa EalaY Alqawomi he came forth upon the people, or party: and he looked upon them: (MA:) accord. to ISk, TalaEotu EalaY Alqawomi means I came to the people, or party: and TalaEotu Eanohumo I became absent, or absented myself, or departed, from them: (S, O:) and Ealayohimo ↓ A^aTolaEotu signifies the same as TalaEotu : (O:) and TalaEotu Eanohumo has the same meaning [also] as TalaEotu Eanohumo expl. above, accord. to ISk; EalaY being put in the place of En : accord. to AZ [likewise], TalaEotu EalaY Alqawomi , inf. n. TuluwEN , means I became absent from the people, or party, so that they did not see me: and also I advanced, or approached, towards them, so that they saw me: thus having two contr. meanings: and accord. to Az, the Arabs said, TalaEotu fiY Aljabali , inf. n. TuluwEN , as meaning I retired, or went back, into the mountain, so that my companion did not see me: [see another explanation of this phrase in what precedes:] and TalaEotu Eano SaAHibiY , inf. n. TuluwEN , I retired, or went back, from my companion: and TalaEotu Eano SaAHibiY [in which Eano seems to be evidently a mistranscription for EalaY ] I advanced, or approached, towards my companion. (TA.) [In all of these phrases, TalaEa and TalaEotu may be correctly rendered He, and I, came forth, or went forth. And hence,] it is said in a prov., h`*ihi yamiynN qado TalaEato fiY AlmaxaArimi [expl. in art. xrm , voce maxorimN ]. (AZ, TA.) ― -b6- For another meaning of TalaEa followed by EalaY , see AiT~alaEa [which is more common as having that meaning]. ― -b7- TalaEa is also syn. with qaSada : so in the phrase TalaEa bilaAdahu (tropical:) [ He tended, repaired, betook himself, or went, to, or towards, his country ]: (K, TA:) and so in the saying, in a trad., h`*aA busorN qado TalaEa Alyamana , (so in the O,) or h*A bur~N , (so in the TA,) (tropical:) [ These are ripening dates, or this is wheat, that have, or has, gone to, or towards, El-Yemen, ] meaning from Nejd. (TA.) ― -b8- And syn. with balaga ; as also ↓ AiT~alaEa : (O, K:) so the former in the saying, TalaEa A^aroDahumo (tropical:) [ He reached, or arrived at, their land ]; (K, TA;) and mataY TalaEota A^aroDanaA (tropical:) [ When didst thou reach, or arrive at, our land? ]: (O, TA:) and so the latter verb in the saying, h`*ihi AlA^aroDa ↓ AT~lE [ He reached, or arrived at, this land ]: (O, K:) and hence, (TA,) EalaY AlA^afoy^idapi ↓ A@l~atiY taT~aliEu , in the Kur [civ. 7], means (assumed tropical:) Whereof the pain shall reach the hearts: (Fr, O, TA:) or which shall rise above the hearts, (O, TA,) [or overwhelm them, ] and burn them. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: i. q. Taraqatohu [i. e. (assumed tropical:) She, or it, or they (referring to irrational things), came to him in the night ]: Aboo-'Alee cites [as an ex.], taTaAlaEuniY xayaAlaAtN lisalomaY kamaA yataTaAlaEu Ald~ayona Algariymu [ Apparitions of Selmà come to me in the night, like as the creditor comes in the night to exact the debt ]: but accord. to another, or others, it is only ↓ yataTal~aEu , because tafaAEala is generally intrans.: so that accord. to Aboo-'Alee, it is like tafaAwaDonaA AlHadiyva and taEaATayonaA AlkaA^osa and tanaA$adonaA AlA^a$oEaAra . (IB, TA.)

sourceDefinition: : see 1, first sentence: ― -b2- and near the middle of the paragraph, in two places: ― -b3- and last sentence, in three places. ― -b4- Also (assumed tropical:) i. q. A^a$orafa [meaning as expl. in the next sentence]; as also ↓ A^aTalaEa , of the class of A^akorama . (Mgh.) One says, AiT~alaEotu mino fawoqi Aljabali and ↓ A^aTolaEotu (assumed tropical:) [ I looked, or looked down, from above the mountain ]. (TA.) And AiT~alaEotu Alfajora (tropical:) I looked at the dawn when it rose. (O, TA. *) And AiT~alaEotu Ealayohi (tropical:) I looked down, or from above, upon him, or it; syn. A^a$orafotu . (TA.) [Hence,] halo A^anotumo muT~aliEuwna faA@T~alaEa , in the Kur [xxxvii. 52 and 53], means (assumed tropical:) Would ye [ be of those who ] look to see ( tuHib~uwna A^ano taT~aliEuwA ) where is your place of abode among the people of Hell? and he (i. e. the Muslim) shall look ( faA@T~alaEa Almusolimu ) and see his [former] associate in the midst of Hell-fire: but some read ↓ hl Antm muToliEuwna faA^aToliEa [in the CK fAT~alaEa , but it is expressly said in the O that the hemzeh is with damm and the T quiescent and the l with kesr; the meaning being (assumed tropical:) Are ye of those who will make me to see? and he shall be made to see; as is indicated in the O and TA]. (K, O.) ― -b5- And (assumed tropical:) He saw. (KL.) You say, AT~lE Ealayohi meaning (assumed tropical:) He saw it. (MA.) [Hence,] it is said in a prov., baEoda A@T~ilaAEK A_iynaAsN (O, TA) i. e. (assumed tropical:) After appearance [or rather sight, is knowledge, or certain knowledge ]. (Fr, TA in art. Ans . [See Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 181.]) ― -b6- And AT~lE Ealayohi , (Msb, TA,) and AT~lEhu , and ↓ tTl~Ehu , and Elyh ↓ TalaEa , inf. n. TuluwEN , (K, TA,) and ↓ A^aTolaEa Elyh , (TA,) (tropical:) He got, or obtained, sight and knowledge of it: (Msb, TA: *) or [simply] he knew it; namely, an affair, or a case, or an event. (K, TA.) One says, AT~lE EalaY baATinihi , (K,) or AD~lE EalaY baATini A^amorihi , (S, O,) (tropical:) He became acquainted with, or obtained knowledge of, or knew, his inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances, or the inward, or intrinsic, state or circumstances of his affair or case. (K, * TA.) And-accord. to some, AiT~ilaAEu AlHijaAbi means (assumed tropical:) The stretching out the head [ and looking over the veil of Paradise or of Hell]; for he who examines into a thing stretches out his head to see what is behind the veil, or covering. (TA voce HijaAbN , q. v.) [And one says also, AT~lE fiyhi , meaning (assumed tropical:) He looked into it: see an ex. voce hadara .] ― -b7- AiT~alaEatohu EayoniY means (tropical:) My eye regarded him with contempt. (TA.) -A2- [ AiT~alaEa is used sometimes for AiDoTalaEa , as is shown in art. DlE : see muDoTaliEN : and see an instance in the first paragraph of art. Elw .] -A3- And accord. to Kr, AiliA T~laAEu signifies also Aln~ajaApu . (TA. [But I think that both words are mistranscribed, and that Kr explained AlA_iTolaAEu as meaning Aln~ijaA='u , i. e. The acquainting with a secret. ])

sourceDefinition: signifies Talaba TuluwEahu (assumed tropical:) [ He sought, or desired, its, or his, coming forth, or appearance ]. (Har p. 47.) [And hence, (assumed tropical:) He sought, or desired, to elicit, or to discover, it: he sought, or desired, information respecting it, minohu of him: and he asked him to tell him a thing. (TA.)

definition: (assumed tropical:) The TaloE [i.
sourceDefinition: (assumed tropical:) The TaloE [i. e. spadix, or spadix in its spathe, and sometimes, the spathe alone,] of the palm-tree: (S, O:) the A_igoriyD [or spadix ] of the palm-tree, from over which the kaAfuwr [or spathe ] bursts open longitudinally; or the flowers of the palm-tree, while in the kAfwr ; (TA;) a thing that comes forth from the palm-tree, as though it were two soles, or sandals, closed together, with the Himol [meaning flowers ] compactly disposed between them, and having the extremity pointed; or the vamarap [or produce ] of the palm-tree, in the first stage of its appearance, the covering [or spathe ] of which is called the kufur~aY (K, TA) and the kaAfuwr , (TA,) and what is within this the A_igoriyD , because of its whiteness; (K, TA;) or the TaloE is what comes forth from the palm-tree and becomes dates if the tree is female; and if the tree is male it does not become dates, but is eaten in its fresh state, or is left upon the palm-tree a certain number of days until there becomes produced in it a white substance like flour, [i. e. the pollen, ] having a strong odour, and with this the female is fecundated; definition: and Tal~aAEu AlA^anojudi (tropical:) [lit.
sourceDefinition: and Tal~aAEu AlA^anojudi (tropical:) [lit. A man wont to ascend mountain-roads; meaning] a man experienced in affairs; wont to surmount them by his knowledge and his experience and his good judgment: or who aspires to lofty things, or the means of attaining eminence: (O, K, TA: [see also vaniy~apN :]) A^anojudN being pl. of najodN ; which means “ a road in a mountain, ” like vaniy~apN [of which vanaAyaA is the pl.]. (TA.) An ex. of the former phrase is presented by a verse of Soheym Ibn-Wetheel cited in art. jlw : and an ex. of the latter by the saying of Mohammad Ibn-AbeeShihádh Ed-Dabbee, said by ISk to be of Ráshid Ibn-Dirwás, waqado yaqoSuru Alqul~u AlfataY duwna ham~ihi waqado kaAna lawolaA Alqul~u Tal~aAEa A^anojudi [ Certainly, or sometimes, or often, poverty withholds the young man from attaining his purpose; and certainly, or sometimes, or often, but for poverty, he would be a surmounter of affairs by his knowledge &c.]. (O, TA.) -A2- qadaHN Tal~aAEN (tropical:) A full drinking-vessel. (TA.) And EayonN Tal~aAEN [or Tal~aAEapN ?] (tropical:) An eye filled with tears. (TA.)

definition: (assumed tropical:) [ A place to which one ascends: or] a place of ascent from a low spot to a place that overlooks.
sourceDefinition: (assumed tropical:) [ A place to which one ascends: or] a place of ascent from a low spot to a place that overlooks. (As, TA.) Hence, (TA,) it is said in a trad. (O, K) of the Prophet, (O,) maAnazala mina AlquroA=ni A=yapN A_il~aA lahaA ZahorN wabaTonN walikul~i HarofK Had~N walikul~i Had~K muT~alaEN i. e. (O, K) (assumed tropical:) Not a verse of the Kur-án has come down but it has an apparent and known [or exoteric ] interpretation and an intrinsic [or esoteric ] interpretation, (TA voce ZahorN , where see more,) [ and every word has a scope, and every scope has ] a place [meaning point ] to which the knowledge thereof may ascend, (O, K, TA,) or, as some say, something that may be violated, God not having forbidden a thing that should be held sacred without his knowing that some one would seek to elicit it. (TA.) ― -b2- And i. q. maA^otFY ; (S, O, K, TA;) muT~alaEu AlA^amori meaning maA^otaAhu ; (S, O, TA;) as also AlA^amori ↓ maTolaEu ; (TA;) i. e. (assumed tropical:) The way, or manner, of attaining to the doing, or performing, of the affair. (TA.) One says, maAlih`*aA AlA^amori muT~alaEN (assumed tropical:) There is no way, or manner, of attaining to the doing, or performing, of this affair. (TA.) And A^ayona muT~alaEu h`*aA AlA^amori i. e. maA^otaAhu (assumed tropical:) [ Where is the way of attaining to the doing, or performing, of this affair? ]. (S, O, TA.) ― -b3- And (tropical:) An elevated place from which one looks towards a low place. (S, O, Msb, K, TA.) To this is likened the scene of the events of the world to come, (S, O, Msb, K, TA,) after death, i. e. the station of the day of resurrection, (TA,) in the saying of 'Omar, lawo A^an~a maA fiY AlA^aroDi jamiyEFA laA^afotadayotu bihi mino hawoli AlmuT~alaEi (tropical:) [ If all that is in the world belonged to me, assuredly I would ransom myself therewith from the terror of the place whence one will look down on the day of resurrection]: (S, * O, Msb, * K, * TA:) or AlmuT~alaE means that which is looked upon of such hardships as the interrogation of [the angels] Munkar and Nekeer, and the pressure of the grave, and its solitude, and the like; and is [for AlmuT~alaEi Ealayohi , or] originally an inf. n. in the sense of AlAiT~ilaAE : or it may be a noun of time, and thus applied to the day of resurrection. (Har p. 344-5.)
